docs.title: Ethereum from Scratch
docs.text:
Ethereum is usually explained badly. Most introductions either hand you a metaphor that falls apart the moment you look closely ("it's a world computer!") or drop you straight into Solidity code without saying what the machine underneath is actually doing.

This site tries something different, with two rules.

Nothing is explained before its prerequisites. Start at What is Ethereum?, work down, and each page assumes you've read the ones above it and nothing more. The site is in seven parts for that reason — the order is the argument. The concept map draws the dependencies that order comes from.

Everything here is permanent. Ethereum upgrades through hard forks, and plenty of tutorials that were accurate when written are now quietly wrong. So this site begins with the part of Ethereum that has not changed since 2015 — and realistically cannot, because altering any of it would break every wallet, library and deployed contract at once.

That makes for a narrower site than it could be. It's also the part worth learning first.

docs.title: How to read a page
docs.text:
The main text of every page is written to be read start to finish with no prior knowledge, and it stands on its own.

Every page opens by saying whether it can go out of date. Ethereum is upgraded every so often, and some of what's true today won't be in five years. So each page says up front whether what follows is permanent or has parts that move — and that label links to the full explanation of how this site handles it. Where a page says permanent, you can trust it without checking the date on anything.

Some pages also carry collapsible boxes, closed by default, in two kinds:

  • The formal version — the precise, specification-level statement of what the page just explained in plain language. Exact notation, exact field widths, edge cases.
  • History — how something used to work, and why it changed. Often the clearest explanation of why the current design is the way it is.

If you're new to Ethereum, you can leave every one of them closed and lose nothing. They aren't continuations of the main text, and they're not material you're expected to get through — they're there for readers who want the exact definition or the reasoning behind a decision. Open them when a page leaves you wanting more precision, and ignore them otherwise.

docs.title: If a word is unfamiliar
docs.text:
Technical terms are linked the first time each page uses one, and every link does two things:

  • Hover it and a short definition appears, without leaving the page. Usually that's enough to carry on reading.
  • Click it and you go to the full entry — either the page that explains the term properly, or the glossary.

So you need never lose your place to look something up, and you can go deeper when a one-line reminder isn't enough.

The glossary also stands alone: it defines every term used anywhere on the site.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
Seven parts, in order. Each assumes the ones before it and nothing else.

Each part is named for the question it answers, and in order they make a sentence:

what it is → who can act → where it runs → what it holds → how it changes → when it's settled → why anyone bothers

That's the whole site in a line. The topic names under each card are what the material is called elsewhere, in case you're looking for something specific.

  • Part 1 · What it is

    What Ethereum actually is, the units it counts in, and the two tools every later page leans on — how bytes are written, and how they're fingerprinted.

    What is Ethereum? · Ether, wei and gwei · Hex and bytes · Keccak-256

  • Part 2 · Who can act

    How control is proved: a secret number, the one-way chain that turns it into an address, and what holding the only copy means.

    Cryptography — Private keys · Public keys · Addresses · Signatures

    Wallets — Seed phrases · What losing your keys means

  • Part 3 · Where it runs

    The machines that hold all this and check every block for themselves — what they are, what software they run, and what it takes to be one.

    What a node is · Clients and the two layers · Running one yourself

  • Part 4 · What it holds

    Everything every node stores, how much of it everyone else can see, and how one 32-byte number commits to all of it.

    Accounts and state — Accounts · The nonce · State · Why accounts, and what they cost · What it reveals

    Contracts — What a smart contract is · What the code actually is · Events and logs · Tokens aren't special

    How it's written — RLP encoding · The Merkle Patricia Trie

  • Part 5 · How it changes

    The only way anything ever happens: what's inside a transaction, why the work has to be metered, and what it costs.

    Transactions · Why metering is necessary · Gas · Fees · Gas costs

  • Part 6 · When it's settled

    How changes get batched and chained, who gets to propose one and why anybody must, and what "confirmed" is actually worth.

    Blocks · The block header · Why somebody has to be chosen · Proof of stake · The chain and reorgs

  • Part 7 · Why anyone bothers

    What keeping this running costs, who ends up paying, what capping a supply buys — and who gets to decide any of it when nobody is in charge.

    Why security has to be paid for · Who pays · Fixed cap or flexible supply · Who decides, when nobody is in charge

Then two things that sit outside the reading path: a glossary defining every term used anywhere on the site, and about — how upgrades are handled, what each one did, and who's writing this.

docs.title: Reading paths
docs.text:
Straight through, part by part, is the order the site is built for. But depending on why you're here, some of it can wait.

New to Ethereum — read in order. Start at What is Ethereum? and work down. Nothing assumes anything you haven't already read.

Here for the economics. The monetary and incentive questions need surprisingly little machinery — just what Ethereum is and what the units are:

What is Ethereum? → Ether, wei and gwei → Why security has to be paid for → Who pays → Fixed cap or flexible supply

Parts 2 to 6 can wait, and picking them up later costs nothing.

Here for the technical detail. Parts 1 to 4, in order. That's nearly everything on the site that has not changed since 2015 — so it's worth learning properly once rather than twice.

Looking for one specific thing. Use the search box, or the glossary for a quick definition with a link to the page that explains it.

Why there's no choice to make up front

Some sites ask you to pick a track before you begin. This one doesn't, because the economics genuinely depends on the technical material — you can't weigh what security costs without knowing what it buys — so the paths overlap rather than diverge. There's one set of pages, and these are just suggested routes through them.

docs.title: What's missing, and why
docs.text:
Gas costs, the fee market, transaction types, the EVM, Proof of Stake and rollups aren't here yet. They're all important, and they're all coming.

They're also the parts that change at hard forks — so they need a different treatment: numbers kept in one place, pages stamped with the upgrade they were written against, and changes taught as history rather than patched over.

How this site handles forks explains the approach in full.

docs.title: Who's writing this
docs.text:
I'm Davide Stocco, and I'm learning Ethereum — this site is how I'm doing it. My reasoning is that you don't really understand something until you can explain it in an order that makes sense to someone who knows nothing, so instead of taking notes I'm writing the explanation I wanted when I started.

The obvious caveat follows: this is written by a learner, not an expert. Pages marked stub are outlines I haven't filled in yet, and if you find a mistake I'd genuinely rather know — corrections are the most useful thing you can send me.

More about me → My website →

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Definitions here are deliberately one or two sentences — just enough to unstick you. Each links to the page that explains the thing properly.

If you arrived from a search engine and a word on some page made no sense, this is where to look.

Scope

This covers every term used on the published pages. It grows as the site does — so if something is missing, it's because no page uses it yet. Terms without a link don't have their own page yet.

docs.title: A
docs.text: ABI (Application Binary Interface) The convention for encoding calls to a contract — which function, and what arguments. Not a protocol rule, just an agreement everyone follows. Account An entry in Ethereum's state, identified by a 20-byte address. Has four fields: nonce, balance, storage root, code hash. Comes in two kinds — EOA and contract. → Accounts Address The 20-byte identifier of an account, written as 40 hex characters. For an EOA it's the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of the public key. → Addresses

docs.title: B
docs.text: Balance How much ether an account holds, counted in wei. Beacon Chain The Proof of Stake chain that ran separately from December 2020, holding no accounts or transactions. The Merge connected Ethereum's execution layer to it. → What is Ethereum? Beige Paper Micah Dameron's rewrite of the Yellow Paper in ordinary prose, covering the same material without the formal notation. Useful for reading; not cited on this site, because it is one person's restatement of the specification rather than the specification, and the project's repository describes it as a beta with errata. If the Yellow Paper is impenetrable, start here and check anything load-bearing against Wood. https://cryptopapers.info/assets/pdf/eth_beige.pdf Block A batch of transactions, added to the chain as a single unit. State is recorded once per block, not per transaction. Byte Eight bits. The unit everything in Ethereum is measured in — addresses are 20 bytes, hashes are 32. → Hex and bytes

docs.title: C
docs.text: Canonical Agreed on and permanently recorded by the network, as opposed to merely having existed. Intermediate states inside a block are real but not canonical. Chain id A number identifying which network a transaction is for — 1 for Ethereum's main network, different values for testnets and other chains. Included in what gets signed, so a signature is valid on one chain only. → Signatures Consensus layer The half of Ethereum that decides the order of transactions, using Proof of Stake. → What is Ethereum? Contract account An account with code attached. It cannot start a transaction — it only runs when something calls it. → Accounts

docs.title: D
docs.text: Determinism The property that the same state plus the same transaction always produces the same result, for everyone. This is what makes independent verification possible, and therefore what makes trust unnecessary. → What is Ethereum?

docs.title: E
docs.text: EIP (Ethereum Improvement Proposal) A numbered, published proposal for changing Ethereum. The authoritative description of any protocol rule. https://eips.ethereum.org EOA (Externally Owned Account) An account controlled by a private key rather than by code — what people mean by a wallet. The only kind that can start a transaction. → Accounts ether Ethereum's native currency. Counted internally in wei, never in decimals. Event What a log is called in the language a contract is written in. An event in source code compiles into a log on the chain — the same relationship as a function and its four-byte selector. The two words get used interchangeably; the log is the protocol-level thing. → Events and logs EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) The machine that executes contract code — a stack machine working on 256-bit words. Every node runs it identically. Execution layer The half of Ethereum that holds the accounts and runs the code. The state machine proper. → What is Ethereum?

docs.title: G
docs.text: Gas The unit measuring computational work. Not money — gas is the amount of work, and the fee is what that work costs. Exists so that computation is paid for and so no contract can run forever. Genesis The very first block, and the starting state it defined — Ethereum's launch in July 2015. "Since genesis" is the usual way of saying "for the whole life of the network"; this site generally says the plainer thing instead. gwei 10<sup>9</sup> wei. The unit fees are normally quoted in. → Ether, wei and gwei

docs.title: H
docs.text: Hard fork A coordinated rule change that every node adopts at an agreed point. Ethereum has had roughly twenty. → Ethereum changes Hexadecimal (hex) Base 16, written with 0–9 and a–f. Used everywhere because one byte is exactly two hex characters. The 0x prefix just means "hex follows". → Hex and bytes

docs.title: K
docs.text: Keccak-256 Ethereum's hash function. Takes any input, returns 32 bytes. Nearly the same as SHA-3 but not identical — the padding differs, so the two give different results. → Keccak-256

docs.title: L
docs.text: Log A record a contract writes for the outside world, attached to a transaction's result rather than to the state. The one thing a contract can write and never read — not its own, not any other's — which is why logs are cheap: no node needs them in order to execute anything. Called an event in source code. → Events and logs

docs.title: N
docs.text: Nibble Four bits — half a byte, and exactly one hexadecimal digit. The unit the Merkle Patricia Trie reads keys in, which is why its branches have sixteen directions and a 32-byte key is 64 nibbles long. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) The United States government agency that publishes technical standards, cryptography among them, as documents called FIPS. It ran the competition that chose Keccak as SHA-3 — and then altered the padding before publication, which is why Ethereum's Keccak-256 and the SHA3-256 standard are different functions. → Keccak-256 Node A computer running Ethereum's rules: it keeps a copy of the state, receives blocks, applies them itself, and rejects any that break the rules. It holds no keys, signs nothing and earns nothing — a validator does those things. → What a node is Nonce A per-account counter of transactions already sent. Prevents the same signed transaction being replayed, and forces strict ordering. → The nonce

docs.title: O
docs.text: Oracle A service that reports off-chain facts to a contract. Necessary because contracts can't see outside the chain — and a point of trust whenever you need one. → What is Ethereum?

docs.title: P
docs.text: Private key A 256-bit number. Whoever knows it can produce valid signatures for the matching address, which is what "owning" ether actually means. → Private keys Proof of Stake The mechanism Ethereum uses to agree transaction order, where validators stake ether rather than spending electricity. Replaced mining at The Merge in September 2022. Public key A point on the secp256k1 curve, derived from a private key by one-way multiplication. An address is derived from it in turn. → Public keys

docs.title: R
docs.text: Receipt The record of what a transaction did — gas used, logs emitted, success or failure. Committed per transaction, unlike state. RLP (Recursive Length Prefix) Ethereum's encoding for turning structured data into bytes. Canonical by design: one piece of data has exactly one valid encoding. → RLP encoding

docs.title: S
docs.text: Script Bitcoin's scripting language. Deliberately stateless and limited, which is the real contrast with Ethereum's contracts — not that Bitcoin lacks code. → What is Ethereum? secp256k1 The elliptic curve Ethereum uses for signatures — the same one Bitcoin uses. → Public keys Smart contract A program stored at an account, run by the network when called. Stateful and general-purpose, but metered and capped. → What is Ethereum? Solidity The language most Ethereum contracts are written in. It is not part of Ethereum — the protocol has no notion of any language, and Solidity's output is bytecode like any other compiler's. A convention among people, in the same position as the ABI. → What the code actually is State Everything Ethereum stores right now: every account and what it holds. → What is Ethereum? State machine A system with some state plus rules for changing it. Ethereum's own formal specification describes it this way. → What is Ethereum? State root A single 32-byte fingerprint committing to the entire state, carried in each block header. Any change to any account changes it.

docs.title: T
docs.text: The Merge The September 2022 upgrade that connected Ethereum's execution layer to the Beacon Chain, retiring mining. Called a merge because two existing systems were joined. → What is Ethereum? Transaction A signed instruction from an EOA that changes the state. The only way anything on Ethereum ever changes. Turing-complete Able to express any computation, loops included. Ethereum's contracts are; Bitcoin's Script deliberately isn't. On Ethereum the limit is gas, not expressiveness. → What is Ethereum?

docs.title: U
docs.text: UTXO (Unspent Transaction Output) Bitcoin's model, where individual coins are the state and each can be spent once. Ethereum uses accounts instead — which is why it needs a nonce. → Accounts

docs.title: W
docs.text: wei The smallest unit of ether. 10<sup>18</sup> wei = 1 ether. All amounts are integers in wei; Ethereum never uses decimals. → Ether, wei and gwei White Paper Ethereum's original proposal, by Vitalik Buterin in 2014 — what the system was for and why it was designed this way, including the case for accounts over Bitcoin's coins. The Yellow Paper says what the rules are; the white paper says why. This site cites it for design arguments and Wood for mechanisms. https://ethereum.org/en/whitepaper/

docs.title: Y
docs.text: Yellow Paper Ethereum's formal specification, by Gavin Wood. The authority on how the execution layer behaves, and the source most often cited here. Dense formal notation — see the Beige Paper for the same material in prose, and the White Paper for why any of it was designed this way. https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf

docs.title: Who's writing this
docs.text:
I'm Davide Stocco. I'm learning Ethereum, and this site is how I'm doing it.

The approach is deliberate: I don't think you understand something until you can explain it in an order that makes sense to someone who knows nothing. So rather than take notes, I'm writing the explanation I wanted when I started — and when a page is hard to write, that's usually a sign I haven't understood the thing yet.

Which means this site has an obvious caveat: it's written by a learner, not an expert. I've tried to be careful, to work from primary sources, and to say plainly when something is beyond what I can explain yet. But if you find a mistake, I'd genuinely rather know. Corrections are the most useful thing you can send me.

More about me: https://sites.google.com/view/davidestocco/

docs.title: How this site is written
docs.text:
A large part of the prose on this site was drafted with an AI assistant (Claude), and you should know that before deciding how much to trust it.

What that looks like in practice: I decide what each page needs to cover and in what order, I question explanations that don't convince me, and I check claims against primary sources. The assistant drafts, suggests structure, and catches gaps — and I've had it argue me out of several things I had wrong, as well as putting things in that I then had to correct.

I'm saying so for three reasons. It's honest, and a page that admits to being written by a learner shouldn't be coy about its tools. It's relevant — AI-drafted technical writing has a known failure mode of sounding authoritative while being subtly wrong, which is precisely why every factual claim here is tied to a reference you can check yourself. And it's standard practice in the research world I come from, where disclosing your tools isn't an apology, it's method.

The references are the safeguard. If a claim on this site isn't cited, treat it as something I believe rather than something I've verified.

docs.title: The site
docs.text:
Built with MkDocs and Material. The source is on GitHub.

Two rules shape it: nothing is explained before its prerequisites, and the published material is restricted to the parts of Ethereum that have never changed — see how this site handles forks for why that matters.

docs.title: Ethereum changes — how this site handles it
docs.text:
Ethereum is not finished, and it was never meant to be. It upgrades through hard forks: coordinated rule changes that every node on the network adopts at an agreed point. There have been roughly twenty since 2015, and more are planned.

Some were substantial. In September 2022, an upgrade called The Merge replaced Ethereum's entire consensus mechanism — the way the network agrees on the order of transactions — swapping mining for staking. In 2021, EIP-1559 rebuilt how transaction fees are calculated. In 2024, blobs were introduced and made transactions on Layer 2 networks dramatically cheaper.

This creates an obvious problem for a site like this one. Plenty of Ethereum tutorials were accurate when written and are now quietly, confidently wrong. A reader has no way of telling which parts have gone stale.

So this site is built around a deliberate choice.

docs.title: Not everything changes
docs.text:
Hard forks sound like they churn everything, but they don't. The churn is concentrated, and a large part of how Ethereum works has not moved since the network launched in 2015:

  • An address has always been the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of a public key.
  • A private key has always been a 256-bit number on the secp256k1 curve.
  • There have always been exactly 1018 wei in one ether.
  • RLP, the encoding Ethereum uses to serialise data, has never been revised.
  • The nonce has always been a simple per-account counter.
  • Every account has always had the same four fields.

None of these can realistically change. Altering any one would break every wallet, library, block explorer and deployed contract simultaneously. They are, for practical purposes, permanent.

docs.title: What this site covers right now
docs.text:
Only that permanent core.

Everything currently published here has been true since 2015 and will almost certainly be true in twenty years. Nothing on this site depends on which fork is live as you read it.

That's a narrower site than it could be. It leaves out gas costs, the fee market, transaction types, Proof of Stake, and rollups — all genuinely important, and all things I intend to cover.

But it's the right place to start, for two reasons. The permanent material is foundational: you cannot understand why a storage write is expensive without first understanding what storage is, and you cannot follow a transaction's signature without knowing what a private key is. And it's honest — I'd rather publish a small site that stays correct than a large one that rots.

docs.title: How the rest will be added
docs.text:
When the fork-dependent sections arrive, they'll follow three rules.

Numbers live in one place. No page will ever hardcode a gas cost. Pages explain why an operation is expensive; a single reference table says how much. When a fork reprices something, one file changes.

Volatile pages say so. Any page whose details depend on the current fork will carry a visible note naming the upgrade it was written against, so you can judge for yourself whether it's current.

Changes are taught as history, not patched over. This is the useful part. EIP-1559 is confusing on its own, but obvious once you know what came before: fee bidding used to be a blind auction where you guessed what everyone else would pay, and usually overpaid or got stuck. The old design explains the new one.

So forks won't be errata buried in a changelog. Where something changed, you'll get the version before, the problem with it, and the version after — because that sequence is genuinely the clearest way to understand the thing as it stands today.

docs.title: If you find something wrong
docs.text:
Please tell me. This site is written in public, by someone learning the material, and corrections are the most useful thing you can offer. Open an issue on the repository.

For anything fork-dependent, the authoritative sources are always:

  • https://eips.ethereum.org — the EIPs themselves
  • https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs — the executable specification
  • https://ethereum.org/en/history/ — the upgrade timeline

docs.title: Accounts
docs.text:
Permanent, except one part. The four fields have been the same since Ethereum launched in 2015. The clean split between the two kinds of account is the part that has started to soften.

Current as of Fusaka (December 2025)

The four fields and the "only an EOA can start a transaction" rule are unchanged since 2015. EIP-7702 weakened the distinction between the two kinds when it shipped in May 2025 — explained in its own box below. Nothing in Fusaka touched accounts.

EIP stands for Ethereum Improvement Proposal: the numbered documents in which every change to Ethereum is proposed, argued over and finally specified. They're the primary sources this site cites, and EIP-7702 is simply the 7702nd.

If you're reading much later, check how this site handles forks.

Account

An entry in Ethereum's state, looked up by a 20-byte address, holding exactly four fields: a nonce, a balance, a storage root and a code hash.

Two kinds exist. An EOA is controlled by whoever holds the matching private key. A contract account is controlled by its own code.

The address is how you find the account, not something the account stores.

Two words in that box need settling before anything else, because both are doing heavy lifting.

The state is the complete record of every account — the thing the state machine page described as "the current situation", as opposed to the history that produced it. Every node keeps a copy. This page only needs that much; its own page comes two pages from here.

EOA stands for externally owned account, and the name is badly chosen, because it suggests the account is somehow outside Ethereum. It isn't. An EOA is on the chain exactly as much as any other account — an entry in the state, with the same four fields, stored by every node.

What's external is only the thing that controls it: a private key, sitting on somebody's device, which the network has never seen and knows nothing about. The account is on-chain; its owner is off-chain.

A contract account is the other way round. What controls it is code, and that code is stored on the chain in plain view, where every node can read it.

So the two kinds differ in where the controller lives, not where the account lives. Both accounts live in the state, and neither could do anything otherwise.

OFF THE CHAIN · your device onlyprivate keyauthorisesON THE CHAIN · every node stores both of theseEOAcodeHash = emptyso: no code of its owncontrolled fromoutside, by that keyCONTRACT ACCOUNTits own codeanyone can read itcontrolled from inside

Worth walking through, because the whole point is in the geometry.

The dashed border is the chain — everything inside it is stored by every node on the network. Both account panels are inside, which is the thing to take away: an EOA is no less on-chain than a contract.

Only the key is outside. It sits on your device, and the arrow crossing the border is the entirety of what an EOA's owner contributes: an authorisation, arriving from somewhere the network cannot see.

The contract's arrow doesn't leave the box. Its controller is the code drawn inside it — stored on the chain, readable by anyone, and looping back to govern the account that holds it. Nothing outside is required, and nothing outside can intervene.

So the two panels hold the same four fields and differ in one respect: where the arrow comes from.

Nobody says “EOA” out loud

It's specification vocabulary. In conversation people say wallet — "send it to my wallet" — which is loose but unambiguous in context.

Worth knowing the term anyway, because it's what you'll meet in every EIP, every client's source code and every technical discussion, always unexplained. This site uses it where precision matters and "wallet" where it doesn't.

docs.title: Where each thing lives
docs.text:
The previous few pages built up a chain of objects — seed phrase, private key, address — and this page adds a fourth. They are easy to run together, so here is the whole picture at once, with the one thing that matters marked: the line down the middle.

  YOUR DEVICE                    EVERY NODE
  ───────────                    ──────────
  seed phrase
      ↓  derives
  private key
      ↓  derives, one way
  address  ········ looks up ········▶  account
                                          nonce
                                          balance
                                          storageRoot
                                          codeHash

Everything on the left is yours and private. Everything on the right is public and held by thousands of machines. The address is the only thing that appears on both sides, and it carries no secret — which is the entire reason it can be handed out.

Three consequences, each of which surprises somebody:

  • The account is not in your wallet. It never was. Your wallet holds keys; the account is an entry in the state that every node stores. So when your wallet shows you a balance, it has asked a node and is displaying the answer — it owns none of that information.
  • Deleting your wallet changes no balance. The account is untouched, because it was never there. What you lose is the key, and with it the ability to authorise anything — which is the whole of the previous page.
  • Neither side determines the other's contents. An address tells you nothing about a balance, and an account holds no trace of the key that controls it. The arrow is a lookup, not a calculation.

And the pairing isn't as neat as it looks, in both directions:

Happens when A key with no account the key is fresh and its address has never been used, so nothing is recorded An account with no key every contract account — plus any address somebody sent ether to in error A wallet usually doesn't store your keys either

One more refinement, since it changes what a backup is.

It's natural to picture a wallet as a folder of private keys. Most modern wallets hold one seed and re-derive the keys whenever they're needed, exactly as the seed phrases page described. The keys are a product, not a stored collection.

Which is why twelve words restore everything, and why "back up your keys" is the wrong instruction — there is usually only one thing to back up, and it sits upstream of all of them.

docs.title: What an account actually looks like
docs.text:
Easiest to start with one in front of you. Take the address 0x7E5F…95Bdf — the one the addresses page derived from the private key 1, picked there because it's the simplest number a key can be and makes every step checkable by hand. Ask a node what that address holds — the lookup itself is explained further down:

nonce        3
balance      1500000000000000000
storageRoot  56e81f17…b421
codeHash     c5d24601…a470

Four values, and that is the entire account. The address isn't in there — it's what you looked the account up by, like a word in an index rather than part of the entry. The balance is in wei, so it reads as 1.5 ether. The nonce says three transactions have been sent from here. The last two are hashes, and the specific ones shown mean nothing stored and no code — more on them shortly.

Now a contract account, same four fields:

nonce        0
balance      0
storageRoot  ⟨fingerprint of its stored values⟩
codeHash     ⟨fingerprint of its code⟩

Neither of those last two is the empty constant, and that is the only thing distinguishing this account from the one above. Same shape, different contents. There is no fifth field marking it as a contract. The difference is entirely in those last two values, and we'll come back to exactly how you read it.

A note on those numbers. The address is real — it's the one private key 1 produces, the most-guessed key in existence — but the nonce and balance shown for it are made up for illustration. The two hashes in the wallet account are genuine fixed constants, and you'll meet them again in a moment. The contract's two are written in words rather than invented hex, because a plausible-looking fake hash is worse than no hash at all.

docs.title: The four fields
docs.text:
Every account, of either kind, holds these and nothing else (Wood, 2014):

Field What it holds nonce A counter — transactions sent, or contracts created balance Ether owned, in wei storageRoot Fingerprint of everything in storage codeHash Fingerprint of the code

The first two are plain numbers, but the word nonce needs defusing immediately, because it invites exactly the wrong guess.

It does not mean "random number" here. The account nonce is a plain sequential counter: it starts at 0 and goes up by one each time the account sends a transaction — 0, 1, 2, 3. It is public, anyone can read yours, and it is meant to be predictable, since your wallet has to know which number comes next and so does every node checking your transaction. A secret or random counter would be unusable.

The confusion is the vocabulary's fault. Nonce is merely short for "number used once", which promises nothing about how the number is chosen.

This site has already used “nonce” in the other sense

So the collision is worth naming, rather than letting you trip over it later.

  • Random, and necessarily unpredictable. The k in signing a message is this kind. Reuse one and your private key can be recovered — that page shows the arithmetic. Bitcoin's mining nonce is similar: a value searched for, essentially at random.
  • Sequential, and entirely predictable. The account nonce on this page. Counting, not guessing.

What they share is only the guarantee in the name: each value is used exactly once. For k that's achieved by drawing unpredictably from a space too large to repeat by accident. For an account it's achieved by adding one. Same promise, opposite methods — and for k, secrecy is essential, while for the account nonce it would break everything.

There are more than two senses in play, in fact — the block header has a nonce, and so do many contracts. The nonce page lists them all in one table.

docs.title: The two fingerprints
docs.text:
These are the fields that needed groundwork, and the groundwork is now in place.

A contract can hold a great deal — thousands of stored values, and a program of some size. None of it is in the account entry. What the account holds is a hash of each: the kind of fingerprint the Keccak-256 page described, where changing any input byte produces a completely different output.

That buys one specific thing. The account entry stays small and fixed-size no matter how much the contract stores, while still committing to every byte of it — you cannot alter one stored value without changing storageRoot, and you cannot change the code without changing codeHash.

What's still deferred is how you hash a collection. Hashing one lump of bytes is simple; hashing a mapping of thousands of keys and values, such that you can prove one entry belongs without presenting all the others, needs a structure. That structure is the Merkle Patricia Trie, and it has a page. Here, it's enough that a fingerprint exists and nothing can change beneath it unnoticed.

An account with no storage and no code still has both fields. They hold the fingerprints of emptiness, which are two fixed constants:

codeHash — the hash of no code at all
    c5d2460186f7233c927e7db2dcc703c0e500b653ca82273b7bfad8045d85a470

storageRoot — the root of an empty trie
    56e81f171bcc55a6ff8345e692c0f86e5b48e01b996cadc001622fb5e363b421

The first is Keccak-256 of nothing at all — the empty-input hash the Keccak page used to check its own implementation against the published value. The second is the root of an empty trie. Every ordinary wallet account on Ethereum carries that identical pair, which is what makes the next section possible.

docs.title: So one account can hold code and storage
docs.text:
Yes, and for a contract that's the normal case. The two fields are independent, which gives the combinations you actually meet:

Account codeHash storageRoot Ordinary wallet empty constant empty constant Contract holding data its code its storage Freshly deployed contract its code empty constant

The missing fourth row — storage but no code — isn't something you meet, because the only thing that can write to an account's storage is that account's own code.

docs.title: And yes, a contract can hold ether
docs.text:
Worth being explicit, since it surprises people. The balance field is on every account, because there is only one kind of entry in the state. A contract isn't a different sort of object with a different shape; it's an account that happens to have code.

It also has to be that way for contracts to be good for anything. An escrow must actually hold the money it's holding. A trading pool must own the assets it trades. If contracts couldn't own ether they could only ever direct other people's, which is a far weaker thing to be.

What differs is how the ether gets out. An EOA's balance moves when its key signs a transaction. A contract's balance moves only if the contract's own code contains instructions to send it — and if the code has no such path, the ether stays there permanently, as unreachable as if the key had been lost. That has happened at scale more than once, and the reason is worth remembering: nobody can override the code, for precisely the reasons the previous page set out.

How contracts work beyond that — what the code is, how it runs, what it costs — is its own page.

docs.title: How an address finds an account
docs.text:
This page has twice said "ask a node" without saying what that involves, and the answer is more specific than it looks it up in a list.

The state is a key–value mapping. The value is the four fields, written out with RLP — Ethereum's way of encoding structured data as bytes, which has its own page. The key is the part worth noticing: it is not the address. It's the address put through Keccak-256 first.

address      0x7E5F…95Bdf
    │
    │  keccak256
    ▼
key          a 32-byte value, which is where to look
    │
    ▼
value        RLP[ nonce, balance, storageRoot, codeHash ]

So nothing about the account is computed from the address. The contents are whatever transactions have put there over time, and no amount of arithmetic on an address could tell you a balance. What the address gives you is where to look — and the precise structure it's looking in, which makes that lookup provable rather than merely fast, is the Merkle Patricia Trie.

docs.title: Why hash the address first?
docs.text:
It seems like a pointless step — the address is already a hash, and already a fixed 20 bytes. There's a reason, and it's a defence.

Without it, anybody could choose where in the structure their account lands. That sounds harmless until you notice that creating an account costs almost nothing and needs no key: send one wei to any address and an entry appears, as the empty-accounts box above describes. Nobody has to control an address to put something at it.

So an attacker could pick a million addresses sharing a long leading prefix, dust each one, and force the structure into a single pathologically deep branch — making every lookup along it slow, for every node, permanently. Choosing the keys was free, and the cost landed on everybody else.

Hashing removes the choice. To place two accounts near each other you'd now have to find two addresses whose hashes share a long prefix, and that's a brute-force search for every account you want to add. The attack goes from free to expensive, which is the whole of the defence.

A secondary benefit falls out: hash outputs are spread evenly, so keys distribute evenly and no region of the structure ends up much deeper than another even by accident.

docs.title: Which kind is it? Look at one field
docs.text:
Suppose somebody hands you an address and you want to know whether it's a person's wallet or a contract. You cannot tell by looking: addresses are 20 bytes either way, and that page made the point that nothing in one reveals which kind it is.

The answer is in the account, and it takes one comparison. Ask any node for the account, then look at codeHash:

  • It equals c5d2…a470 → there is no code → it's an EOA.
  • It's anything else → there is code → it's a contract.

That's the entire test. Which is worth dwelling on for a second, because of what it implies: no field says which kind of account this is. Nothing was declared when the account came into being, and there's no flag anybody set. The kind is read off from what the account holds.

Everything else follows from that one difference:

EOA Contract account Controlled by whoever holds the private key its own code Comes into being when an address derived from a key is first used a transaction deploys code Can start a transaction yes no Its nonce counts transactions sent contracts created

Both can hold ether, both are addressed identically, and both appear in the state the same way.

Why there's no type field — or an owner, or a name

Four fields is a strikingly short list, so it's worth asking what isn't there. Each absence is deliberate.

No type, as above. It would be redundant, and redundancy in consensus data is a liability: two fields that can disagree need a rule for which one wins. Deriving the type from codeHash makes disagreement impossible.

No owner. For a contract there's nothing to put — control is whatever the code says, which might be one key, five keys, a vote, or nobody. For an EOA it would be the public key, which is exactly what the address already commits to.

No name, no creation date, no history. The state answers what is true now and nothing else. How an account reached its current contents is recoverable from the blocks, so putting it in the state would mean every node storing a second copy of something it already has.

The pattern recurs all over Ethereum: the state holds the minimum from which everything else can be derived. Anything inferable is left out, because storing it anyway only creates a way for a node to be wrong.

docs.title: Nothing creates an account
docs.text:
With the concrete picture in place, one consequence is worth drawing out.

"Opening an account" is a thing you do at a bank — an application, an approval, a record created in your name. None of that has an equivalent here. The addresses page established that nothing creates an address: all 2160 exist already, and a wallet merely derives one. Accounts inherit that. An account isn't created; it begins to be recorded the first time there's something to record.

So an address nobody has ever used is not in the state at all. Not stored as a row of zeros — absent. Which is indistinguishable from an account holding nothing, and that's the point: zero balance and no stored entry describe the same situation. Ask a node for the balance of an untouched address and it answers zero, because that's the correct answer, not because it found a record saying so.

Which makes “empty” an awkward category

A case where a tidy idea needed patching.

Early on you could create entries that existed while holding nothing: send zero ether to an untouched address and a record appeared with a zero balance, a zero nonce and no code. Functionally identical to absence, but occupying space on every node — and millions were made cheaply as a result.

EIP-161 (Wood, 2016) fixed it in the Spurious Dragon upgrade of 2016, by deleting such accounts at the end of any transaction that touched them — so "holds nothing" and "isn't recorded" converged again.

More than trivia, because of what it reveals: everything in the state is something every node must store, forever, at a real cost. Storing nothing therefore has to cost nothing, or the accounting breaks. That pressure turns up again and again once you reach gas.

docs.title: Only an EOA can start anything
docs.text:
This is the most clarifying fact about how Ethereum runs, and it's routinely assumed to work the other way.

Nothing on Ethereum happens by itself. There are no timers, no scheduled jobs, no background processes. A contract cannot wake up at midnight, cannot poll a price, cannot notice that a deadline has passed. It has no thread of its own and no way to get one.

A contract's code runs only when something calls it. Follow any chain of calls back far enough and it begins in the same place: a transaction, signed by a private key, sent from an EOA. Contracts can call other contracts, and one transaction can touch dozens — but all of it descends from a single signature at the root.

onesignaturetransactioncontract Acontract Bcontract CRemove the signature and nothing to its right can happen.

Two reasons it has to be this way:

  • Somebody has to pay. Execution is metered and the fee comes from the account that sent the transaction. Self-starting code would be work with no payer.
  • Somebody has to be the cause. Every node must reach the same result, so all of them must run the same operations in the same order. Spontaneous execution would require agreement on when it fired — and there is no shared clock to agree with.

Which raises an obvious question: plenty of things on Ethereum visibly happen without anyone pressing a button. They aren't exceptions — somebody is being paid to send those transactions, and the contracts page takes that apart.

One thing here is changing: EIP-7702

The rule above holds. The tidy statement of the previous section doesn't, quite.

EIP-7702 (Buterin et al., 2024), live since Pectra in May 2025, lets an EOA set its codeHash to point at contract code. So "EOAs have no code" is no longer strictly true, and the compare-against-the-constant test now has an exception.

What it's for: giving ordinary wallets abilities that used to require a contract account — batching several actions into one transaction, letting somebody else pay your fee, setting spending permissions. The same goals ERC-4337 (Buterin et al., 2021) pursues as a layer on top.

What it does not change: an EOA still needs a key to authorise anything, and transactions still originate only from EOAs. Both rules this page rests on survive. What's blurring is the tidy two-kinds taxonomy — which is why this page carries a date stamp at the top, and why you should hold that taxonomy loosely.

So is an account the same thing as a wallet?

No, and the words get used interchangeably constantly.

  • An account is the entry in the state. It exists whether or not any software knows about it.
  • A wallet is the program on your device. It holds keys and builds transactions, and Ethereum has never heard of it.
  • An EOA is an account whose key some wallet happens to hold.

So "my wallet has three accounts" means one piece of software holding keys for three addresses. The accounts aren't in the wallet, and losing the wallet doesn't touch them — as the previous page laboured.

Harmless in conversation. A problem the moment you read a specification, where "account" never means "app".

docs.title: Why this design needs a nonce
docs.text:
One last consequence, to set up the next page.

Ethereum records balances where Bitcoin records individual coins. The state machine page covered the comparison, and Buterin (2014) argues the case at length. Here is what the choice costs.

The difference is roughly cash versus a bank statement. Bitcoin is the cash: you hold particular notes, paying someone means handing over specific notes, and you get different ones back as change. The notes are the money, and each individual one either exists or has been spent. Ethereum is the statement: there are no notes at all, just a number beside your address that goes up and down.

That distinction decides whether replay is even possible.

A Bitcoin transaction consumes specific coins — it names them. Submit it twice and the second attempt fails on its own terms, because the coins it names are already gone: not merely disallowed, but meaningless, like trying to hand over a note you no longer have. The protection is a property of the thing being spent.

An account has no such property. "Send 1 ether from A to B" names nothing that gets used up. It's a valid instruction before it executes and an equally valid instruction afterwards, because A's balance is just a number and the instruction never referred to any particular part of it. A signed transaction would be a reusable cheque: anyone who saw it could submit it again, and every copy would verify perfectly.

So the protection has to be supplied separately, and it's supplied as a counter. That's the nonce.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The account is not in your wallet. Your wallet holds keys; the account is held by every node. The address is the only thing on both sides of that line, and it carries no secret.
  • An account is an entry in the state, looked up by address, with exactly four fields: nonce, balance, storageRoot, codeHash. The address isn't one of them.
  • The lookup key is keccak256(address), not the address — so nobody can choose where their account sits, which stops an attacker dusting a million chosen addresses to force one deep, slow branch.
  • EOA means externally owned — what controls it sits outside Ethereum, namely a person with a key. A contract's controller is code on the chain.
  • The account nonce is a sequential counter, not a random number. It shares only the "used once" guarantee with the random nonces elsewhere in cryptography.
  • storageRoot and codeHash are fingerprints, letting a fixed-size entry commit to unbounded data. The structure behind them is the Merkle Patricia Trie.
  • An account with neither carries the two constants for empty — c5d2…a470 and 56e8…b421.
  • The kind of account is read off codeHash, not declared. There is no type field, because the type is derivable.
  • Nothing creates an account. An unused address is absent from the state, which is indistinguishable from holding nothing.
  • Only an EOA can start a transaction. No timers, no scheduled jobs. Anything that looks automatic is somebody paid to send a transaction, racing others for the reward.
  • EIP-7702 has begun blurring the EOA/contract split without changing either rule above.
  • Balances aren't consumable the way coins are, so replay protection must be added separately — by the nonce.

Next: The nonce — the counter that stops a signed transaction being reused.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Buterin, V., Weiss, Y., Tirosh, D., Nacson, S., Forshtat, A., Gazso, K., & Hess, T. (2021). ERC-4337: Account Abstraction Using Alt Mempool. Ethereum Improvement Proposals. Pursues contract-account capabilities for ordinary users without a protocol change. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4337
  • Buterin, V. (2014). Ethereum white paper: A next-generation smart contract and decentralized application platform. Argues the case for an account model over Bitcoin's transaction outputs, including the replay problem it creates. https://ethereum.org/en/whitepaper/
  • Buterin, V., Wilson, S., Dietrichs, A., & lightclient (2024). EIP-7702: Set Code for EOAs. Ethereum Improvement Proposals. Lets a key-controlled account carry contract code, weakening the EOA/contract distinction. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7702
  • Wood, G. (2016). EIP-161: State trie clearing (invariant-preserving alternative). Ethereum Improvement Proposals. Activated in Spurious Dragon; deletes accounts left empty at the end of a transaction, so that "holds nothing" and "not recorded" describe the same thing. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-161
  • Wood, G. (2014). Ethereum: A secure decentralised generalised transaction ledger. Ethereum project yellow paper. §4.1 defines the account state as the four-field tuple, and gives the empty-code and empty-trie constants. https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf

docs.title: The nonce
docs.text:
Permanent. The way the nonce works has never been revised.

Nonce

Literally "number used once" — which is all the word promises, and says nothing about how the number is chosen. Ethereum reuses it for several unrelated mechanisms, listed at the end of this page.

This page is about the account nonce: a counter stored in every account. A transaction declares which value it is claiming, the network accepts it only if that value is the one the account is due next, and the counter then advances — so no number can ever authorise two things.

It counts; it is not random. What it counts and where it starts depend on the kind of account, and both are below.

docs.title: The account nonce, concretely
docs.text:
Take an ordinary wallet account. It has sent three transactions. Its nonce is 3. The next transaction you sign must say nonce: 3, and once it's in a block the account's nonce becomes 4.

That really is the whole mechanism. The reason it's worth a page is not the counter — it's what the counter prevents, and the very practical trouble it causes when it gets out of step.

Why the name misleads, when most nonces really are random

The confusion is reasonable: elsewhere in cryptography a nonce almost always is a random value, and nothing in the word rules that out.

The k used when signing is the famous example: it must be unpredictable, and reusing one leaks your private key. The account nonce is the opposite kind. It counts, it's public, and anybody can read yours.

Being predictable isn't a weakness here, it's a requirement — your wallet has to know which number comes next, and so does every node checking your transaction. A secret counter would be unusable.

docs.title: The problem it solves
docs.text:
The accounts page ended on this, so briefly: a signed transaction without a nonce would be a reusable cheque.

"Send 1 ether from A to B" names nothing that gets consumed. The instruction is as valid after it executes as before, because A's balance is only a number and the instruction never referred to any particular part of it. So anybody who saw your transaction — and everybody sees every transaction — could submit the identical bytes again. The signature would still verify, because it's a signature over those bytes, and the bytes haven't changed.

Your 1-ether payment becomes a hundred-ether payment, by somebody else's choice, with your valid signature on every copy. Buterin (2014) names this as the cost of choosing an account model, and the counter as the answer to it.

The nonce closes it completely. Your transaction says nonce: 3, and the moment it's included your account is due nonce 4. The replayed copy still says 3, which is now wrong, so every node rejects it without even looking at the signature.

docs.title: Why Bitcoin needs no such thing
docs.text:
Because of the difference set out on What is Ethereum? — Bitcoin records individual coins, Ethereum records balances.

A Bitcoin transaction names the specific coins it spends. Submit it twice and the second attempt isn't rejected by a rule — it's meaningless, because the coins it names no longer exist. The protection is a property of the thing being spent.

Ethereum has nothing consumable to lean on, so it adds a counter instead. Same protection, supplied by bookkeeping rather than by the structure of money.

The nonce doesn't protect you across chains

Worth knowing, since the two defences get confused.

Many networks run Ethereum's rules with their own history. Your nonce means nothing on another chain — it keeps its own count for your address, so a transaction valid here could be replayed there, where the same key controls the same address.

That's the job of a second field, the chain id, introduced by EIP-155 (Buterin, 2016) and covered on the signatures page.

  • nonce — stops the same transaction twice on this chain
  • chain id — stops it being carried to another chain

Neither substitutes for the other.

docs.title: Strictly in order, no gaps
docs.text:
Here is the part with consequences. The rule isn't "a nonce you haven't used yet" — it's exactly the next one.

If your account's nonce is 5, then a transaction with nonce 5 is valid and a transaction with nonce 7 is not. Not invalid forever; invalid for now. It becomes valid the instant nonce 6 is included, and not a moment before.

That's a condition of validity rather than a preference: the specification lists a matching nonce among the tests a transaction must pass before it may be applied at all (Wood, 2014).

one account’s queuethe protocol takes them in this order, with no skipping3done4done5fee too low6waiting7waiting8waiting…this one is stuck— and so is everything to its right6, 7 and 8 may each offer a generous fee. It makes no difference: theprotocol will not accept nonce 6 until nonce 5 has happened, so noblock can contain them. A queue with one jam at the front is a queuethat has stopped.

Why so strict? Because the alternative is ambiguity. If gaps were allowed, a node holding nonces 5 and 7 would have to decide whether 6 is coming, and two nodes could reasonably decide differently — one applying 7, the other waiting. They would disagree about the state, which is the one thing the design cannot tolerate. A strict sequence means every node knows, with no judgement involved, exactly which transaction from your account comes next.

docs.title: Why transactions get stuck
docs.text:
This is the most useful thing on the page, because nearly everyone meets it and almost nobody is told why.

Suppose you send a transaction with nonce 5 and attach a fee too low for anyone to want to include it. It sits unconfirmed. Annoying, but you'd expect it to affect only that one transaction.

It doesn't. It blocks every later transaction from the same account, however much each of those offers, because none of them can legally be included before nonce 5 is. Your whole account is frozen behind one cheap transaction — and nothing in any wallet's interface explains that this is what has happened.

What nodes do with the later ones varies, and this is worth knowing because it shapes what you see:

  • The protocol's rule is about blocks: a block containing nonce 6 without 5 having happened is invalid. Flat rule, no discretion.
  • A node's waiting room is softer. Most clients will hold a transaction whose nonce is in the future, hoping the gap fills — often labelled queued as against pending. They may also drop it after a while, or refuse to hold more than a few.

So "stuck" has two flavours that look identical from outside: the gap transaction nobody will mine, and the later ones no block may legally contain yet.

docs.title: Unsticking one
docs.text:
You cannot delete a transaction. Nothing on Ethereum can be withdrawn once broadcast — there's no instruction for it and nobody to ask. What you can do is replace it.

Sign a new transaction with the same nonce and a fee high enough to be worth including. Now two transactions claim nonce 5, and at most one of them can ever be included, since the account's nonce can only pass 5 once. Nodes keeping a waiting room generally prefer the better-paying of the two and discard the other.

Two details that matter in practice:

  1. You must re-sign. The nonce is part of what you signed, so you cannot edit a broadcast transaction — the signature wouldn't match. A replacement is a genuinely new transaction that happens to reuse the number.
  2. The fee must be meaningfully higher. Clients won't swap one transaction for a near-identical one, or the network could be flooded with trivial replacements. A small increase is usually refused.

To cancel rather than retry, send something harmless at that nonce instead — most wallets do this by sending zero ether to your own address. It still has to be included and still costs a fee, but it consumes the number, and the queue behind it starts moving.

Cancelling is a race, not a command

The original transaction remains perfectly valid the whole time. If someone includes it before your replacement lands, it happened — your cancel simply becomes the one that's now invalid.

So a cancellation is an attempt to win a race against your own earlier transaction, not an undo. The longer it has been sitting there, and the better it pays, the likelier you lose.

Why did my wallet send two transactions with the same nonce by accident?

Because asking "what nonce is next?" has two answers, and tools don't always pick the same one.

  • Counting only what's confirmed on chain gives you the account's actual nonce.
  • Counting confirmed transactions plus the ones you've already broadcast gives you the next free number.

Use two wallets, or one wallet and one script, and they can each read the confirmed count, each decide the next nonce is the same number, and sign two different transactions with it. Only one can ever be included. The other is not merely rejected — it becomes permanently invalid the moment its rival is mined.

Which is occasionally useful and mostly an accident. If you're signing from more than one place at once, something has to track the count.

docs.title: Contract accounts have a nonce too
docs.text:
Same field, different meaning: for a contract, the nonce counts how many contracts that account has created.

That isn't an unrelated reuse of the field. It serves the same purpose — making sure a number is never used twice — because a contract's address is computed from the creating address and that creator's nonce, as the addresses page described. The nonce is what stops two deployments from the same account landing on the same address.

A contract's nonce starts at 1, not 0

A small asymmetry, and a deliberate one.

An EOA begins at nonce 0. A newly created contract begins at 1, a rule introduced by EIP-161 (Wood, 2016) in the same upgrade that cleared out empty accounts.

The reason is the address calculation above. A contract that still had nonce 0 could compute an address for its own first deployment that collided with an address derived some other way, and starting the count at 1 removes the overlap. One of those fixes that looks arbitrary until you notice what it rules out.

docs.title: What the nonce is not
docs.text:
Four things it gets mistaken for:

  • Not a timestamp. It says how many transactions you've sent, not when. An account that sent three transactions years apart has nonce 3.
  • Not global. Every account keeps its own, independently. There is no network-wide transaction counter.
  • Not secret. Anybody can read any account's nonce, and they must be able to.
  • Not a measure of anything but transactions sent. Receiving ether doesn't change your nonce — receiving requires no transaction from you. An account can hold a fortune and still have nonce 0.

That last one is the useful test: the nonce counts what you did, never what happened to you.

docs.title: Other things called a nonce
docs.text:
The word is reused all over Ethereum for things that have nothing to do with each other beyond the "used once" promise. Worth having the list in one place.

Where What it is Chosen how Account the counter this page is about counting, 0 upwards Transaction the field in which a transaction declares which account nonce it is claiming copied from the account Block header a leftover from proof of work now always zero Signing (k) the secret value in ECDSA random, and must be unpredictable Inside contracts whatever a contract's author decided up to them

They share the name and nothing else. The value is chosen by counting, or at random, or fixed at zero, or however a contract's author felt; by the protocol, your wallet, the signer, or a stranger. And the cost of repeating one ranges from trivial to catastrophic: reuse an account nonce and your second transaction is simply rejected, while reuse a signing k and your private key can be reconstructed from the two signatures.

So there's no general account of nonces to give — "used once" is the whole of the overlap, and a page about that would be a page about a word. Each mechanism is instead covered where its own subject lives: k with signatures, the dead field with the block header, the declared value with transactions, and contract counters with contracts. This page takes the account nonce because this section is about accounts.

Two of them still deserve a second look here, because they're the two that get mistaken for this one.

The account nonce and the transaction nonce are different fields. The account holds the count; the transaction states the number it claims. Validity is the test that the two agree. It's easy to read "the nonce" as one thing in one place, but there are two copies and the whole mechanism is the comparison between them.

The block header's nonce is a fossil. Under proof of work, miners searched for a value that made the block's hash small enough — that search was mining, and the nonce was where the answer went. Proof of stake abolished the search, and EIP-3675 (Kalinin et al., 2021) requires the field to be exactly 0x0000000000000000 from the transition block onward. It stays in the header because the header's shape is baked into too much code to change for nothing, so every block since the Merge carries eight bytes of zeros where the puzzle answer used to be.

And the contract ones aren't protocol at all. A contract accepting signed instructions from off-chain has the same replay problem this page opens with, and no account nonce to lean on, because the signature isn't a transaction. So contracts keep their own counters — token approvals, account-abstraction operations, anything with an off-chain signature. Each is a convention its author invented, enforced only by that contract's code.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The account nonce is a per-account counter. For a wallet account it counts transactions sent and starts at 0, and it's part of what you sign.
  • It exists to stop replay: without it a signed transaction could be submitted again and again, and every copy would verify.
  • Bitcoin needs no equivalent because its transactions name specific coins, which can only be spent once. Balances offer no such protection, so a counter supplies it.
  • Nonces must be used in strict order with no gaps — nonce 7 is invalid until 6 has been included — because gaps would let two nodes reasonably disagree about what comes next.
  • Therefore one underpriced transaction blocks every later one from the same account, no matter what they pay.
  • You can't delete a transaction, only replace it: same nonce, higher fee, newly signed. Cancelling means winning a race against your own earlier transaction, which you may lose.
  • For a contract the nonce counts contracts created, and it starts at 1. It keeps deployment addresses from colliding.
  • The nonce counts what you sent — never what you received.
  • "Nonce" is reused for several unrelated things: the account's counter, the transaction field that claims it, the block header's dead proof-of-work field, the secret k in signing, and whatever counters contracts keep for themselves.

Next: State — the whole collection of accounts, and how a tiny block header commits to all of it.
