  • Buterin, V. (2016). EIP-155: Simple replay attack protection. Ethereum Improvement Proposals. Adds the chain id, which handles the replay case the nonce cannot — the same transaction carried to a different network. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-155
  • Kalinin, M., Ryan, D., & Buterin, V. (2021). EIP-3675: Upgrade consensus to Proof-of-Stake. Ethereum Improvement Proposals. Requires the block header's nonce to be the zero constant from the transition block onward. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-3675
  • Wood, G. (2014). Ethereum: A secure decentralised generalised transaction ledger. Ethereum project yellow paper. Defines the nonce as a field of the account state and makes the matching nonce a condition of transaction validity. https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf
  • Wood, G. (2016). EIP-161: State trie clearing (invariant-preserving alternative). Ethereum Improvement Proposals. Specifies that a newly created contract's nonce begins at 1, closing an address-collision case. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-161

docs.title: State
docs.text:
Permanent, except one part. That the state is a mapping from addresses to accounts, and that each block commits to it with a single root, has held since 2015. The structure producing that root is the part under active replacement.

Current as of Fusaka (December 2025)

Nothing here has changed in Ethereum's lifetime. The long-running proposals to replace the structure behind the state root — and to let untouched state expire — would change the mechanism without changing what the root promises. None has shipped. How this site handles forks.

State

The complete set of every account and what it holds — each address paired with its four fields.

It is not stored in the blocks. Every node keeps its own copy and updates it as blocks arrive. What a block carries is a state root: one 32-byte fingerprint of the whole state, which lets every node check that its copy matches everybody else's.

This page needs four things about blocks, all of which What is Ethereum? established and none of which needs the blocks section to understand:

  • A block is a batch of transactions — a hundred or two — added to the chain as a single unit.
  • Its transactions are ordered, and applied one after another in that order.
  • Whoever assembles a block is its proposer. Anyone may; who gets to, and when, is the blocks section's business.
  • The state is committed once per block, after every transaction in it has run — not once per transaction.

That's the whole of the vocabulary borrowed from later pages. Everything else here is accounts and hashing, both of which you already have.

docs.title: The state is one enormous mapping
docs.text:
Nothing more structurally complicated than a dictionary. The key is an address; the value is the four fields the accounts page laid out.

0x7E5F…95Bdf  →  nonce 3   balance 1500000000000000000   (no code)
0xd8dA…96045  →  nonce 847 balance 2000000000000000      (no code)
0xA0b8…eB48   →  nonce 1   balance 0    code, and storage
      ⋮

Hundreds of millions of entries, and that's the lot. Ask "what is Ethereum's state?" and the honest answer is that table, as it stands right now.

Two things follow immediately, and both matter more than they look.

The state has no history in it. It says 0x7E5F has sent three transactions. It does not say when, to whom, or what they were. It is a snapshot, not a record.

The state is the only thing you need to go on. To check whether a new transaction is valid, a node needs balances and nonces — which are in the state. It does not need to know how those values came about.

docs.title: The state is not in the blocks
docs.text:
This is the misconception worth killing early, because almost everyone arrives with it.

A block does not contain the state. It contains transactions — instructions — and each node applies them to the copy of the state it already has. The state is the result of running every block ever produced, and it lives on each node's disk, not on the chain.

Which raises the obvious problem. If every node computes the state privately, how does anyone know they all got the same answer? Thousands of independent machines, each with their own copy, each claiming it's correct.

They could exchange their copies and compare. That would work and is completely impractical: the state is measured in hundreds of gigabytes, so agreeing on every balance by sending every balance around is not a mechanism, it's a bandwidth bill. (No figure is given here on purpose — it's a moving target, and any number printed on this page would be wrong within months.)

docs.title: The state root
docs.text:
So they do the other thing. Each block header carries a single 32-byte value — the state root — which the proposer says is the fingerprint of the whole state after that block's transactions have been applied (Wood, 2014).

Note says. The root is a claim, not a fact. Whoever built the block ran the transactions on their own copy, fingerprinted the result, and wrote the number down. Nothing about it is self-evidently true, and the entire mechanism is that it's a claim anybody can test.

block headera few hundred bytesstateRoot32 bytesthe statehundreds of gigabytesone account’s four fieldsanother accountanother account… hundreds of millions morenone of this is in the blockChange one wei in one account and the root changes completely. So twonodes agreeing on 32 bytes agree on every balance, every nonce, andevery byte of every contract’s storage.

docs.title: Why a matching root means matching state
docs.text:
Two steps, and they differ in kind.

Different data gives a different root. That's the Keccak-256 property: change one wei in one account and the output is unrecognisable. So if your copy of the state and mine differed in any respect at all, our roots would differ.

Running that backwards gives the useful direction. Our roots are identical, therefore our states are identical — because if they weren't, the roots couldn't be.

That reversal isn't quite airtight, and it's worth being exact about why. Two different states yielding the same root is a collision, and the reason to discount it isn't logic, it's that nobody can find one — the 2128 of the collisions box on the Keccak page. So the guarantee is computational, not mathematical, which is the same strength of claim everything else here rests on.

docs.title: What a node actually does
docs.text:
The step that makes this work is easy to miss: the node isn't starting from nowhere. Before this block arrived, it had already checked its state against the previous block's root. So it knows its starting point matches everybody else's.

Which means it holds all three inputs:

  • the same starting state, already verified
  • the same transactions, which came in the block
  • the same rules, which are the protocol

Three identical inputs to a deterministic function must produce one identical output. So the node doesn't merely compare roots — it knows in advance what the root has to be. Then:

  1. Apply the block's transactions to its own copy of the state.
  2. Compute the root of the result.
  3. Compare with the root the header claims.

Match, and it has independently confirmed its state is identical to the proposer's — every account, without having seen any of theirs. It never has to trust the state it was handed, because it never was handed any.

Mismatch, and it rejects the block. And notice the mismatch is unambiguous rather than merely worrying: because the node verified its own starting point one block ago, the fault cannot be in where it began. It is in the block.

This is an induction running back to the very first block — my state was right then, I applied the same instructions everybody else did, so my state is right now — and it's why a node needs no copy of anybody else's state, ever.

What this stops, concretely

Suppose a proposer wants to credit itself an extra 1,000 ether.

Building that state is easy, and fingerprinting it honestly is easy. The problem is the number it must then publish: it disagrees with the root every honest node computes from the same transactions, so every one of them rejects the block.

And there is no number it could write instead, because the correct root is fixed by things everybody already has — the previous state and the transactions in the block. The proposer isn't being asked for information nobody else can obtain. It's being asked to state a value that others will independently derive, which leaves it nowhere to put a lie.

Which is the asymmetry the whole design turns on. Producing the state is expensive; checking the claim about it costs a 32-byte comparison.

Why a plain hash of the whole state wouldn't do

A fair question: hash the lot and you get 32 bytes, so why does the next section need a special structure?

Because of what the root is asked to do besides matching.

It must be cheap to update. A node applies a block, changing perhaps a few hundred accounts out of hundreds of millions. Re-hashing the entire state for each block would be absurd. The real structure lets a change be pushed up one path, touching a handful of values.

It must support proofs about parts. Somebody should be able to prove "this account holds this balance" against the root, without presenting the whole state. A flat hash can't: the only way to verify it is to have all the data, which defeats the point for anyone running a light client — software that follows the chain without storing the state.

Both needs point to the same answer — a tree of hashes, where each node commits to its children. That's the Merkle Patricia Trie, and it gets its own page.

docs.title: The commitment is per block, not per transaction
docs.text:
One detail worth pinning down, because it bounds what a root can tell you.

If a transaction lands in block N, it runs against the state at the end of block N−1 plus the effects of every transaction ordered before it inside block N. That intermediate state is real, and no root is published for it. Ethereum commits once per block, after all of it has run.

History: it used to commit per transaction

Not always the case, and the change is instructive.

Until the Byzantium upgrade in 2017, every transaction receipt — the record a node produces for each transaction, saying what happened when it ran — carried the state root as of that transaction — a published commitment after each one, not merely each block. EIP-658 (Johnson, 2017) replaced that field with a plain status code: 1 for success, 0 for failure.

The reason was cost against use. Computing an intermediate root per transaction is real work for every node, and almost nothing consumed the result, whereas did this transaction succeed? was the question everyone actually asked and previously had to infer.

So Ethereum once published exactly this commitment, looked at the price, and sold it for a single bit of far more useful information.

A consequence worth carrying forward: a transaction never names the state it expects, and could not usefully do so. That belongs with transactions, where it's unpacked.

docs.title: Storage is a state inside the state
docs.text:
An account's storageRoot is where this turns recursive, and it's neater than it first sounds.

A contract's storage is its own private mapping: 32-byte keys, called slots, to 32-byte values. Nothing else can read or write it directly — only the contract's own code, which is why the accounts page could say storage without code never occurs.

slot 0x00…00  →  0x00…0539    (say, a stored number)
slot 0x00…01  →  0x00…7E5F…   (say, an address)
      ⋮

That mapping is fingerprinted exactly the way the whole state is — same structure, same guarantees — and the resulting root is what sits in the account's storageRoot field. So:

  • the state root commits to every account,
  • and each account's storage root commits to every slot that account holds.

A tree of accounts, where some leaves carry a tree of their own. Change one slot in one contract and that contract's storage root changes, so that account's entry changes, so the state root changes. One 32-byte number at the top is a statement about every stored value on Ethereum.

Storage keys get hashed too, for the same reason addresses do

The state is keyed by keccak256(address) rather than the address, as the accounts page explained, so nobody can choose where in the structure their account lands.

Storage does the same: the trie is keyed by keccak256(slot). And here the defence matters more, not less. An address takes work to grind; a slot number is simply a number a contract writes to, free to choose outright. If raw slots were keys, a contract could write to a million slots sharing a long prefix and make its own storage pathologically deep for everybody storing it.

docs.title: State and history are different things
docs.text:
Both get called "the blockchain", and separating them explains what a node actually keeps.

  • History is the chain of blocks: every transaction ever sent, in order. It only gets added to.
  • State is where that history has left things. It gets rewritten constantly.

History is a recording. State is the current position. And the surprising part:

You can throw away the history and keep using the chain. You cannot throw away the state.

To validate the next block, a node needs balances, nonces, code and storage — all present-tense, all in the state. It does not need last year's transactions. They produced the state it's holding, and having done so, they are no longer load-bearing.

This isn't a thought experiment. EIP-4444 (Kadianakis et al., 2021) proposes exactly it: execution clients stop serving and may delete block bodies and receipts past a cutoff, keeping the chain fully functional. That the proposal is even coherent is the clearest evidence the two things are separable.

Hence the kinds of node you'll meet, which are differences in how much history is retained:

Keeps Can tell you Archive state at every past block what your balance was two years ago Full current state, plus enough history to re-derive everything, but old queries need recomputation Pruned current state, little history the present, authoritatively

All three validate new blocks identically, because all three hold the current state. The difference is only what questions about the past they can answer.

So is Ethereum's data permanent or not?

Both, in different senses, and the distinction is worth having because the word immutable gets used far too loosely.

What cannot be altered is the history, by anyone, because every block commits to the one before it. Nobody can quietly rewrite a transaction from 2017.

What is not guaranteed to be retained is a copy of it on any particular machine. Pruning is a local choice about disk, not a change to the chain. The data is immutable; your access to it depends on somebody having kept it.

So "stored on the blockchain forever" is two claims wearing one coat: it can't be changed is a protocol guarantee, while it will always be available to you is a bet on other people's storage.

docs.title: The state only grows
docs.text:
One closing fact, with consequences all over the rest of the site.

Nothing removes an account. A balance can fall to zero, a contract can become useless, a key can be lost — and the entry stays, because the protocol has no notion of state going out of date. The only deletions in Ethereum's history were the narrow cleanup of genuinely empty accounts the accounts page described.

So the state rises monotonically, every node stores all of it, and the cost of running one rises with it. That's the state growth problem — not a bug anybody introduced, but the direct price of having chosen accounts, which is the next page's subject.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The state is a mapping from every address to its four fields — a snapshot of the present, containing no history.
  • Blocks don't contain the state. They contain transactions; each node applies them to its own copy.
  • Each block header carries a state root: 32 bytes the proposer claims fingerprint the whole state. Two nodes agreeing on it agree on everything — a computational guarantee, since the alternative is finding a hash collision.
  • A node already verified its state against the previous block's root, so it has the same starting state, the same transactions and the same rules — and therefore knows what the new root must be before it looks.
  • A node applies a block, computes the root, and compares. So it verifies the state without ever being sent any.
  • A plain hash wouldn't work: the root must be cheap to update and must support proofs about parts. Both need a tree — the Merkle Patricia Trie.
  • The root commits to the state after a whole block, never mid-block. Ethereum once published a root per transaction and traded it in 2017 for a success-or-failure bit.
  • Storage nests the same idea: each contract's slots have their own root, which sits in its account entry.
  • Storage keys are hashed like addresses, and the defence matters more there, because a contract picks its slot numbers freely.
  • History can be discarded; state cannot. Nodes differ in how much history they keep, not in whether they hold the state.
  • Immutable conflates two claims: the data can't be changed, but your access depends on somebody retaining it.
  • The state only ever grows, because nothing expires. That's the price of accounts.

Next: Why accounts, and what they cost — the trade this whole section has been describing.

docs.text:
• Johnson, N. (2017). EIP-658: Embedding transaction status code in receipts. Ethereum Improvement Proposals. Activated in Byzantium; replaced the per-transaction intermediate state root in receipts with a status code. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-658
  • Kadianakis, G., lightclient, & Stokes, A. (2021). EIP-4444: Bound Historical Data in Execution Clients. Ethereum Improvement Proposals. Proposes that clients stop serving and may prune block bodies and receipts past a cutoff — which is only coherent because state and history are separable. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4444
  • Wood, G. (2014). Ethereum: A secure decentralised generalised transaction ledger. Ethereum project yellow paper. Defines the world state as a mapping from addresses to account states, and the state root as the header field committing to it. https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf

docs.title: What it reveals
docs.text:
Permanent. That the state and every transaction are readable by anyone is not a parameter somebody chose and could unchoose. It is the condition that makes independent verification possible at all. What people do about it changes constantly, and this page describes those efforts as classes rather than products.

Pseudonymous

Identified by a persistent name that isn't your legal one.

Ethereum is not anonymous and not identified — it is pseudonymous. Your address is a stable label that follows you across everything you do, and it is not attached to your name until it is, at which point everything it ever did becomes attached too.

That "until" is the whole subject of this page.

docs.title: The thesis
docs.text:
Every page so far has relied on something without examining it: anyone can check. Nodes recompute balances, verify signatures, and reject invalid blocks, which is why nobody has to be trusted.

Checking requires seeing. A node cannot verify that a transfer doesn't overdraw an account without reading the balance; it cannot confirm a signature without the message. So the property the whole site rests on has a precondition, and the precondition is that everything is readable by everybody.

Verifiability and privacy are the same dial. You do not get the first without paying the second.

That isn't a flaw anyone introduced, and it isn't fixable by being more careful. It is the trade the design makes, and the useful thing is to understand which way it was set and what that costs.

docs.title: What's actually public
docs.text:
More than people expect, and permanently.

Every balance, for every address that has ever held anything.

Every transaction — sender, recipient, amount, the data it carried, what it cost, whether it succeeded. Including the ones that failed, which still happened and still appear.

Every contract's code, and every value in its storage. This is the one that surprises developers: marking a variable private in a contract's source controls which other contracts may read it through the language. It does nothing whatsoever about people. The storage slot is a 32-byte value in the state, and anybody with a node can read it.

And intentions, briefly, before they happen. A transaction sits in the mempool before inclusion, visible to anybody watching. So what you are about to do is public for a few seconds before it is done — which is the window most front-running lives in.

What's not public is the one thing that matters: your private key, which never leaves your device. The protocol hides the thing that grants control and publishes everything else.

docs.title: Why pseudonymity is weaker than it sounds
docs.text:
"My address isn't my name" feels like adequate protection. It is much thinner than that, for a reason that has nothing to do with cryptography.

A pseudonym accumulates. Every transaction you make from an address joins a permanent, public, unforgeable record attached to that one label. Nobody can forge entries and nobody can remove them. Over time that record becomes a detailed account of behaviour — amounts, timing, counterparties, what you interacted with and when.

And it collapses all at once. The record isn't linked to you until one link exists: an exchange that knows your identity and your withdrawal address, a published donation address, a name registered to your address, a payment to someone who knows you. The moment any single link is made, it doesn't reveal one transaction. It reveals the whole history, backwards.

This is not hypothetical, and it has been demonstrated against a system that tries harder than Ethereum does. Meiklejohn et al. (2013) clustered Bitcoin activity into real-world identities using public data and a handful of heuristics — against users who were already generating a fresh address per payment, which is the practice the account model discourages.

Ethereum hands over by design what that research had to reconstruct.

Why the account model makes this worse, specifically

The previous page listed privacy as one cost of choosing accounts. Here is the mechanism.

Bitcoin wallets generate a new address for each payment, so one user's activity is scattered across many unlinked labels, and linking them is the work those researchers had to do.

Ethereum pushes the other way. An address is a persistent place — where your token balances live, where a name points, where a contract expects to find you, where a lending position is recorded. Reusing it isn't carelessness, it's what the model is for.

So the same property that makes undercollateralised lending and reputation conceivable makes surveillance straightforward. They are one fact seen from two sides, which is why this page sits where it does rather than in a section of its own.

docs.title: Why you can't simply hide the amounts
docs.text:
The obvious fix is to encrypt the sensitive parts and leave the rest. It fails immediately, and the reason is worth following.

A node validating a transfer must establish that the sender's balance covers it. If the balance is hidden, the node cannot do that — so it would have to take somebody's word, which is precisely the thing the design exists to avoid. Hiding data from the verifier doesn't make the system private; it makes it trusted.

So confidentiality here can't be a matter of withholding information. The node still has to end up convinced. What it needs is a way to be convinced without being shown — and that is a real technique, usually called a zero-knowledge proof.

The everyday version: proving you are over eighteen without disclosing your date of birth. The bouncer needs certainty, not your birthday, and the two are separable. Or a bank's letter saying this customer can cover £5,000 — the recipient learns what they need and not the balance. The difference with a zero-knowledge proof is that nobody has to trust the bank: the argument itself is checkable, and checking it reveals nothing beyond the fact it was valid.

Applied here, a transaction would carry a proof that the sender's balance covered this amount and the arithmetic was done correctly, which a node could verify without learning any balance at all. The verification still happens. What's removed is the node's need to see.

That is an active field rather than a finished one, and it's a different design from the one this site describes. The point for now is just this: "hide the amounts" is not a small change. It changes what checking means.

docs.title: What the transparency buys
docs.text:
Worth stating plainly before the costs, because it is easy to forget that this side exists.

You can audit the whole thing yourself. Total supply, who holds what, whether a contract actually has the reserves it claims — all checkable by anybody with a node, without asking permission and without anyone's cooperation. There is no equivalent for a bank, a payment network, or a company's internal ledger.

You can prove a specific fact compactly. "This address held this much at this block" is a short proof against the state root, as the state page described. Verifiable without handing over the rest.

And bugs are findable by outsiders. A contract holding money with a flaw in it can be examined by anyone, which is why serious problems are often found by people with no relationship to the project.

That combination — universal auditability with no gatekeeper — is genuinely unusual, and it is what the privacy cost is buying.

docs.title: Who it costs, and how
docs.text:
The costs are specific, and they fall unevenly.

Anyone paid on-chain. A salary paid to an address publishes that salary — to colleagues, to counterparties, to anyone who learns the address. Most employment arrangements assume this information is private, and most legal systems treat it as such.

Any business. Counterparties, volumes, margins and timing are visible to competitors. Ordinary commercial confidentiality simply isn't available.

Anyone whose address becomes known, which is most people eventually. And the exposure is retroactive: it isn't "from now on, my transactions are public", it's "everything I have ever done is now public, including from before I had any reason to be careful".

That retroactivity is what makes this different from ordinary data protection, and it deserves its own statement:

Published data cannot be unpublished. A privacy technique adopted tomorrow does nothing about the record already written.

Every other privacy regime assumes some ability to delete, restrict or expire. Here there is none, by construction — the data's permanence is the same property that makes the chain's history trustworthy.

docs.title: The mitigations, as classes
docs.text:
Four approaches exist. Naming them as classes rather than products is deliberate: specific tools on this subject date quickly, and some carry legal context this site is not the place to summarise.

Use a fresh address per purpose. Effective and cheap, and the account model fights it — you lose the accumulated balances, names and positions that made the address useful. Works for receiving, poorly for anything persistent.

Pool with others, so that which participant did what is no longer determinable from the chain alone. The classic approach, and the one whose legal treatment varies most by jurisdiction.

Move the activity off the main chain, so only summaries are published. Reduces what is visible without changing what the main chain does with what it does see.

Prove rather than reveal. Attach a zero-knowledge proof instead of the data, so a node can confirm the rules were followed without learning the amounts — the over-eighteen trick above, applied to balances. The most promising of the four and the least finished.

Each is a different point on the same dial, and none of them moves the dial for the record you have already written.

docs.title: So is Ethereum private?
docs.text:
The question is badly formed, and that's worth saying rather than answering it.

"Private" suggests a property the system either has or lacks. What actually exists is a set of specific answerable questions: what can be inferred, about whom, by whom, and for how long? On Ethereum the answers are roughly everything financial, about anybody whose address is known, by anyone at all, for ever.

Which is a defensible arrangement and an extreme one. Economic treatments of privacy describe disclosure as a trade rather than a good: it creates value by letting people verify and enforce things, and destroys value by exposing people to anyone who would use the information against them (Acquisti et al., 2016).

So there is no amount of disclosure that is simply correct. It depends who ends up holding the information, and what they want it for — your salary disclosed to a tax authority and your salary disclosed to a burglar are the same fact with opposite consequences. Which is why the question is never "how private is this?" but "visible to whom, and what can they do with it?". Regulated markets spend enormous effort tuning that trade: what must be disclosed, to whom, in what detail, and — crucially — after what delay.

Ethereum has no tuning. There is no "disclose to regulators only", no "publish after ninety days", no "aggregate figures but not individual positions". The dial is welded at one end, and the weld is what makes the verification work.

So the honest summary is not that Ethereum is private, or that it isn't. It's that Ethereum made a policy choice structurally, where everyone else makes it adjustably — and bought something real with it.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Verifiability and privacy are the same dial. Nodes can check everything because they can see everything; the site's central claim has transparency as its precondition.
  • Public: every balance, every transaction including failed ones, every contract's code and every value in its storage — private in source code restrains other contracts, not people. Plus your intentions briefly, while a transaction waits in the mempool.
  • Not public: your private key. The protocol hides what grants control and publishes the rest.
  • Ethereum is pseudonymous, which is weaker than it sounds: a pseudonym accumulates a permanent record, and one link to the real world reveals that record backwards.
  • Clustering chain activity into identities has been demonstrated against users who were rotating addresses (Meiklejohn et al., 2013). Ethereum discourages rotating them.
  • "Just hide the amounts" isn't a small change. A verifier that can't read a balance must trust someone. Confidentiality therefore needs a zero-knowledge proof — convincing the node without showing it, the way you can prove you're over eighteen without giving your birthday. The checking still happens; the seeing doesn't.
  • What it buys: universal auditability with no gatekeeper, compact proofs of specific facts, and bugs findable by outsiders.
  • What it costs falls on anyone paid on-chain, any business, and anyone whose address becomes known — retroactively, which no other privacy regime assumes.
  • Published data cannot be unpublished. No mitigation helps the record already written.
  • "Is Ethereum private?" is the wrong question. What can be inferred, about whom, by whom, for how long — and the answers are everything financial, anybody known, anyone at all, for ever.

Next: What a smart contract is — the second kind of account, and what its code can and cannot see.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Acquisti, A., Taylor, C., & Wagman, L. (2016). The economics of privacy. Journal of Economic Literature, 54(2), 442–492. Surveys privacy as a trade rather than a good — disclosure enabling verification and enforcement while exposing the disclosed — which is the frame this page applies to a system that resolved the trade structurally. https://doi.org/10.1257/jel.54.2.442
  • Meiklejohn, S., Pomarole, M., Jordan, G., Levchenko, K., McCoy, D., Voelker, G. M., & Savage, S. (2013). A fistful of bitcoins: Characterizing payments among men with no names. Proceedings of the 2013 Internet Measurement Conference, 127–140. Clusters public chain activity into real-world identities using heuristics alone, against users who were already generating a fresh address per payment. https://doi.org/10.1145/2504730.2504747

docs.title: Why accounts, and what they cost
docs.text:
Permanent. Accounts were chosen before Ethereum launched in 2015 and the decision has never been reopened, so the costs described below are permanent ones. Work on reducing those costs is still going on, which is why the last section describes general approaches rather than naming particular proposals.

The account model

Recording value as balances against persistent addresses, rather than as individually spendable units that are consumed when spent.

Bitcoin does the latter: a payment destroys specific coins and creates new ones. Ethereum does the former: a payment edits two numbers, and the accounts they belong to go on existing, untouched in every other respect. The specification puts it as a mapping from addresses to accounts (Wood, 2014) — a mapping, with entries that persist, rather than a set of items that get used up.

Everything on this page follows from that one difference.

docs.title: One property, and a long invoice
docs.text:
The previous three pages described the account model. This one argues it, because it was a choice and it cost real things.

Here is the whole argument in a sentence: persistence buys programmability, and everything awkward about Ethereum is the invoice.

accounts persistWHAT IT BUYSWHAT IT COSTSprograms can exist at alla lasting identitycomposabilityorder starts to matterthe state only growsparallel execution is hardyou must hold ether to actThe two columns are not separate lists. They are the same property, readtwice.

That last line is the thing to hold on to. The costs aren't flaws that happen to sit beside the benefits — they are the benefits, described by someone who didn't want them.

docs.title: Programs need somewhere to live
docs.text:
This is the one that justifies everything else, and it's worth stating starkly: Bitcoin cannot hold a program, and no amount of engineering would let it. Not because its scripting language is limited — because there is nowhere for a program to be.

A coin is consumed when spent. It has no address, no permanence, nothing you could send a second message to. A program needs to exist between the times it's used: somewhere to keep its code, somewhere to keep what it remembers, and a name people can reach it at.

An account is exactly that. It has an address that never changes, a codeHash for the program and a storageRoot for what the program remembers — the four fields the accounts page listed. So contracts aren't an addition to the account model, they're a consequence of it. The state machine page said Bitcoin lets you agree on who owns what while Ethereum lets you agree on what a program computed. This is why that's possible.

docs.title: A lasting identity
docs.text:
Because an address persists and accumulates, things can be attached to it: a name, token balances, a borrowing position, a voting record, a reputation. None of that is a feature anybody built into the protocol. It's a side effect of having somewhere durable to write.

Which is also the privacy cost, seen from the other side. They are not two facts. An address that accumulates a history is simultaneously what makes undercollateralised lending conceivable and what makes surveillance straightforward, and any page presenting those as separate items is hiding the trade.

docs.title: Composability
docs.text:
Contracts can hold balances, including balances of things other contracts define, and can call each other. That works because accounts are addressable and survive between transactions — a contract can be pointed at, and will still be there next block.

Most of what gets described as innovation on Ethereum is this: existing pieces addressed and combined. It needs persistent, nameable places to compose, which is the account model again.

docs.title: Order starts to matter
docs.text:
Two Bitcoin transactions spending different coins are independent. Neither refers to anything the other touches, so their order is arbitrary.

Two transactions from one Ethereum account are a sequence. Each depends on the balance and the counter the other leaves behind, so "which came first" is a question with a required answer. That's why the nonce exists, and why one underpriced transaction blocks every later one from the same account — a problem with no UTXO equivalent, because UTXO transactions were never in a queue to begin with.

docs.title: The state only grows
docs.text:
A UTXO is destroyed when spent: the set shrinks as well as grows, and it stays roughly proportional to money actually in use. An account persists whatever happens to it. Balance at zero, contract abandoned, key lost years ago — the entry stays, because the protocol has no notion of state going out of date.

So the state rises monotonically, every node stores all of it, and the cost of running one rises forever. The only deletion mechanism Ethereum has ever had is the narrow cleanup of genuinely empty accounts.

docs.title: Parallel execution is hard
docs.text:
If transactions name the coins they spend, a client can look at two of them, see they touch nothing in common, and safely run them at once. The independence is visible in the transaction itself.

Account transactions don't declare what they'll touch. A call to a contract may read or write anything that contract can reach, which is only known once it runs. So the safe default is one at a time, in order — and every scheme for executing Ethereum transactions in parallel is an attempt to recover information the UTXO model gives away for free.

docs.title: Privacy is the default casualty
docs.text:
Bitcoin wallets generate a fresh address for each payment, so a user's activity is spread across many unlinked addresses. Ethereum does the opposite: address reuse is universal and necessary, because contracts, token balances and names all need an address that stays put.

The consequence is that one address is one linkable history, permanently and publicly. And this isn't theoretical even in the system that does use fresh addresses — Meiklejohn et al. (2013) showed Bitcoin activity could be clustered into real identities using heuristics over the public chain, against users who were changing addresses. Ethereum hands over, by design, what those researchers had to work to reconstruct.

This is the loose end the public keys page left: the old advice against reusing an address had substance, and Ethereum spent it deliberately for a stable identifier.

docs.title: You must hold ether to act
docs.text:
A Bitcoin fee comes out of the inputs being spent — it's the difference between what goes in and what comes out, so paying is part of the payment.

An account has no inputs to shave. The fee comes from the sender's ether balance, which means holding a thing is not enough to be able to move it. An account with a million in tokens and no ether can receive anything and send nothing, exactly as the ether page described. Entire mechanisms exist to work around this, letting a third party pay on your behalf, and all of them are compensating for a cost the account model introduced.

And anyone can make every node store more

A smaller cost, worth knowing because it shows the shape of the problem.

Creating an account needs no key and no permission: send one wei to an untouched address and an entry appears. So the state isn't only your liability — it's a public resource any stranger can enlarge, cheaply, for everybody.

Early Ethereum was exploited this way until EIP-161 cleared out entries left genuinely empty, which the accounts page covers. That was the first patch on this, and the fact that a patch was needed at all is the tell.

docs.title: What it quietly avoids
docs.text:
Less obvious, and the honest accounting requires it: several things are simply absent from Ethereum because of this choice, and their absence is why nobody notices them.

  • No dust. A tiny UTXO becomes unspendable once the fee to move it exceeds its value — real money, permanently stranded in fragments. A balance is one number, so no part of it can be too small to use.
  • No coin selection. Bitcoin wallets run algorithms to decide which coins to spend, trading off fees, privacy and future flexibility. Ethereum wallets contain no such code, because there is nothing to select.
  • No change. No change outputs, no change addresses, and none of the machinery or confusion they generate.
  • Constant-size transfers. A Bitcoin transaction grows with its input count, so consolidating many small coins is expensive precisely when you can least afford it. An Ethereum transfer is the same size whatever the balance behind it.
  • Cheap balance proofs. "This address holds this much" is a short proof against the state root. Bitcoin's headers commit to no equivalent set, so a light client cannot be handed a compact proof of someone's balance at all.

Notice that three of those five are ordinary users not losing money to something they'd never have understood. That belongs in the ledger as much as the costs do.

docs.title: The bill nobody has paid yet
docs.text:
The sharpest version of all this is not technical, and it's where the account model's real unsettled problem lives.

You pay once to write state. Every node then stores it forever.

A one-time fee against a perpetual liability. The payment is made by one party, at one moment, at a price set by a fee market concerned with present congestion — while the cost falls on thousands of operators who were not consulted, cannot refuse, cannot charge for it, and will carry it indefinitely.

You have already met the far end of this. Running one yourself described the disk requirement as the thing that rules machines out, and as something that only ever rises — that is this externality, arriving as a shopping constraint. The two are one fact: what looks like a hardware problem to an operator is a pricing problem to the protocol.

That's a textbook externality, and the classic description of what follows is Hardin's (1968): a resource nobody owns, which each user is individually rational to consume and collectively ruinous to exhaust. It reframes state growth from an engineering nuisance into a pricing failure — and that reframing matters, because it tells you no amount of faster disks fixes it. Cheaper storage changes the rate. It doesn't change the sign.

The protocol does have one crude lever: it refunds gas when you clear storage, paying you a little to shrink the state. The refunds have been reduced over time because they were gameable, and they only ever applied to people willing to delete their own data. Nothing addresses the general case.

The genuine responses fall into three classes — named as classes, not products, because which of them ships is exactly what this site doesn't try to predict:

  • Rent. Charge for occupied state over time, so a perpetual cost meets a perpetual payment.
  • Expiry. Let state untouched for long enough fall out of what nodes must keep, with some way to revive it.
  • Statelessness. Arrange that validators don't need the state to validate, which doesn't shrink it but moves who must hold it.

None has shipped. All three have been argued over for years. The problem is permanent; the solutions are plans — and that distinction is the whole reason this page is fork-proof and the gas-costs page is not.

History: the trade as the designers saw it

Worth reading how this was argued before the consequences were known, because it was not presented as obvious.

Ethereum's white paper (Buterin, 2014) sets the two models against each other and credits the UTXO side with real advantages — privacy, a degree of parallelism, and simpler proofs for light clients checking payments. The case for accounts was made on space savings, fungibility, and simplicity for developers.

Which reads, a decade on, like an understatement of what was being bought and an underestimate of what was being spent. The white paper's list doesn't mention state growth, because nobody had a large state yet.

That's not a criticism. It's the ordinary condition of design decisions: the benefits are visible at the time and the bills arrive later. Worth knowing it was a judgement call rather than a discovery.

docs.title: The two models side by side
docs.text:
Prose first, because a table alone reads as a scorecard and this is a trade:

Coins (Bitcoin) Accounts (Ethereum) A payment destroys units, creates new ones edits two numbers Can hold a program no — nothing persists to hold it yes Replay protection the coin is already spent a nonce must be added Transaction order arbitrary between independent payments a strict sequence per account Data held by nodes grows and shrinks with use grows only Parallel execution independence is visible must be inferred Privacy by default fresh address per payment one address, one history Paying the fee out of what you're spending from a separate ether balance Stranded small amounts dust is a real problem cannot occur Proving a balance no committed set to prove against short proof against the state root

docs.title: So was it the right call?
docs.text:
The honest answer is that the question is badly formed, because the two systems are no longer trying to do the same thing.

If Ethereum were a payment network, this trade would look poor: it gave up privacy and bounded storage to gain programmability it wouldn't need. But the programmability is what Ethereum is. Judging the account model against Bitcoin's purposes is like judging a database against a receipt.

What can be said firmly is narrower and more useful:

  • The benefit was real and unobtainable otherwise. No clever scripting gets you contracts without persistence.
  • The costs were real and mostly unforeseen in their eventual size, state growth above all.
  • The one that remains genuinely unsolved is the pricing of permanent storage, not any of the engineering.

Which is a reasonable thing to know about any system you rely on: not whether it was built correctly, but which of its bills are still outstanding.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The account model records balances against persistent addresses instead of consuming individual units. Everything else follows from that.
  • Persistence is what makes programs possible. A coin is destroyed when spent, so there is nowhere for code or memory to live. Contracts are a consequence of accounts, not an addition to them.
  • The same persistence gives a lasting identity — which is why names, token balances and lending positions work, and why privacy is the default casualty. One property, not two.
  • It makes order matter, hence the nonce and head-of-line blocking; makes parallel execution hard, since transactions don't declare what they'll touch; and requires you to hold ether to move anything at all.
  • It also silently removes dust, coin selection, change addresses and transaction sizes that grow with your history — three of which are users not losing money.
  • The unsolved problem is pricing, not engineering: you pay once to write state and every node stores it forever, which is an externality rather than a nuisance. Faster disks change the rate, not the sign.
  • Responses divide into rent, expiry and statelessness. None has shipped. The problem is permanent; the solutions are plans.
  • It was a judgement call, argued at the time with UTXO's advantages acknowledged, and its largest cost unforeseen.

Next: What it reveals — the cost this page listed in one line, which deserves rather more than that.

  • Hardin, G. (1968). The tragedy of the commons. Science, 162(3859), 1243–1248. The standard treatment of a resource that is individually rational to consume and collectively ruinous to exhaust — the shape of the state-growth problem, which is a pricing failure rather than a technical one. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.162.3859.1243

The header field list has grown at several forks: baseFeePerGas in London, withdrawalsRoot in Shanghai, blob fields and the parent beacon block root in Cancun. Write this page from the current specification, not from any secondary source including this outline.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• What is in a header, and what does each field commit to?
  • Which fields are roots, and what does each one fingerprint? (State, transactions, receipts, withdrawals.)
  • Why is the header so small, when it commits to so much? (Because the roots do the work — see the Merkle Patricia Trie.)
  • Which fields are vestigial, kept only for compatibility after the switch to Proof of Stake?
  • Which fields exist because of a specific fork, and what problem did each solve?

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• Take a real header apart field by field, reusing the RLP decoder built for that page and the self-proving trick from transactions: hash the header bytes and show the result is the block hash everybody quotes. That demonstrates in one step what the page argues in prose — that a few hundred bytes commit to the whole block.

  • This is the most fork-volatile page on the site. Date-stamp it clearly and expect to revisit it after every upgrade.

  • The vestigial fields are genuinely interesting — difficulty and nonce survive as fixed values, which tells a small story about how upgrades preserve compatibility. Good candidate for a ??? info "History" box.
  • One table, one row per field, with a "why it exists" column. That column is what makes this teaching material rather than a spec dump.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• What is a block? (A batch of transactions, plus the metadata needed to place it in the chain.)
  • Why batch at all, rather than processing transactions one at a time? (Agreement is expensive: agreeing once per batch amortises it. Also connects to why state is recorded per block.)
  • How are blocks linked? (Each names the hash of its parent — which is what makes rewriting history expensive.)
  • Who decides what goes in a block, and in what order? (A proposer, with wide discretion. The consequences of that discretion are an economics question — see MEV.)
  • What limits a block's size? (A gas limit, not a byte limit — the constraint is work, not space.)
  • What's the difference between a block being produced and being final?

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• Keep this page structural. Who proposes and why they're trusted is consensus, and it comes later.
  • "Linked by parent hash" is the whole of why a chain is hard to rewrite. Give it room — it's one idea that pays for itself repeatedly.
  • The gas-limit-not-byte-limit point surprises people and is worth stating plainly.

Next: The block header

docs.title: Proof of stake
docs.text:
Stub — not written yet

This page is an outline. Delete this box when you fill it in.

Current as of: (fill in the fork and date)

Nearly every number on this page is a parameter a fork can change — the amount a validator stakes, slot and epoch timings, committee sizes, reward and penalty rates. Give each one the date it was true and the source it came from. The requirement this mechanism satisfies is on the previous page and does not move.

Expect this page to need revisiting. It is the most fork-dependent page on the site after gas costs.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• What is a validator, as distinct from a node? (The node page draws the line: a validator is a node plus a paid job. Restate it, because this is where the job gets described.)
  • What does staking actually mean? (Locking ether as a deposit that can be reduced. Not a payment, not a purchase — collateral, which is why the previous page's "something to lose" requirement is met.)
  • What are the two jobs? (Proposing a block when it's your turn, and attesting — voting that somebody else's block looks valid. Almost all of a validator's work is the second, which surprises people.)
  • How is the proposer chosen? (Pseudorandomly, in proportion to stake, from the active set. The why is the previous page; the how and its parameters belong here with a date.)
  • What is a slot, and an epoch? (The timing structure that turns "eventually" into a schedule — and the reason "when it's settled" is answerable at all.)
  • What is finality, precisely, and how does it differ from "confirmed"? (The sharpest thing on the page. A block can be in the chain and still be revertible; finality is the point at which reverting it would require destroying an enormous amount of staked value. Set up carefully, because the chain and reorgs depends on it.)
  • What is the difference between being offline and being dishonest? (Offline leaks a little stake slowly; equivocating — signing two conflicting things — is slashing, and costs a large amount at once. The asymmetry is deliberate and worth explaining: carelessness should be survivable, contradiction should not.)
  • Can you get your stake back? (Yes, with exit and withdrawal mechanics — which did not exist at first and were added later. Good history-box material.)
  • What does this cost the network, as opposed to the validator? (Issuance: new ether paid to validators. Hand straight to why security has to be paid for, which is the page that treats it as an economic question.)

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• The why belongs on the previous page. If this page starts arguing that somebody must be chosen, the split has failed. This page answers how, with dates.
  • Finality is the payload. Everything else here is machinery; finality is the thing a reader actually needs, because it's what makes "is my transaction settled?" a question with an answer. Give it room and keep it honest — including that finality is economic rather than absolute.
  • Explain why attesting dominates: thousands of validators voting on each block is what makes the chain's history expensive to rewrite, and a reader who thinks proposing is the main job has the mechanism upside down.
  • No client names, no validator counts, no yield figures. All three date within months, and a yield figure in particular invites being read as advice.
  • Resist explaining reorgs — the next page. Resist explaining the fee market — that's fees. This page is selection, voting and penalties.
  • History box worth having: proof of stake ran as a separate chain for nearly two years before being connected in 2022, which is the clearest way to explain why Ethereum has two layers at all. Ties to clients and the two layers.
  • The comparison with proof of work goes here, not on the previous page, because what each costs and who it favours are empirical claims that age.

Next: The chain and reorgs — why the recent tip is less certain than what came before.

docs.title: Why somebody has to be chosen
docs.text:
Stub — not written yet

This page is an outline. Delete this box when you fill it in.

Permanent. The requirement follows from the design and from arithmetic. How Ethereum currently satisfies it is the next page, and that one carries a date.

docs.title: The thesis this page exists to argue
docs.text:
Determinism does not pick an order. It only guarantees that given an order, everybody computes the same result — which the node page showed as three machines reaching one state root without consulting each other.

But transactions arrive at different nodes in different orders, and nothing in the rules says which order is right. So the ordering has to come from somewhere outside the rules: somebody proposes, everybody else checks. That role then has to be paid, has to be costly to obtain, and has to carry a penalty — and each of those three follows from a problem, not from a preference.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• Why is an order needed at all? (Two transactions spending the same balance are each individually valid; only their sequence makes one of them fail. The nonce page established that accounts make order matter — this is the network-level consequence.)
  • Why can't nodes work the order out among themselves by a rule? (The obvious rule is "by timestamp", and there is no shared clock — the same objection the accounts page raises against self-starting code. Any rule needing agreement about when is a rule needing the thing it's trying to produce.)
  • So why not just let anybody propose whenever? (Then everybody proposes, and the network has thousands of candidate orderings and no way to choose. Proposal has to be a scarce right.)
  • Why must the role be paid? (It costs hardware, bandwidth and attention. An unpaid role gets filled by whoever has a motive other than payment — which is a worse set of people than those who want the money.)
  • Why must the right to propose be expensive to acquire? (If it's free, acquiring a majority of it is free. Any scheme where identities are cheap can be swamped by one party pretending to be many — the problem that makes naive voting useless here. Name the problem; don't dress it up.)
  • And why penalties rather than only rewards? (With rewards alone, misbehaving costs nothing but a forgone bonus. For a proposer to be deterrable, there has to be something they already hold that can be taken.)
  • Why can't users vote? (Voting needs a register of who counts as a user, which is precisely what a system with no identities cannot have. Every answer to "who votes" is an answer to "who is in charge".)
  • What, then, is the irreducible requirement? (A scarce, verifiable, costly claim to the right to propose, with something at stake behind it. Proof of work and proof of stake are two ways of meeting it; the requirement is older than either.)

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• This is the mechanism-design page, and Davide's own field — write it as an argument in the register of why accounts, and let him pick the outside frame rather than choosing one for him. The obvious candidates are the literature on costly signalling and on Sybil-resistance.
  • Keep proof of stake out of it entirely. The test of whether this page works: every sentence should still be true if Ethereum changed consensus mechanism tomorrow. That is what makes it permanent while the next page isn't.
  • The two strongest hooks already exist elsewhere on the site and should be used: there is no shared clock (accounts), and order matters because accounts make it matter (nonce). This page is the point where those two converge.
  • Worth a history box on the Byzantine-generals framing — the problem of agreeing on one order among parties who can't be assumed honest predates cryptocurrency by decades. Verify the citation properly before using it; it's the kind of reference that gets attributed loosely.
  • Don't let this become "proof of work versus proof of stake". The comparison is interesting and belongs on the next page, where it can be dated.

Next: Proof of stake — how Ethereum meets that requirement now.

docs.title: Events and logs
docs.text:
Permanent. The structure of logs, and the rule that contracts cannot read them, have not changed since 2015.

Log

A record a contract writes for the outside world, attached to a transaction's result rather than to the state.

It holds the address that emitted it, up to four 32-byte topics meant for searching, and a lump of data of any length.

A contract can emit one and can never read one — not another contract's, not even its own.

docs.title: One thing a contract cannot read back
docs.text:
Everything else a contract touches, it touches both ways. It writes storage and reads storage. It sends ether and reads its own balance. It calls another contract and receives what that call returned.

Logs are the single exception, and the Solidity documentation states it flatly: "The Log and its event data is not accessible from within contracts (not even from the contract that created them)" (Solidity documentation, v0.8.26).

So a contract can speak and cannot listen. Whatever it emits is gone, as far as it is concerned — written down somewhere it has no access to.

That asymmetry is the design, not a limitation of it. Everything else on this page follows from it, including the price.

docs.title: Why the rule exists
docs.text:
Work backwards from what reading logs would require.

If a contract's behaviour could depend on a log, then every node would have to keep every log forever — because any call might consult one, and a node that had discarded old logs could no longer compute the same answer as a node that hadn't. Logs would become part of the state in all but name: permanent, universally replicated, and necessary for execution.

That is precisely the cost the design refuses. Keeping logs outside execution means a node needs none of them in order to validate a block. It can store them, serve them, prune them, or never keep them at all, and its ability to check the chain is unaffected.

Which is why pruning is possible, and why the three sizes of node on the state page differ in history without differing in what they can verify. Logs are on the discardable side of that line, and a contract being able to read them would have moved them.

docs.title: Event or log?
docs.text:
The two words are used interchangeably and mean different things, one level apart. Worth taking slowly, because the difference is the same one the previous page was about.

A log is what exists. An address, up to four topics, and some data. Bytes in a block. That is the whole of it, and it is all the protocol knows.

An event is a declaration in source code — a description, written by the contract's author, of a log they intend to emit. In Solidity it looks roughly like this:

event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value)

That line creates nothing and costs nothing. It is a schema: it names three fields, says what type each is, and marks which of them should be searchable. Then, somewhere in the contract's code, the author emits a Transfer with actual values, and the compiler turns that into the instruction that writes a log.

docs.title: What the compiler does with it
docs.text:
The declaration decides how the log is laid out. Emitting the event above produces:

topic 0    keccak256("Transfer(address,address,uint256)")
topic 1    the "from" address          ← indexed, so it became a topic
topic 2    the "to" address            ← indexed, so it became a topic
data       the value                   ← not indexed, so it went in the data

Two things to notice there.

The first topic is the event's identity — the Keccak hash of its name and argument types. That is what makes "find every Transfer" a question anybody can ask, and it is the same trick as the four-byte function selector, taken at full 32-byte length instead of truncated.

And the names are gone. from, to and value appear nowhere in the log. What survives is three values in fixed positions. The meaning lives in the positions, and the positions only mean something to somebody who has the declaration.

docs.title: Which is the previous page's problem again
docs.text:
A log on its own is an address and four 32-byte blobs. To read it as "this address sent that address this much", you need the event declaration — and the declaration is source code, kept off-chain by people, exactly like everything else on the previous page.

So the division is consistent all the way down:

What it is Where it lives Event a declaration naming the fields source code, off-chain Log the bytes that result in a block, on every node that kept it

The protocol has never heard of events, in precisely the way it has never heard of Solidity or of functions. A log is bytes with meaning attached by convention — the same arrangement as the ABI, and as RLP, where position carries the meaning and nothing in the encoding says what the positions are for.

docs.title: Why they are cheap
docs.text:
Because nothing has to be able to find them later.

A storage slot is expensive for a reason the why accounts page set out: writing one obliges every node to hold that value, indefinitely, available for instant lookup during execution. You pay once and the network carries it forever.

A log imposes none of that. It is never read by the machine, so no node is required to keep it retrievable, and nothing breaks if every node forgets it. The price reflects exactly that — which makes logs the clearest case on this site of cost following structure. Storage is dear because of what it commits others to; logs are cheap because they commit others to nothing.

So the practical advice follows from the mechanism rather than from folklore: if only humans and software outside Ethereum will ever need a value, emit it rather than storing it. Storing it would be buying a guarantee nobody needs.

docs.title: Finding one among millions of blocks
docs.text:
Here is the problem logs create. They are cheap to write, so there are an enormous number of them, scattered across every block ever made — and the natural question is always "show me every log from this contract", which sounds like reading everything.

The trick is in each block header, and it is the neatest piece of machinery in this part of the site.

logsBloom · 256 bytes in every block headerlooking for X: all three positions set — might be here. Open the block.looking for Y: one position clear — certainly not here. Skip it.A no is always right. A yes only means maybe — and that asymmetry is the wholevalue, because almost every block gets a no.

Every block header carries a bloom filter — 256 bytes summarising every address and topic in that block's logs (Wood, 2014). It does not record what is there. It records enough to answer one question: could this block contain a log matching what I'm after?

And the answer comes in two strengths:

  • No — definitive. The block cannot contain it, and there is no need to look.
  • Yes — provisional. It might, and you now have to open the block and check properly.

The lopsidedness is the point. A structure that can be certain in only one direction sounds like a poor one, until you notice which direction gets used: a searcher looking for one contract's logs gets a confident no from almost every block in history, and needs to read only the handful that said maybe. The occasional false maybe costs one wasted look. Nothing is ever missed, because a no is never wrong.

Why it can be wrong in one direction and not the other

The mechanism in one paragraph, without the arithmetic.

Each address and topic is hashed, and the hash is used to pick a few fixed positions out of the 2048 available. Those positions are set to 1. To test for something, compute its positions and look: if any of them is 0, the thing was definitely never added, because adding it would have set that position.

The gap is that positions are shared. Enough other entries can collectively set every position your item would have set, so a yes may be coincidence. There is no way to tell the difference from the filter alone — hence maybe.

So the error is one-directional by construction, not by luck: bits are only ever turned on, so a missing bit is proof of absence and a present bit is merely consistent with presence.

docs.title: What topics are for
docs.text:
Topics are the searchable part. Everything in a log's data is invisible to the filter and to any index; only the address and the topics can be searched on.

The first topic is conventionally the hash of the event's signature — the same Keccak trick as a function selector, except taken at full length rather than truncated to four bytes. That is what lets a searcher say "find me every transfer" rather than "find me every log from this contract and then read them all".

Solidity lets you mark up to three further parameters as indexed, which become the remaining topics. Everything else goes into the data, where it can be read once you have the log but cannot be used to find it.

The limit is a cost decision. Indexing is what makes searching cheap for everybody else, so it is rationed — and the choice of what to index is a genuine design decision made once, at writing time, by somebody guessing what people will later want to search for.

docs.title: What logs are not
docs.text:
The closing caution, and the reason to be careful using them as data.

A contract can do something and announce nothing. Emitting a log is a choice its author made, line by line. There is no rule that state changes must be announced, and no way to tell from the outside whether something happened quietly.

So the honest description is uncomfortable but exact:

Logs look like a record of events. They are a record of announcements.

Which is the same warning the previous page reached from the other direction, and the reason the smart contracts page lists three ways of counting a contract's use that disagree. If you are measuring activity from logs, you are measuring what authors chose to publish — a reasonable proxy, and not the thing itself.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A log is a record a contract writes for the outside world: an emitting address, up to four 32-byte topics, and data of any length.
  • A contract can emit a log and can never read one — not another's, not its own. That asymmetry is the design.
  • The reason: if execution could depend on logs, every node would have to keep every log forever. Keeping them outside execution means a node needs none of them to validate a block, which is what makes pruning possible.
  • An event is a declaration in source code — a schema naming the fields and marking which are searchable. A log is the bytes that result. The protocol has never heard of events.
  • The declaration decides the layout: topic zero is the hash of the event's name and argument types, indexed fields become the remaining topics, and the rest goes in the data.
  • The field names never reach the log. Reading one as anything but blobs requires the declaration, which is off-chain source — the previous page's problem exactly.
  • Logs are cheap because they commit nobody to anything. Storage is dear because it obliges every node to hold a value retrievably, forever. Cost follows structure.
  • So: if only software outside Ethereum will need a value, emit it rather than storing it.
  • Each block header holds a bloom filter, 256 bytes, that answers could this block hold this log? — definitively no, or provisionally yes. Almost every block answers no, which is what makes searching practical.
  • The one-sided error is structural: bits are only ever turned on, so a missing bit proves absence while a present bit is merely consistent with presence.
  • Only the address and topics are searchable; data can be read but not found. Topic zero is conventionally the hash of the event signature.
  • Logs record announcements, not events. A contract can act and say nothing, so activity measured from logs is what authors chose to publish.

Next: Tokens aren't special — what you actually own when you own one.

docs.text:

States that up to three parameters may be indexed, that the hash of the event signature is one of the topics unless the event is anonymous, and that a log and its data are not accessible from within contracts, including the contract that created them.
