Defines the log entry, the receipt it travels in, and the 2048-bit bloom filter carried in the block header as the union of the blooms of that block's receipts. https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf

docs.title: What a smart contract is
docs.text:
Permanent. What a contract is follows from accounts and hasn't changed since 2015. What it costs to run, and which operations exist, are fork-dependent and belong to later pages.

Smart contract

A program stored at an account, under the codeHash field the accounts page described.

It runs only when something calls it, it runs identically on every node, and it can reach nothing outside Ethereum. Those three constraints are not limitations of the current implementation — they are what make it work at all.

docs.title: Neither smart nor a contract
docs.text:
The name is the first obstacle, and worth clearing before anything else, because most people meet the term years before the mechanism.

It isn't smart. There is no judgement in it, no interpretation, no capacity to notice that something has gone wrong. It does exactly what its code says, including when the code says something its author didn't mean. A contract cannot be reasoned with, cannot be asked what it intended, and has no way to behave sensibly in a situation nobody wrote down.

It isn't a contract. There are no parties, no offer and acceptance, no consideration, no court, no remedy. The word imports a set of expectations from law that are all false here: that intent matters, that ambiguity gets resolved reasonably, that breach has consequences someone will impose. None of that exists. There is a program, and it runs.

The term is older than Ethereum by about two decades. Szabo (1997) used it for embedding contractual terms into hardware and software so that breaking them becomes impractical rather than merely actionable — a vending machine being the primitive ancestor, enforcing payment, then goods with no lawyer involved. Ethereum's contracts are related to that idea and narrower than it. They don't enforce agreements. They execute.

Keep the word, since everybody uses it. Just don't let it do any reasoning for you.

docs.title: What it actually is
docs.text:
Go back to the four fields. A contract account has the same ones as any other: nonce, balance, storageRoot, codeHash. What makes it a contract is simply that codeHash isn't the empty constant — there is code, so the account is controlled by that code rather than by any key.

A contract is therefore not a special kind of object. It's an account with a program attached, which is why it can hold ether, receive transactions, and be looked up exactly like a wallet account. That was the point of choosing accounts in the first place — Buterin (2014) presents contracts as what the model is for, rather than as something built on top of it.

Two consequences people find surprising, both established earlier:

Nobody holds its keys, because there are none. Control is the code, and the code is public.

It cannot act on its own. The accounts page argued this at length: no timers, no scheduled jobs, no thread of its own. A contract is inert between calls, and everything that looks automatic is somebody being paid to send a transaction.

docs.title: How it gets there
docs.text:
A contract is created by a transaction carrying code instead of a recipient — a deployment. Once that transaction is included, the code is written to an account and stays there.

The address is computed, not chosen. It comes from the creating account's address and that account's nonce, hashed together (Wood, 2014) — which is why a contract's nonce counts deployments rather than transactions, and why two deployments from one account can never collide.

A useful consequence: you can know the address before the contract exists. Deployment is predictable, so ether can be sent to, or code written referring to, an address that will only be occupied later. That underpins several arrangements you'll meet, and it's possible only because address derivation is arithmetic rather than allocation.

docs.title: How it runs
docs.text:
When a transaction calls a contract, every node runs the code — independently, against its own copy of the state, arriving at the same answer. That's the determinism the site opened with, finally doing real work: thousands of machines can agree on what a program computed because the program cannot do anything that might come out differently anywhere.

Which brings us to the part worth the page.

docs.title: What it can do
docs.text:
A short list, and worth having before the absences, because the absences only mean something against it.

  • Read and write its own storage. Its private mapping of 32-byte slots, fingerprinted as storageRoot. Nothing else can write it; anybody can read it.
  • Send ether, from the balance it holds.
  • Call other contracts, and be called by them. This is what composability is made of.
  • Create contracts, which is why its nonce counts deployments.
  • Read some chain context — its own balance, who called it, how much was sent, the current block's number.
  • Emit a log.

That last one needs a sentence, because it's the odd one out. A log is a record a contract writes that is not part of the state: it goes into the block alongside the transaction, where anything outside Ethereum can read it. The peculiarity is that a contract can write a log and cannot read one — not its own, not anybody's. Logs exist for the benefit of the outside world, which is why they're the practical way to watch what a contract has been doing, and why they're cheap: no node has to keep them available for execution. Events and logs takes it from there.

And that's the whole of it. Six capabilities, all of them inside Ethereum.

docs.title: What it cannot do, and why that's the point
docs.text:
A contract is a program with almost everything taken away. The list of absences is short and total:

It cannot Because read a clock two nodes would read different times make a network request the response could differ, or not arrive generate a random number the result would differ per node read a file, or anything else on the machine nothing outside the state is shared start itself nothing schedules it, and nobody would pay

Every one of those absences is the price of reproducibility. A program able to fetch a web page would get different answers on different machines, and the network would stop agreeing about what happened. So each capability is missing not because nobody implemented it, but because having it would destroy the one property that makes the whole arrangement work.

That inversion is what to take from this page. A contract is interesting because of what it is forbidden to do. The absences are the design.

Two of those need qualifying, because the honest version is sharper

"No clock" isn't quite right. A contract can read a timestamp — but it's a number the block's proposer wrote down, not a reading from a clock. It is approximately the real time, because other nodes reject a block whose timestamp is implausible, and it is not trustworthy to the second, because the proposer chooses it. So contracts have an approximate, partly adversarial notion of time, which is a more awkward thing than none at all.

"No randomness" needs the same care. There are values on the chain that look random and a contract can read them. The difficulty is structural: anything a contract can read, the party assembling the block can read first — and can often choose whether to include the transaction at all. So a contract's "random" number is knowable in advance by exactly the person with the most incentive to exploit it.

Both have one shape. The constraint isn't that information is unavailable; it's that anything available to the contract is available to whoever orders the transactions. That's a recurring trap rather than a solved problem.

So how does a contract learn anything about the world — a price, a result, a temperature? Somebody sends it in. A party puts the data on-chain in an ordinary transaction, and the contract reads it from the state like anything else. Those parties are oracles, and the arrangement deserves clear eyes: the contract isn't observing the world, it's trusting whoever reported it. Any claim that a contract is "trustless" stops at that boundary.

docs.title: Can a contract be changed?
docs.text:
The code at an address cannot change. That much is true, and it's the basis of everything said about immutability.

The trouble is it doesn't mean what it's usually taken to mean, because behaviour isn't determined by one contract's code. The common pattern: the contract you interact with holds an address in its storage and forwards calls to the code found there. Storage is writable. So changing one stored value changes what the whole thing does, without altering a byte of the code you were told was immutable.

That isn't a loophole or an abuse — it's a widely used, openly documented technique. But it makes "immutable" a claim to check rather than accept:

  • Is the code at this address fixed? Almost always yes.
  • Can its behaviour change? Only by reading it to find out.

A good instance of a pattern this site keeps hitting: a true statement about the protocol — code at an address is fixed — and a false impression it creates, that the thing therefore can't change.

docs.title: How a call says which function to run
docs.text:
A short section, because the mechanism is a convention rather than a rule and people assume the reverse.

The protocol has no concept of a function. A call arrives as bytes, and the contract's own code decides what to make of them. What makes transfer(address,uint256) mean anything is an agreement everybody follows: the first four bytes of a call are the leading four bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of the function's signature (Solidity documentation, v0.8.26), with the arguments in a defined layout after it.

Two things worth noticing. Keccak-256 is doing this job too — the same function behind addresses and the state root also decides what a function is called. And because four bytes is short, two different signatures can in principle produce the same selector: rare, and a real source of trouble when it happens.

The whole arrangement is the ABI — the application binary interface — and nothing in the protocol enforces it. It's a shared convention, like the derivation path on the seed phrases page — universally followed, nowhere required.

docs.title: How many times has a contract been used?
docs.text:
A question with an instructive answer: nothing records it.

A contract account has only the four fields, and its nonce counts contracts it created, not calls it received. There is no counter anywhere. So this is a question about history, not state — and a node that pruned its history cannot answer it, however perfectly it validates the present.

Reconstructing it from the chain gives three different numbers, depending on what you count:

  • Transactions sent to the address. Undercounts, often badly — it misses every call arriving from another contract, since those aren't transactions.
  • Events it emitted. The practical method, and cheap at scale. Misses any execution that emitted nothing, which is the author's choice.
  • Re-executing everything with tracing. Complete, expensive, and needs a node that kept the history.

The warning for anyone using chain data: published usage figures aren't comparable unless you know which was counted, and sources rarely say. Same family as addresses are not people, which the previous page argued, and a failed transaction still happened and still cost gas.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A contract can read and write its own storage, send ether, call and create other contracts, read some chain context, and emit a log — and nothing else. All of it inside Ethereum.
  • A smart contract is a program stored at an account, identified by its codeHash not being the empty constant. Not a special object — an account with code.
  • It is neither smart nor a contract: no judgement, no parties, no remedy. The word predates Ethereum by two decades and meant something broader (Szabo, 1997).
  • Nobody holds its keys, because there are none. Control is the code, and the code is public.
  • Its address is computed from the creator's address and nonce, so it is predictable before the contract exists.
  • Every node runs the code and gets the same answer — possible only because of what the code is forbidden to do.
  • It cannot read a clock, reach the network, generate randomness, or start itself. Each absence is the price of reproducibility, not a missing feature.
  • The sharper version: anything available to a contract is also available to whoever orders the transactions — which is why on-chain randomness and timestamps are traps rather than tools.
  • Outside data arrives only because somebody sends it in — an oracle. The contract isn't observing the world; it's trusting a reporter.
  • Code at an address can't change; behaviour can. The usual pattern forwards calls to an address held in storage, and storage is writable. "Immutable" is a claim to check, not accept.
  • Functions are a convention: four bytes of a Keccak-256 hash of the signature, by agreement. The protocol knows nothing about functions.
  • Nothing counts how often a contract is used. It's a history question, answerable three ways that disagree.

Next: What the code actually is — bytecode, source, and why "verified" is a claim rather than a fact.

docs.title: Tokens aren't special
docs.text:
Stub — not written yet

This page is an outline. Delete this box when you fill it in.

Permanent. That tokens are contracts rather than a protocol feature has been true since the first one, and the standards that describe them are finalised documents that cannot be revised.

docs.title: The thesis this page exists to argue
docs.text:
Ethereum has one native asset: ether. Everything else people hold — every stablecoin, every governance token, every NFT — is not a thing the protocol knows about. It is a contract keeping a mapping from address to number, and "owning" one means there is a number recorded against your address in somebody else's storage.

Which sounds reductive and is the literal mechanism. The consequences are not reductive at all, and they explain most of what surprises people about holding tokens.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• What is a token, mechanically? (A contract with a mapping of address → balance, and functions to change it. That's all. Show how small the essential idea is.)
  • So what do you own? (The central answer. Not an object. An entry in a particular contract's storage — which means your ownership is exactly as good as that contract's code and its author's intentions.)
  • Why does your wallet show tokens it doesn't hold? (It queries token contracts for your address and displays the answers. A token you have never heard of can appear in your wallet because somebody wrote your address into their contract — you did not receive anything.)
  • Why do you need ether to move a token? (The fee is payable only in ether, as the ether page said. Hence the account with a fortune in tokens and nothing it can do — this is where that situation is finally explained rather than mentioned.)
  • What is a standard, and why does it matter? (ERC-20 and ERC-721 are agreed function names and behaviours, not protocol rules. A contract that follows them works with every wallet; one that doesn't is still a valid contract that nothing can read. Conventions all the way down, like the ABI and the derivation path.)
  • Can a token's author take yours, or stop you moving it? (Often yes, and this is the section that earns the page. Whatever the code allows, the author can do — freeze, mint, blacklist, upgrade. Whether any given token permits it is a question about its code, not about Ethereum.)
  • What is an approval, and why is it the biggest practical hazard? (Permission for another contract to move your tokens, granted once and lasting until revoked. Explain the mechanism and why the risk is structural rather than a bug: the token contract has no idea whether the spender deserves it.)
  • Is an NFT different in kind? (No — same shape, mapping address to a token identifier rather than a quantity. And what it points at is usually a URL, so "owning the artwork" is a claim about somebody's web server.)

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• This is probably the highest-value page in this part, because tokens are what most people mean by "smart contracts" and the gap between the folk model and the mechanism is enormous.
  • Argue it in the why accounts register: one thesis — ownership is a number in somebody else's storage — and every consequence derived from it rather than listed.
  • Do not name tokens or projects. Mechanisms and classes only, per FORKS.md. The mechanisms are permanent; the products are not, and naming them would also read as commentary on specific assets.
  • Resist the temptation to editorialise about the asset class. State the mechanism and let the reader conclude — the same discipline the governance page needs.
  • The approvals section is where a reader could be protected from real loss, so be precise and avoid advice that dates. The structural point — permission persists until revoked, and the token contract cannot judge the spender — is permanent.
  • Ties to collect: ether-only fees, the account model's persistent identity, logs as the only usable record of transfers, and the "immutable" caveat from what a smart contract is.

Next: RLP encoding — how all of this gets written down as bytes.

docs.title: What the code actually is
docs.text:
Permanent. That a contract's code on-chain is bytecode, and that source is something kept elsewhere by people, has been true since 2015 and follows from the design rather than from any current practice.

Bytecode

The actual contents of a contract's code: a sequence of bytes, each one an instruction for the machine that runs contracts, with constants mixed in between them.

No variable names, no function names, no comments, no types. Those exist in source code, which is a separate file kept by people somewhere else and has never been on the chain at all.

When somebody writes a contract, they write it in a programming language — text with names, comments and structure, meant for people to read. The most widely used one is Solidity, though several others exist.

That text never reaches the chain. It goes through a compiler, a program that translates it into instructions a machine can execute, and only that output is sent.

So two different things get called "the code", and almost everything confusing here comes from running them together:

  • Source — what a person wrote and can read. Kept on somebody's computer.
  • Bytecode — what the compiler produced. The only one Ethereum has ever seen.

docs.title: What is actually at the address
docs.text:
Ask a node for the code at a contract's address and you get something like this:

6080604052348015600f57600080fd5b50...

That is the code. Not a description of it — the thing itself.

And it is readable, in a narrow sense. Each byte is an instruction, so the beginning of that run says:

60 80     PUSH1 0x80      put the value 0x80 on the stack
60 40     PUSH1 0x40      put the value 0x40 on the stack
52        MSTORE          write one to memory at the other

Three instructions, entirely unambiguous — and they tell you nothing about what the contract is for. They are the opening move of almost every Solidity contract: housekeeping, done before any of its actual business starts.

That gap — between what the code does and what it is for — is this page's subject.

docs.title: Where the bytecode is kept
docs.text:
The accounts page said an account holds four fields, one of which is codeHash — a 32-byte hash, not the code itself. So where is the code?

On every node. All of it, on each of them.

Code is part of the state, and the state is the thing every node holds a complete copy of. So every node that can check a block holds the bytecode of every contract that exists — exactly as it holds every balance and every storage slot. Nothing is kept on one special machine, nothing has to be fetched from anybody, and there is no question of which node has it. They all do.

Then why keep the code out of the account entry at all?

Three reasons, all about size.

The entry stays small. An account is four fields and must be a fixed, tidy size whether its code is fifty bytes or fifty thousand. Holding a 32-byte hash achieves that; holding the code would not.

Identical contracts share one copy. Two deployments of the same bytecode have the same codeHash, so there is nothing to store twice. The account entries differ; the code they point at is one object.

And code never changes. Once deployed it is fixed, so unlike a balance it never needs rewriting — which makes it exactly the sort of thing to keep to one side and refer to, rather than carry around.

docs.title: Which is why code has a size limit
docs.text:
Because every node holds the code, and every node loads it whenever the contract is called, a contract's size is not its author's private cost. It lands on every machine in the network, every time anybody calls it.

So there is a cap. A contract's bytecode cannot exceed 24,576 bytes — a consensus rule since 2016, and a deployment producing more is rejected outright. The motivation was exactly the arithmetic above: calling a contract costs work in proportion to its code size, so without a limit a single contract could make every node do unbounded work, with the lightest clients suffering worst (Buterin, 2016).

Two consequences worth having.

Long source is free; complex logic is not. Comments, descriptive names, whitespace and documentation are all discarded by the compiler, so they cost nothing on chain. What produces bytecode is branching, arithmetic and storage work. The cap constrains complexity, not verbosity.

And it is part of why Ethereum systems are many contracts rather than one. Split the logic across several that call each other; put shared routines in one and delegate to it; keep heavy computation off-chain and have the contract check the result. The composability this site keeps describing as an elegance is also a constraint — you compose partly because you must.

docs.title: How a node knows it has the right code
docs.text:
By hashing it.

Hand a node some bytes claiming to be a contract's code and it hashes them, compares the result with the codeHash in that contract's account, and rejects them if they differ. Nothing is taken on trust, which is the same move as everywhere else on this site.

And codeHash is itself covered by the state root, which the block header commits to. So the commitment runs all the way down:

block header → state root → the account entry → codeHash → the code

Alter one byte of a contract's code and its hash changes, so the account entry changes, so the state root changes, so the block header is wrong. A contract's code is committed to exactly as firmly as anybody's balance (Wood, 2014).

And how does it get called?

Mechanically: a transaction naming the contract's address as its recipient, carrying some bytes as input. The node looks up the account, fetches the code by its codeHash, and runs it with those input bytes available to it.

The caller never sends the code. They couldn't usefully — the node already has it, and would reject anything whose hash didn't match the codeHash at that address. Which is also why calling an address reliably runs the code committed there: the caller has no say in what executes.

Code travels inside a transaction exactly once, at deployment, because that is the one moment no node has it yet. After that it is addressed, not transmitted.

Which bytes mean which function is the ABI convention from the previous page — the protocol just hands the code whatever was sent. The anatomy of the transaction that does this belongs with transactions.

docs.title: Where the source went
docs.text:
Nowhere. It was never sent.

what you readsourcenames, comments,types, structure,intentcompilerwhat the chain holdsbytecodeone byte perinstruction, andnothing elseno way backThe compiler throws away everything that made the source readable. Nothingon the chain ever held it, so nothing on the chain can give it back.

A compiler's job is to produce something a machine can execute, and everything that made the source comprehensible to you is surplus to that: the names you chose, the comments you wrote, the types you declared, the structure you imposed. All of it is used during compilation and then discarded.

So the relationship is one-way in the practical sense. Given the source you can always produce the bytecode. Given the bytecode you cannot produce the source, because the information isn't missing from the chain — it was never in the bytecode to begin with.

docs.title: So what does "verified" mean?
docs.text:
Open a contract on a block explorer and you may well see readable Solidity, with names and comments, laid out in files. Given everything above, where did that come from?

Somebody uploaded it. The author, usually, or anyone who had it. They supplied the source and the exact compiler settings; the explorer compiled it itself and checked whether the result matched the bytecode already at that address. If it matched, the source is displayed and the contract is marked verified.

So "verified" is a precise and limited claim:

Somebody produced source that compiles to exactly these bytes.

That is genuinely useful — it is very strong evidence that the source you are reading is the source that produced the contract, because producing different source that compiles to identical bytes is not something you can do by accident or easily on purpose.

But notice what it is not. It is not the protocol telling you anything. The chain holds bytecode and has no opinion about source, so verification happens entirely off to one side, performed by a party who chose to do it.

Why verification can fail for honest code

Two details that explain most confusion around this.

An exact match means exact. Compiling the same source with a different compiler version, or different optimiser settings, produces different bytes — so verification needs the settings, not just the source. This is why a contract whose source is genuinely correct can fail to verify: the submitter mis-remembered which version they used. Failure to verify is evidence of a mismatch, not of dishonesty.

And the bytecode usually carries a pointer to its own description. By default the Solidity compiler appends, to the end of the runtime bytecode, a small structure containing the compiler version and a hash of a metadata file describing the source (Solidity documentation, v0.8.26).

Which is a neat twist on this whole page. The chain does not hold the source — but it very often holds a fingerprint of a description of the source, which is enough to tell you whether a file somebody hands you is the right one. The source still lives elsewhere; the chain just carries a receipt for it.

docs.title: Who is trusting whom
docs.text:
Worth being exact, because the arrangement is easy to misread in both directions.

If you read the verified source on an explorer, you are trusting that explorer to have done the comparison honestly and correctly. Not a wild trust — it is checkable, and a false claim would be caught by anyone who repeated the exercise — but it is trust, and it is not the protocol's guarantee.

If you want no trust at all, do what the explorer did: take the source, compile it with the stated settings, and compare the result against the bytecode you fetched from a node yourself. This is reproducible by anybody, which is what makes the whole arrangement work.

And if you read nothing at all, which is the usual case, you are trusting that somebody else has looked.

docs.title: Unverified is not the same as suspicious
docs.text:
A contract with no verified source works exactly as well as one with it. Verification is a convenience for humans and has no bearing on execution.

What you lose is help. The bytecode is still there, still public, still identical for everybody — you simply have to read machine code instead of Solidity. Plenty of perfectly ordinary contracts are unverified because nobody got round to it.

It is a reason for care, though, and the reason is narrow: the easiest way to check what a contract does has been removed, so the effort required to find out has gone up. Treat it as a cost, not as a confession.

docs.title: What bytecode can and cannot tell you
docs.text:
Tools exist that read bytecode and reconstruct something source-like — decompilers. They work, within limits worth understanding.

What comes back is structure. The control flow, the arithmetic, which storage slots are read and written, which other contracts are called. All of that is in the bytecode and can be recovered.

What does not come back is meaning. A decompiler can tell you that storage slot 3 is compared against the caller's address and the function stops if they differ. It cannot tell you that slot 3 is the owner, that the check is an access control, or that the author intended it to protect a withdrawal. Names are precisely the part that was thrown away.

So the honest statement, and the one that sharpens the previous page's section on immutability:

You can always read what a contract does. You can never read what it was for.

The smart contracts page said code at an address is fixed and the code is public, which together sound like total transparency. They aren't. Both are true, and the thing you most want to know — is this contract doing what its authors said it does — is not settled by either.

docs.title: The protocol has never heard of Solidity
docs.text:
Last and bluntly, because it is easy to assume otherwise.

Ethereum has no notion of Solidity, or of any programming language. It does not know a compiler exists. The rules describe bytes and what the machine does with them, and nothing in the specification mentions a language, a type, or a function name (Wood, 2014).

Every language that targets Ethereum is an arrangement among people outside the protocol — the same position as the ABI, the derivation path on seed phrases, and the wordlist on that same page. Conventions sitting on top of something that knows nothing about them.

This is true of any published program, with one difference

Nothing above is special to Ethereum. Any compiled binary you download is machine code whose source you are trusting somebody about, and "reproducible builds" is a whole field devoted to exactly the comparison an explorer performs.

The difference is not that Ethereum's code is readable. It is that everybody is reading the same copy. Nobody can serve you a different binary from the one other people run, because the bytes are at an address in a state that thousands of machines hold identically — and you can fetch them yourself and check their hash.

Which is a smaller claim than "contracts are transparent" and a much more useful one.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Two things get called "the code": the source a person wrote, and the bytecode a compiler produced. Only the second has ever been on the chain.
  • A contract's code on-chain is bytecode: one byte per instruction, with constants between them. No names, no comments, no types.
  • Every node holds every contract's code, because code is part of the state. The account entry holds only a codeHash, which is a key into that node's own storage rather than a reference to anywhere else.
  • A node checks it has the right code by hashing it and comparing. codeHash is covered by the state root, so a contract's code is committed to as firmly as anybody's balance — and identical contracts share one stored copy.
  • Source was never on the chain. The compiler uses it and discards everything that made it readable, so the relationship is one-way: source gives bytecode, bytecode cannot give source.
  • Bytecode is readable as instructions and tells you nothing about purpose. The opening bytes of nearly every Solidity contract are memory bookkeeping.
  • "Verified" means somebody produced source that compiles to exactly these bytes. Strong evidence, performed off-chain by a party who chose to, and not a statement by the protocol.
  • It needs the exact compiler version and settings, which is why honest code sometimes fails to verify.
  • The bytecode usually ends with the compiler version and a hash of a metadata file describing the source — so the chain holds a receipt for the source even though it never held the source.
  • Reading verified source means trusting the explorer's comparison; you can repeat it yourself, which is what makes it trustworthy.
  • Unverified is a cost, not a confession. The contract works identically; you just have to read machine code.
  • Decompilers recover structure, never meaning. So: you can always read what a contract does, and never what it was for.
  • Code is capped at 24,576 bytes, because every node must load it when the contract is called. Verbosity is free; complexity is not — which is part of why systems are built from many contracts rather than one.
  • The protocol has no notion of any language. Solidity is a convention among people, like the ABI.

Next: Events and logs — the one thing a contract can write and cannot read.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Buterin, V. (2016). EIP-170: Contract code size limit. Ethereum Improvement Proposals. Caps a contract's code at 24,576 bytes, on the grounds that calling a contract costs work proportional to its code size and an uncapped contract would impose unbounded work on every node. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-170
  • Solidity documentation, v0.8.26. Contract metadata. States that the compiler appends the IPFS hash of the canonical metadata file and the compiler version to the end of the runtime bytecode, encoded in CBOR with its length in the final two bytes. Version-pinned deliberately: the latest URL moves, and the default behaviour has changed between versions. https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/v0.8.26/metadata.html
  • Wood, G. (2014). Ethereum: A secure decentralised generalised transaction ledger. Ethereum project yellow paper. Specifies code as a byte array and the machine's behaviour over it, with no reference to any source language — Appendix H lists the instruction set that gives each byte its meaning. https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf

docs.title: Addresses
docs.text:
Permanent. Address derivation and EIP-55 checksums have never changed.

An address is the thing you actually paste into a wallet:

0xd8dA6BF26964aF9D7eEd9e03E53415D37aA96045

Address

The last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of a public key — 40 hex characters, conventionally written with 0x in front.

It is the identifier everything on Ethereum is recorded against: balances, contract code, storage. Nothing distinguishes an address whose key someone holds from one nobody has ever computed.

Twenty bytes, forty hex characters. This is the last step of the chain and the simplest one: hash the public key and keep the end of it.

docs.title: The derivation
docs.text:
private key          32 bytes
         │
         │   × G
         ▼
    public key           64 bytes
         │
         │   keccak256
         ▼
       hash              32 bytes
         │
         │   keep the last 20
         ▼
     address             20 bytes

Private key to public key by curve multiplication, public key to hash by Keccak-256, then discard all but the last 20 bytes. That's the whole derivation, and it's specified in exactly those terms — the rightmost 160 bits of the hash (Wood, 2014).

Try it: the whole chain, end to end

Private key (hex) Random key

Every step runs in your browser — the curve multiplication, the hash, the truncation.

Step 1 — start at 1 again. The public key is G, exactly as on the previous page, and the address that falls out is 0x7E5F4552091A69125d5DfCb7b8C2659029395Bdf. That is a real address with a real transaction history, because private key 1 is the most-guessed key in existence.

Step 2 — look at the greyed-out part of the hash. Those first 12 bytes are computed and then thrown away. Only the last 20 survive.

Step 3 — press Random key a few times. This is precisely what a wallet does when it creates an account: pick a number, derive, hash, truncate.

docs.title: One private key gives exactly one address
docs.text:
Worth stating plainly, because the answer isn't obvious and wallets make it look otherwise.

Every step in that chain is deterministic. Multiplying by G has one answer. Keccak-256 has one answer. Taking the last 20 bytes has one answer. So a given private key produces one public key, which produces one address, and it will produce the same one on any machine, forever. There's no choice to make and no parameter to vary.

So how does your wallet show you a dozen addresses?

Because the wallet has a seed, not a key

This is the distinction from the private keys page, and it's where it starts to matter.

                 seed
                  │
      ┌───────────┼───────────┐
      ▼           ▼           ▼
  key #0       key #1      key #2        ← many keys, from one seed
      │           │           │
      ▼           ▼           ▼
  address 0   address 1   address 2      ← one address each

The seed sits upstream and can generate an unlimited supply of private keys by a repeatable procedure. Each of those keys then yields exactly one address, by the chain on this page.

So "many addresses from one thing" is true of a seed and false of a private key. Which is why writing down twelve words can restore a whole wallet, while a single private key only ever restores a single account.

Mechanics under wallets and seed phrases.

One key can control several addresses, though

A separate point, and easy to conflate with the above.

A key is derived into one address. But that address can go on to create contracts, and each contract gets an address of its own — computed from the creator's address and nonce, as the contract-addresses section below explains. Deploy ten contracts and there are ten more addresses under your control.

Contracts can also simply be configured to obey a particular address, which is how multi-signature and smart-contract wallets work.

So the precise statements are:

  • derived from your key: exactly one address, always
  • controlled by your key: as many as you care to create

The chain on this page is about the first. Nothing about control is visible in an address.

docs.title: Why keep only 20 bytes?
docs.text:
Keccak-256 produces 32 bytes and an address is 20, so 12 bytes — 96 bits — are deliberately thrown away.

The reason is size. As the public keys page argued, an address is an identifier: it gets stored, transmitted, logged and typed constantly. Trimming 32 bytes to 20 is a 37% saving, paid out on every transaction and every storage slot, forever.

The cost is a smaller space of possible addresses — 2160 rather than 2256.

Is 2¹⁶⁰ enough?

A fair question, since discarding 96 bits is a deliberate weakening.

2^160 ≈ 1.46 × 10^48

But the number to compare against isn't 2256. The questions that matter are whether anyone could find two public keys hashing to the same address, or hit a specific address that already holds something.

Finding a collision takes about 280 operations by the birthday bound — roughly 1024. Vastly beyond anything ever computed, but a far thinner margin than the 2128 the rest of the stack enjoys. It's the main reason 20 bytes is occasionally criticised as too thrifty.

Finding a specific address is 2160, which is hopeless in the same way guessing a private key is hopeless.

So: comfortable, but the least comfortable link in the chain. A deliberate trade of margin for size.

docs.title: Every address already exists
docs.text:
A consequence of this design that surprises people: nothing creates an address.

All 2160 of them are equally valid right now. The overwhelming majority have never been used and never will be. An "unused" address isn't absent from the state — it simply holds nothing, which is indistinguishable from not existing.

So you can send ether to an address nobody controls, and it will sit there permanently. There is no check, because there is nothing to check against: the network cannot tell an address whose private key exists from one whose key nobody has ever computed. They are identical objects.

This is why mistyping an address is unrecoverable, and why the next section exists.

docs.title: The capitalisation is a checksum
docs.text:
You'll meet the same address written both ways:

0xd8da6bf26964af9d7eed9e03e53415d37aa96045
0xd8dA6BF26964aF9D7eEd9e03E53415D37aA96045

Both are the same address. Hex is case-insensitive, so as a number they're identical and either will work.

But the mixed-case version carries information. EIP-55 (Van de Sande & Velicanu, 2016) hides a checksum in the choice of which letters are capitalised:

  1. Take the lowercase address and hash it with Keccak-256.
  2. Walk the address and the hash together, one character at a time.
  3. Where the address has a letter a–f, capitalise it if the matching hash character is 8 or more. Leave digits alone.

The capitalisation is therefore determined entirely by the address — so a wallet can recompute it and compare.

Try it: check or compute a checksum

Address

Step 1 — as given, the checksum is valid.

Step 2 — break it. Change one capital letter to lowercase, or the reverse. The checksum fails and the offending character is highlighted.

Step 3 — paste an all-lowercase address. It reports no checksum present, which is correct: a single-case address is valid and simply carries no protection.

Step 4 — change a digit rather than the capitalisation. Now it's a different address, so the tool computes a different, perfectly valid checksum for it. Which is the point of the next section.

docs.title: What it catches, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
It catches typos. Mistype a character in a checksummed address and the capitalisation almost certainly stops matching, so a wallet refuses it before anything is sent. The chance of a random error still checksumming correctly is around 1 in 240.

It does not catch substitution. Hand someone a different address, correctly checksummed, and it validates perfectly — because it is a correct checksum, for the wrong address. EIP-55 protects you from your own slips, not from being deceived.

That distinction is worth being firm about, because "the checksum passed" gets treated as a safety guarantee and is nothing of the kind.

History: EIP-55 is retrofitted, and it shows

Addresses had no checksum at all for Ethereum's first year. Mistype one and the funds went somewhere nobody controlled, with no warning.

Fixing that properly would have meant changing the address format — which would have broken every wallet, contract and tool simultaneously. EIP-55's trick is that it changes nothing. The bytes are identical. The capitalisation was free information nobody was using. An old tool handing a lowercase address to a new one still works.

The price of that compatibility is that the checksum is optional. A lowercase address remains valid, so a wallet cannot insist on a checksum — only verify one when it happens to be present. A format designed with a checksum from the outset would have made it mandatory.

Neat engineering, and a good illustration of what retrofitting costs: not the mechanism, but its enforceability.

docs.title: Contract addresses
docs.text:
Contracts have addresses that look identical — 20 bytes, same format, same checksum rules — but they can't be derived from a public key, because a contract has no private key.

A contract's address comes instead from the address that created it and that creator's nonce, hashed in much the same way. Which makes it predictable before the contract exists: you can know the address of your next deployment in advance.

Nothing in an address reveals which kind it is. The two are told apart by what the account holds, not by how the address looks.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• An address is the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of the 64-byte public key.
  • The hash's first 12 bytes are computed and discarded, to keep identifiers short.
  • There are 2160 addresses and all of them already exist. Sending to an unowned one loses the funds permanently, and nothing can warn you.
  • Mixed-case addresses carry an EIP-55 checksum in which letters are capitalised. Lowercase addresses are equally valid, with no protection.
  • The checksum catches typos, not deception.
  • Contract addresses derive from the creator's address and nonce, and look exactly the same.

Next: Signatures — how a private key proves control of an address without revealing itself.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Van de Sande, A., & Velicanu, V. (2016). EIP-55: Mixed-case checksum address encoding. Ethereum Improvement Proposals. Specifies the capitalisation rule, and supplies the test vectors used to verify the tool above. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-55
  • Wood, G. (2014). Ethereum: A secure decentralised generalised transaction ledger. Ethereum project yellow paper. Defines an address as the rightmost 160 bits of the Keccak-256 hash of the public key, and gives the separate rule for contract addresses. https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf

docs.title: Keccak-256
docs.text:
Permanent. Ethereum's hash function since it launched in 2015, specified as such throughout the Yellow Paper (Wood, 2014). Addresses, the state root, transaction hashes and function selectors all depend on it, so it cannot be changed.

Keccak-256

A hash function: it takes any input at all — a word, a book, a transaction, a gigabyte of video — and returns a fixed-size fingerprint. Keccak-256's output is always exactly 32 bytes, which is 64 hex characters.

The same input always gives the same fingerprint. A slightly different input gives an unrecognisably different one. And there is no way to work backwards from a fingerprint to what produced it.

Try it: hash anything

Input

Type anything. Empty the field, paste a paragraph, use emoji. The output is always 32 bytes — that's the first thing to notice, and it already tells you something important: the hash cannot contain the input, because the input can be larger than the output.

docs.title: The four properties
docs.text:
Everything Ethereum does with hashing rests on these, and nothing else.

1. Deterministic. The same input always gives the same output — on every machine, in every language, forever. Hash hello here, hash it in ten years on different hardware, and you get the same 32 bytes. This is what makes hashes usable in a system where thousands of computers must agree.

2. Fixed size. Any input, 32 bytes out. A single character and the complete works of Shakespeare both come out the same length.

3. Avalanche. Change the input by the smallest possible amount and nearly every character of the output changes. Not "the output changes a bit" — the output is unrecognisable.

4. One-way. Given an output, there is no practical way to find an input that produces it. Easy forwards, infeasible backwards.

docs.title: Avalanche, demonstrated
docs.text:
The third property is the one people underestimate, so it's worth seeing. Two inputs differing by one letter:

Try it: the avalanche effect

Input A Input B

hello and hellp differ in a single letter. Yet 61 of the 64 hex characters differ — the output isn't similar, it's unrelated.

Worth trying: make the two inputs identical. Every character matches, every time. That's determinism and avalanche together — wildly sensitive to any change, and perfectly stable when there's none.

docs.title: Nearly every character, but only half the bits
docs.text:
The tool reports two numbers, and the gap between them is worth a moment: 61 of 64 characters changed, but only 132 of 256 bits.

That isn't a contradiction. Recall from hex and bytes that each hex character is exactly four bits. A character looks different if any one of its four bits flipped — so characters are a much blunter instrument than bits.

If the function is doing its job, each output bit flips with probability one half. The chance that all four bits of a character survive untouched is then:

(1/2)^4  =  1/16

So a character changes 15 times out of 16, and across 64 characters you'd expect about 64 × 15/16 = 60 of them to change. We observed 61.

Half the bits is the design target; nearly every character is what that looks like in hex. The bit figure is the precise statement of the property, and the character figure is what you actually see.

And half is not an accident. If similar inputs produced similar hashes, you could hill-climb your way to a desired output: tweak the input, check whether you got closer, tweak again. Avalanche destroys that strategy, because "closer" carries no information at all.

docs.title: Why it can't be reversed
docs.text:
The honest answer is simpler than people expect: the output is too small to hold the input.

Hash a one-megabyte file and you get 32 bytes. Eight million bits in, 256 bits out. The information is not hidden — it is gone. There is no key, nothing encrypted, nothing to decrypt. Most of the input was discarded by construction.

Which means infinitely many inputs share any given hash. That sounds alarming until you ask how you'd find one.

Collisions exist, and that's fine. Finding one is the problem.

Since inputs are unlimited and outputs number only 2256, collisions must exist — two different inputs with the same hash. This is the pigeonhole principle and it isn't a weakness.

The security claim isn't "no collisions exist". It's that nobody can find one. And 2256 is a number that resists intuition:

2^256 ≈ 115,792,089,237,316,195,423,570,985,008,
        687,907,853,269,984,665,640,564,039,457,
        584,007,913,129,639,936

Roughly 1077 — comparable to estimates of the number of atoms in the observable universe. A machine testing a billion billion hashes per second, running since the universe began, would have covered an utterly negligible fraction of it.

So "one-way" is an economic claim, not a mathematical impossibility. The same distinction appears everywhere in this subject: not cannot, but costs more than any conceivable benefit.

docs.title: How it works: the sponge
docs.text:
The page so far has treated the function as a box you drop bytes into. The inside is worth a look, because Keccak's shape is unusual and it's what the next section's one-byte difference actually modifies.

The design is called a sponge (Bertoni et al., 2011), for the obvious reason: it absorbs, then it squeezes.

block 1block 2block 3…136 bytes each, XORed in — nothing else entersRATE136 bytes (1088 bits) · input in, hash outCAPACITY64 bytes (512 bits) · the input never reaches it136 + 64 = 200 bytes, which is the whole state: 1600 bits32 bytes outAfter each block the permutation stirs all 1600 bits together, so the capacitydoes change — but only as a side effect of input that went into the rate.24 rounds of the permutation per block · state is 25 lanes of 64 bits

There is a state of 1600 bits, starting at all zeros. That's the whole memory of the function — no matter how much data you hash, this is all it ever holds.

The 1600 isn't arbitrary. The permutation is defined over a 5 × 5 grid of 64-bit lanes, and 25 × 64 = 1600. That grid is the shape the five round steps are written in terms of, so the state size follows from the design rather than the other way round. In bytes it's 200, which is the number to hold onto: 136 + 64.

The state is split in two, and the split is the entire security story:

  • the rate, 1088 bits or 136 bytes, which your input is allowed to touch
  • the capacity, 512 bits, which it is not

Hashing then goes:

  1. Pad the message so its length is a multiple of 136 bytes.
  2. Absorb. Take the first 136-byte block and XOR it into the rate. Leave the capacity alone.
  3. Permute. Run the whole 1600 bits through a fixed scrambling function, 24 rounds of it. This mixes rate into capacity and back.
  4. Repeat 2 and 3 for every remaining block.
  5. Squeeze. Read the first 256 bits of the state. That's your hash.

docs.title: Why the capacity is the point
docs.text:
An attacker trying to steer the output controls the input — and therefore controls what gets XORed into the rate, exactly. If that were the whole state, they would have complete knowledge of it at every step, and the function would be a calculation they could run backwards.

The capacity denies them that. 512 bits of the state are never written by the message directly. They change constantly, but only as a side effect of the permutation stirring the rate into them. So each block arrives into a state the attacker has not fully specified, and that gap compounds with every block absorbed.

docs.title: Nothing here is random
docs.text:
Worth heading off straight away, because "the attacker can't control the capacity" sounds like it must involve randomness somewhere. It doesn't. There is no randomness anywhere in Keccak — that would contradict the determinism at the top of this page, which is the property the whole of Ethereum rests on.

The state begins at all zeros. Every step afterwards is fixed arithmetic. Anybody who hashes the same input gets the same 1600 bits at every stage, capacity included, on any machine, forever. You could print the capacity out at each step and compare notes; two people doing it would agree exactly. It is neither secret nor unpredictable, and there is nothing to "check for randomness" because nothing claims to be random.

What the capacity actually is, is not independently choosable. The attacker picks the input and thereby fixes everything, including the capacity — but only via the permutation. To make the capacity take some particular value they'd have to work backwards from that value to an input producing it, and that is precisely the problem the permutation is built to make infeasible. They can always compute what the capacity will be. They cannot choose the rate and the capacity to suit them at the same time.

So the security doesn't come from hidden information. It comes from the input and the state being tied together by something that is cheap to run forwards and hopeless to run backwards — the same asymmetry the one-way section above described, applied to the function's own internals.

That's also why the number is 512 rather than something smaller: it's sized so the capacity is never the weakest link. With a 256-bit output, the binding limit is the birthday bound on the output itself — the 2128 of the collisions box above — not anything about the internal state.

The permutation, in one paragraph

Each of the 24 rounds applies five steps, traditionally named with Greek letters: θ mixes each bit with the parity of two nearby columns, ρ rotates each of the 25 lanes by a different fixed amount, π moves the lanes around, χ is the only non-linear step and the one that makes the whole thing irreversible in practice, and ι XORs in a round constant so that the rounds aren't identical to each other.

You don't need the detail to use the function, and this site's implementation doesn't need you to trust it — the rotation amounts and round constants are computed from the specification's own formulas rather than copied from a table, then checked against the published test values. A transcription error in a table of 24 constants would be invisible on inspection and fatal in use.

docs.title: Keccak-256 is not SHA-3
docs.text:
This causes real confusion and real bugs, so it's worth being precise.

Keccak, designed by Bertoni, Daemen, Peeters and Van Assche (Bertoni et al., 2011), won an open competition to become SHA-3. The competition was run by NIST — the United States standards agency, which publishes the cryptographic standards most of the world ends up using.

Between Keccak winning and the standard being published, NIST changed the padding: the bytes appended to the input before hashing (NIST, 2015). Ethereum had already adopted the original Keccak and kept it.

So Ethereum uses Keccak-256, and the NIST standard is SHA3-256, and they are not the same function. The difference is a single byte: 0x01 where the standard uses 0x06.

One byte, and the outputs share nothing:

Try it: Keccak-256 against SHA3-256

Input

Both functions use the identical permutation, the identical structure, the identical number of rounds. They differ by one byte of padding — and almost every character of the output differs as a result. Avalanche doesn't care where the difference came from.

The empty string is the pair worth remembering, since both turn up constantly in different contexts:

keccak256("")  =  c5d2460186f7233c927e7db2dcc703c0e500b653ca82273b7bfad8045d85a470
sha3_256("")   =  a7ffc6f8bf1ed76651c14756a061d662f580ff4de43b49fa82d80a4b80f8434a

What goes wrong in practice: a library function named sha3 may implement either one, depending on its age and author. Call the wrong one and nothing errors — you simply get a hash that no other Ethereum tool agrees with. Addresses won't match, signatures won't verify, and nothing tells you why.

If you take one thing from this page: when Ethereum says SHA-3, it means Keccak. Check which your library gives you.

docs.title: Where Ethereum uses it
docs.text:
Almost everywhere, which is why this page comes first in the cryptography section:

Use What gets hashed Addresses a public key — the last 20 bytes of the hash become the address Address checksums the address itself, to detect typos Transaction hashes the signed transaction State and storage roots every node of the trie Function selectors a function's name and parameter types Contract addresses the creator's address and nonce

In each case the job is the same: compress something arbitrary into a fixed-size identifier nobody can forge.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
Two misconceptions worth killing off.

It isn't encryption. Encryption is reversible by design — that's its entire purpose. Hashing is not, and there's no key. "Decrypting a hash" is not a difficult problem; it's an incoherent request.

It isn't random. It's perfectly predictable: the same input always yields the same output. Hash output looks random, and that's useful, but anyone with the input can reproduce it exactly. Using a hash as a source of randomness is a well-trodden route to losing money, because whoever supplies the input chooses the result.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Keccak-256 takes any input and returns exactly 32 bytes.
  • It is deterministic — the same input gives the same output everywhere, forever.
  • Avalanche: a one-letter change rewrites nearly every character of the output — half the bits, which in hex means about 60 of the 64 characters. Similar inputs tell you nothing about each other.
  • It is one-way because the output is too small to hold the input. The information is gone, not hidden.
  • Collisions must exist; the claim is that nobody can find one, and 2256 is why.
  • Keccak-256 is not SHA3-256. One padding byte apart, and completely different outputs.
  • It is neither encryption nor a source of randomness.

Next: Private keys — where a 256-bit number starts being worth something.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Bertoni, G., Daemen, J., Peeters, M., & Van Assche, G. (2011). The Keccak reference, version 3.0. The designers' own specification of the sponge construction and the permutation. https://keccak.team/files/Keccak-reference-3.0.pdf
  • National Institute of Standards and Technology (2015). SHA-3 Standard: Permutation-Based Hash and Extendable-Output Functions. FIPS PUB 202. The standard whose padding differs from Ethereum's. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.FIPS.202
  • Wood, G. (2014). Ethereum: A secure decentralised generalised transaction ledger. Ethereum project yellow paper. Specifies Keccak-256 as Ethereum's hash function throughout. https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf

docs.title: Private keys
docs.text:
Permanent. 256-bit keys on the secp256k1 curve, unchanged since Ethereum launched in 2015.

A private key is a number. That's the whole of it.

Private key

A randomly chosen integer, 256 bits long — which from hex and bytes you'll recognise as 32 bytes, or 64 hex characters.

Whoever knows it can produce signatures for the matching address, and that is the whole of what owning ether consists of.

Not a file, not a password, not a certificate issued by anyone. Nobody assigns it to you and no record exists of it anywhere.

Try it: make one

Generate a key

Press it a few times. Nothing was registered, nobody was asked, no server was contacted — your browser picked a random number. That is the entire process, and it's the first genuinely strange thing about Ethereum: an account is not issued to you, it's a number you happened to choose.

Never send anything to a key from this page

To be precise about the risk, because it's easy to overstate and easy to understate.

Nothing is at risk right now. The key you just generated controls an account that has never been used and holds nothing. There is nothing to steal.

The danger is only if you ever put value behind it. And it's absolute, because of something worth stating plainly: the private key is the complete secret. There is nothing above it, beneath it, or alongside it — no password, no second factor, no account to lock. Anyone holding that number can sign for that address, and the network cannot tell them from you.

This key has been generated in a browser and displayed on a screen, in a tab that is probably in your history, on a page any installed extension could read. That's fine for looking at. It is permanently unfit for holding anything, and no amount of later care fixes it.

For real value, use wallet software that generates a key and never shows it to anyone, including you.

docs.title: How is one number enough?
docs.text:
A natural objection: if a key is just a number, surely someone can guess it?

They can't, and the reason is the size of the number. Private keys run up to about 2256:

2^256  =  115,792,089,237,316,195,423,570,985,008,
          687,907,853,269,984,665,640,564,039,457,
          584,007,913,129,639,936

Roughly 1077. Written out, it's 78 digits. That number resists intuition completely, so rather than reach for an analogy, here's a calculation you can run yourself.

Try it: how long to guess a key?

Suppose every person alive were hunting for your key, each testing keys as fast as a modern machine can manage, for the entire history of the universe.

Keys per second For how many years

The defaults are 8 billion people × a billion keys per second each (8 × 1018), running for 13.8 billion years — the age of the universe.

The result is around 1 in 1040. Not "difficult". Not "takes a long time". After exhausting the universe's entire history with every human being and every machine, they would have searched a fraction of the keyspace too small to write comfortably.

Try making the numbers absurd — a trillion keys per second, a trillion years. It barely moves.

This is why a key needs no protection beyond secrecy. There's no account to lock, no rate limit to enforce, nobody to appeal to. The number itself is the security, and guessing is not a strategy.

docs.title: The valid range
docs.text:
Almost any 256-bit number works, but not quite all of them. A private key must be at least 1 and less than a specific constant called the order of the curve, written n:

n = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFEBAAEDCE6AF48A03BBFD25E8CD0364141

That's defined by secp256k1, the elliptic curve Ethereum uses (SECG, 2010) — the same one Bitcoin uses. Keys have to fall below it because of how the public key is derived; the arithmetic happens in a group with exactly n elements, so numbers at or above n simply wrap around to ones below it.

How much of the range is excluded? Almost none.

The gap between n and 2256 is:

2^256 - n  =  432,420,386,565,659,656,852,420,866,394,968,145,599

Which looks enormous until you compare it to the space it sits in. The proportion of 256-bit numbers that are too large to be valid keys is about:

3.7 × 10^-39      —  roughly 1 in 2.7 × 10^38

So if you pick a random 256-bit number, the chance it's out of range is far smaller than the chance of guessing someone's key. Real implementations do check, and loop if the draw fails, but the branch essentially never runs.

This is also why "a private key is a random 256-bit number" is a perfectly good working definition, even though it's not exactly true.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
A private key does exactly one useful thing: it produces signatures.

A signature is a way of proving you know a secret without telling anyone the secret.

That sounds impossible, and with an ordinary password it is. If you prove you know a password by typing it in, whoever is on the other end now knows it too — you've handed over the very thing you were proving you had. Every proof costs you the secret.

A signature escapes that. Give your private key a message — say, "send 1 ether to Anna" — and it computes a value with two properties:

  • Anyone can check that the value could only have been produced by someone holding the key for a particular address.
  • The value reveals nothing about the key. You can publish a thousand signatures and the key stays secret.

And a third property, which matters just as much: the signature is bound to that one message. Change a single byte — the amount, the recipient — and it stops checking out. So a signature isn't a reusable token the way a password is. It authorises exactly one thing, once.

It's not much like a handwritten signature

The word is unhelpful, because the everyday version works the opposite way.

Your handwritten signature is the same every time, which is precisely its weakness: anyone who has seen it can attempt a copy, and a copy works on any document.

A digital signature is different for every message. Signing two transactions gives two unrelated values, and neither is any use on a third. So there's nothing to copy. Seeing a million of someone's signatures tells you nothing you could use.

Closer analogies are all imperfect, but the useful intuition is a lock that produces a different, publicly-checkable receipt for each thing you lock — rather than a stamp that leaves the same mark.

Transaction signing on Ethereum has worked this way with secp256k1 keys since the beginning (Wood, 2014). How the computation actually works is the subject of signatures; for now, only the properties matter.

That's the mechanism behind every claim of ownership on Ethereum. Which leads to a definition worth stating bluntly, because it surprises people:

"Owning" ether means knowing a number.

Nothing in the state records that an account belongs to you. The chain holds only a balance against an address, entirely public, visible to everybody. What distinguishes you from everyone else looking at it is that you can produce valid signatures for it and they can't.

And the key is the whole secret, not one factor among several. Nothing else is checked: no password, no second device, no identity. A signature is valid or it isn't, and producing a valid one requires only the number.

So there's nothing to steal except the number — and nothing to lose except the number, which is the subject of what losing your keys means.

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
Two things follow from the key, in order:

  1. The key is multiplied into a public key — easy to compute forwards, infeasible to reverse.
  2. The public key is hashed into an address.

Each step is one-way, which is why an address reveals nothing about the key behind it.

Seed phrases are not this

If you've used a wallet, you've probably met twelve or twenty-four words rather than a 64-character number, and may reasonably assume that's the private key.

It isn't. Those words are a seed, and a repeatable procedure turns one seed into many private keys.

The direction matters, because it's easy to get backwards. The seed sits upstream of your keys, not above them as some higher authority:

seed  ──►  private key  ──►  address

So a seed is a convenient way to produce and re-produce keys — which is why writing down twelve words can restore a whole wallet. But it is not a second secret guarding them. Once a private key exists, it stands alone: whoever has it can sign, and the seed is irrelevant to that.

Ethereum itself has never heard of seed phrases. They're a wallet convention, and the protocol sees only keys and signatures. Covered under wallets and seed phrases.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A private key is a random 256-bit number. Nothing more.
  • Nobody issues it. You pick it, and the network never needs to know you did.
  • There are about 1077 possibilities, which is why guessing is not a strategy — every human searching for the age of the universe covers around 1 in 1040 of the space.
  • It must be below the curve order n, which excludes about 1 in 1038 of all 256-bit numbers — so in practice, any random number will do.
  • Its one job is producing signatures, and therefore "owning" ether means knowing a number.

Next: Public keys — the one-way step that turns the key into something you can safely publish.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Standards for Efficient Cryptography Group (2010). SEC 2: Recommended Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters, version 2.0. Defines secp256k1, including the group order n quoted above. https://www.secg.org/sec2-v2.pdf
  • Wood, G. (2014). Ethereum: A secure decentralised generalised transaction ledger. Ethereum project yellow paper. Appendix F specifies the use of secp256k1 for transaction signing. https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf

docs.title: Public keys
docs.text:
Permanent. secp256k1 has been Ethereum's curve since it launched in 2015.

A private key is a number you keep. A public key is what you get by running that number through a one-way calculation, and it's safe to publish.

Public key

A point on the secp256k1 curve, computed from a private key by multiplying a fixed, published point by it. Two coordinates, 32 bytes each, so 64 bytes in total.

Easy to compute from the private key and infeasible to reverse — which is what makes it safe to publish.

The calculation involves an elliptic curve, which sounds forbidding and mostly isn't. You need three things from this page: what a public key is, why the step can't be reversed, and which of its several written forms Ethereum actually uses.

docs.title: The curve
docs.text:
secp256k1 is the set of points satisfying one equation:

y² = x³ + 7

docs.title: "Over a finite field" means clock arithmetic
docs.text:
Every number in that equation is kept inside a fixed range by wrapping round, exactly the way a clock does. Four hours after eleven o'clock is three, because the hours wrap at twelve. Written as arithmetic:

11 + 4 = 15,  and  15 wraps to 3   (because 15 − 12 = 3)

That's arithmetic modulo 12. secp256k1 does the same thing, with an enormous prime instead of twelve:

p = 2²⁵⁶ − 2³² − 977

So whenever a calculation on the curve produces a number at or above p, you subtract p until it fits. Every coordinate is a whole number between 0 and p − 1 — no decimals, no square roots in the ordinary sense, and nothing ever grows without limit.

Two consequences matter. There are finitely many points, which is what makes the set a usable mathematical object. And the points are integer pairs, not positions on a smooth line.

docs.title: So why does everyone draw a curve?
docs.text:
Because the same equation over the real numbers really is a smooth curve, and it's the easiest way to show how point addition works. Here it is:

x y y² = x³ + 7 over the real numbers — a genuine curve, and what every diagram of this shows.

That picture is honest about the structure and misleading about the shape.

Now keep the equation exactly as it is and change only one thing: every calculation wraps round, in the clock sense above. The modulus is doing all the work here — it isn't a detail alongside the equation, it's the entire difference between the two pictures.

Here's what that does, with 97 as the modulus. Ask whether x = 1 has a point on the curve:

x³ + 7  =  1 + 7  =  8

Over the real numbers you'd need y = √8 ≈ 2.828 — not a whole number, so there's no integer point there at all. With wrapping, try y = 28:

28²  =  784
784  =  8 × 97 + 8      so 784 wraps round to 8   ✓

Which is exactly x³ + 7. So (1, 28) is on the curve, even though 28 is nothing like √8. Wrapping lets large coordinates satisfy the equation, and that's why the solutions end up scattered rather than lying along a line.

Doing that for every x from 0 to 96 gives:

x → 96 96 The same equation, with the arithmetic wrapped at 97 instead of carried out over the reals. 78 points, and nothing remotely curved.

Same equation, no curve. The wrapping is what destroys the shape: a coordinate that would have carried on climbing instead falls back to the bottom of the range, so neighbouring values of x land nowhere near each other. What's left is scattered dots, symmetric about the middle because y and p − y are both solutions.

secp256k1 is this second picture, with 97 replaced by a prime of 78 digits and roughly 10⁷⁷ points rather than 78. Nobody draws that.

So when you see a smooth curve with points labelled on it, read it as a diagram of the rules, not a map of the territory. The rules carry over exactly; the shape does not.

Why the real-number picture is still worth having

The geometry is where point addition comes from, and it's genuinely visual. To add two points P and Q on the real curve:

  1. Draw a straight line through them.
  2. That line crosses the curve at exactly one more place. Call it R.
  3. Reflect R across the horizontal axis. That reflection is P + Q.

Only R gets reflected. P and Q stay exactly where they are — they're the inputs, and the answer appears somewhere else entirely.

reflect P Q R P+Q

P and Q are the two points being added. The dashed chord through them meets the curve a third time at R. Reflecting R across the horizontal axis gives P + Q. Note that neither P nor Q moves — only R is reflected.

That's the chord construction. When you add a point to itself there's no second point to draw a line through, so you use the tangent at that point instead — and the rest is the same. Hence "chord and tangent".

The reflection in step 3 looks arbitrary and isn't: it's what makes the operation behave like addition, so that adding points is associative and every point has an inverse. Without it the structure doesn't work.

Over a finite field the same algebraic formulas apply, and they still produce a valid third point. There's simply no line to draw any more. The arithmetic survives the move; the picture doesn't.

docs.title: Deriving a public key
docs.text:
The curve comes with one fixed, published point called the generator, written G. Everyone uses the same one — it's part of the standard, not something you choose:

G.x = 79BE667E F9DCBBAC 55A06295 CE870B07 029BFCDB 2DCE28D9 59F2815B 16F81798
G.y = 483ADA77 26A3C465 5DA4FBFC 0E1108A8 FD17B448 A6855419 9C47D08F FB10D4B8

Those two numbers are in the specification (SECG, 2010) and have been identical for every Ethereum and Bitcoin key ever made. Keep them in view — the tool below lets you check them.

Your public key is then:

public key = private key × G

That's it. Take G, add it to itself as many times as your private key says, and the point you land on is your public key. Since a private key is around 10⁷⁷, "as many times as your private key says" isn't something anyone does literally — see the box further down.

Worth being clear about what you end up with, because it catches people out:

The public key is a point. Not a string, not a hash — a pair of coordinates, x and y, each a 32-byte number. Any hex string you see called "a public key" is just one of several ways of writing that pair down.

So the whole derivation is two steps and no more:

a number you chose          ──×G──►      a point on the curve
   (private key)                            (public key)
Try it: private key to public key

Private key (hex) Random key

The two coordinates at the top are the public key. The byte strings below them are the same point written in the different formats explained later on this page — not extra things, just other spellings.

Work through it in this order; each step shows something different.

Step 1 — check the tool is honest. The field starts at 1, so it's computing 1 × G, which should be G itself. Compare the x and y it gives you against the two values printed above. They match, which means everything below is trustworthy.

Step 2 — type 2. That's G + G. Notice the coordinates have nothing in common with G's. Not larger, not similar — unrelated.

Step 3 — type 3, then 4, then 5. Watch the x coordinate as you go. There's no drift, no pattern, no sense in which 5 is "further along" than 4. This scattering is the entire security of the scheme, and it's the thing to take away from this page.

Step 4 — press Random key, a few times. This is what a wallet actually does when it makes you an account.

Step 5 — try to break it. Enter 0, or ffffffff... (64 f's, which is above the curve order). Both are rejected, for the reason given on the private keys page.

docs.title: Why it can't be reversed
docs.text:
Going forwards is fast. Going backwards — given a public key, find the private key — is the discrete logarithm problem, and nobody has a practical method.

The reason is the same one that makes Keccak-256 one-way, and it's worth noticing the parallel: the output gives you nothing to follow.

Try the tool with 1, then 2, then 3. The coordinates jump about with no pattern. They don't increase. "Close to the right answer" doesn't exist, because a private key one away from yours produces a point bearing no resemblance to yours. So there's no gradient to climb, no way to narrow the search, nothing to do but guess — and guessing is hopeless at this scale.

Then how is the forward direction fast?

A fair question, since adding G to itself 10⁷⁷ times is obviously not happening.

The trick is doubling. Rather than stepping one G at a time, you repeatedly double — G, 2G, 4G, 8G, 16G — and add together whichever of those you need. Any number up to 2²⁵⁶ is the sum of at most 256 such powers, which is exactly what its binary representation tells you.

So the whole computation is around 256 doublings and at most 256 additions, and it finishes in well under a millisecond. The tool above is doing it in your browser.

The asymmetry is the entire point: about 256 operations forwards, no known shortcut backwards. Multiplying is cheap; dividing is not available.

docs.title: The several written forms
docs.text:
A public key is a pair of coordinates, each 32 bytes, so 64 bytes in total. But you'll meet it written several ways, which is a common source of confusion:

Form Size What it looks like Raw 64 bytes x then y Uncompressed 65 bytes 0x04 then x then y Compressed 33 bytes 0x02 or 0x03 then x

The 0x04 prefix in the second form is a marker meaning "uncompressed point follows". It is not part of the key, and this trips people up constantly — see the note below.

Compressed form drops y entirely, which works because the curve equation nearly determines it. Given x, the equation y² = x³ + 7 has exactly two solutions, and they always have opposite parity — one even, one odd.
