So a single byte recording which one it was (02 for even, 03 for odd) is enough to recompute y. Half the size, no information lost.

Ethereum hashes the 64-byte form, with no prefix

When deriving an address, Ethereum hashes the raw 64 bytes — x followed by y, and no 0x04 prefix.

The Yellow Paper is explicit about this — address derivation takes the 64-byte representation (Wood, 2014).

Include the prefix and you hash 65 bytes instead of 64, which by the avalanche property gives you a completely unrelated hash, and therefore a completely wrong address. Nothing errors; you just get an address that isn't yours.

This is probably the single most common mistake when implementing address derivation by hand.

docs.title: Why this curve?
docs.text:
The name decodes piece by piece: sec for the standards group that published it, p because the field is a prime one, 256 for the size in bits, k for Koblitz, and 1 because it's the first curve of that kind in the list (SECG, 2010).

Bitcoin chose it, and Ethereum followed — which brought along a decade of implementations, review and hardware support.

History: who Koblitz was, and what a Koblitz curve is

Koblitz is a person. Neal Koblitz was one of two mathematicians who, working independently in the mid-1980s, proposed using elliptic curves for cryptography — the other was Victor Miller. Until then elliptic curves were a subject in pure number theory with no particular connection to keeping secrets.

A Koblitz curve is one whose constants are chosen to have deliberate structure rather than being picked arbitrarily, because structure makes the arithmetic faster.

You can see it in secp256k1's own numbers. The equation is y² = x³ + 7, with no x term at all and a tiny constant, and the field prime sits just below a power of two:

p = 2²⁵⁶ − 2³² − 977

Both choices speed up the computation. But they have a second property that turned out to matter more: they're plainly visible. Anyone can see why each constant is what it is, because there's nothing to see — a 7, and a prime chosen to sit near a round binary number.

That becomes the interesting part when you compare it with the alternative, which is the next box.

There was another candidate, and the choice is interesting

The obvious alternative was secp256r1, where r stands for random. It's the curve NIST recommends and most of the wider internet uses.

The two were generated differently. secp256k1's parameters are structurally derived — a Koblitz curve, with the small constant 7 and a prime close to a power of two, chosen because they make the arithmetic fast and the choices visible. secp256r1's parameters come from hashing an unexplained seed value, and nobody has said where that seed came from.

There is no published attack on secp256r1, and this is not evidence of one. But "we can see exactly why every constant is what it is" is a property cryptographers value for its own sake, and it's part of why the k1 curve was attractive for a system meant to need no trusted authority.

docs.title: Why have both a public key and an address?
docs.text:
A reasonable question, since the address is just a hash of the public key and carries no extra information. Why not use the public key directly as the thing people send to?

Because the two do different jobs.

The public key does the cryptography. It's the mathematical object that signature verification needs: checking a signature means checking it against a public key, and there's no way round that.

The address does the naming. It's what goes in a transaction's recipient field, gets stored in contracts, is typed into wallets and read down the phone. For that job the public key is a poor choice, for one blunt reason:

Size Public key 64 bytes — 128 hex characters Address 20 bytes — 40 hex characters

An address is less than a third the size. It appears in every transaction, in storage, in logs, in every interface — so that saving is paid out constantly, in storage costs, bandwidth and human effort.

And here's the part that makes it work: you don't need to publish the public key separately. A signature lets anyone recover the public key that produced it. So the public key is available exactly when verification needs it, and need never be stored or sent on its own.

So: short identifier for naming, full key recovered on demand for the maths. The hash in between costs nothing and, as the box at the end of this section explains, happens to buy a little extra protection too.

docs.title: When your public key becomes visible
docs.text:
Which leads to a detail worth knowing, because it isn't obvious.

Receiving ether reveals nothing. People send to your address — and a hash can't be reversed, so an unused account exposes only the address.

Your public key becomes known the first time you sign something. A signature lets anyone recover the public key that produced it; that's how verification works at all. So the moment you send your first transaction, your public key is on the chain for good.

This doesn't put anything at risk today. The public key is meant to be public, and the private key stays unreachable behind the discrete logarithm problem.

So why mention it at all? Because it's a second lock, and it only matters if the first one ever fails.

When the distinction would actually matter

Everything on this page rests on the discrete logarithm problem being hard. Suppose one day it isn't — because someone finds a flaw in the curve, or because a sufficiently large quantum computer is eventually built. Shor's algorithm, published in 1994, would solve discrete logarithms efficiently on such a machine.

Machines capable of this do not exist, and when or whether they will is genuinely unknown. Treat any confident timeline with suspicion.

But note the asymmetry if it ever happened:

  • An account that has transacted has published its public key. Anyone who could break the curve could compute its private key.
  • An account that has never transacted has published only its address — a Keccak hash. Breaking the curve wouldn't help, because you'd first have to reverse the hash to get the public key, and hashes resist quantum attack far better than curves do.

So untouched accounts sit behind two different kinds of problem rather than one. That's the entire practical content of "your public key is secret until you sign".

And it's where the old advice against reusing addresses came from. Once you've spent from an address, its public key is published for good. Anything you send to that same address afterwards sits behind the curve alone — the hash layer is spent. Use a fresh address for each receipt and every balance keeps both layers until the moment you spend it.

Bitcoin wallets do this automatically, generating a new address for every payment. Ethereum does the opposite: address reuse is universal, and deliberately so, because contracts, token balances and ENS names all need an address that stays put. A stable identifier is worth more in practice than a speculative hedge against a machine that doesn't exist.

That's a real trade-off Ethereum has chosen, not an oversight. Worth knowing it was chosen — and it's one instance of a larger pattern, since the same persistence that makes an address worth reusing is what makes it worth watching. Why accounts, and what they cost takes that apart.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A public key is a point on the secp256k1 curve: two coordinates, 32 bytes each.
  • It's computed as private key × G, where G is a fixed published point everyone shares.
  • Forwards takes about 256 doublings; backwards is the discrete logarithm problem, with no known shortcut.
  • It's one-way for the same reason hashing is: the output offers nothing to follow. Neighbouring private keys give unrelated points.
  • Three written forms — raw (64 bytes), uncompressed with an 0x04 prefix (65), compressed (33).
  • Ethereum hashes the raw 64 bytes. Including the prefix silently produces the wrong address.

Next: Addresses — the last step, and the one that finally produces something you'd paste into a wallet.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Standards for Efficient Cryptography Group (2010). SEC 1: Elliptic Curve Cryptography and SEC 2: Recommended Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters, version 2.0. SEC 1 defines the point encodings used above; SEC 2 defines secp256k1 itself, including the generator G and the field prime. https://www.secg.org/sec2-v2.pdf
  • Wood, G. (2014). Ethereum: A secure decentralised generalised transaction ledger. Ethereum project yellow paper. Appendix F specifies the use of secp256k1 and the 64-byte public key form for address derivation. https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf

docs.title: Signatures
docs.text:
Permanent. ECDSA over secp256k1, unchanged since Ethereum launched in 2015.

The private keys page described what a signature is for: proving you know a secret without revealing it. This page is about how Ethereum actually uses that — and it opens with the fact that surprises nearly everyone.

Signature

Three numbers — v, r and s — computed from a message and a private key. They prove that the key's holder authorised that exact message, while revealing nothing about the key.

On Ethereum they do one thing more: the signer's address can be recovered from them. Which is why a transaction never has to state who sent it.

docs.title: A transaction never says who sent it
docs.text:
Transactions get a page of their own later. Only one thing about them matters here.

A transaction is a short list of fields — how much, to whom, what data, how much fee — followed by three numbers called v, r and s, which together are the signature.

There is no "from" field. Nowhere does a transaction state its sender.

Instead, the sender's address is recovered from the signature. Given the signed message and those three numbers, anyone can compute the public key that must have produced them — and from that, the address.

This isn't optional or occasional. When a node receives a transaction it has to establish who sent it before it can do anything at all: whose balance to check, whose account nonce to compare against, whose account to take the fee from. Recovery is how it finds out, so every node runs it on every transaction it ever sees. The Yellow Paper defines the function for exactly this purpose (Wood, 2014).

So the signature doesn't accompany a claim of identity. The signature is the claim.

Which is rather elegant once it lands. A forged "from" field would be worthless, so Ethereum doesn't have one. The only way to appear as the sender of a transaction is to produce a signature that recovers to your address, and the only way to do that is to hold the key.

docs.title: What actually gets signed
docs.text:
Not the transaction — the hash of the transaction, via Keccak-256.

That has a useful consequence. Since the hash covers every field, changing any single byte of the transaction changes the hash, and a signature over the old hash recovers to a different address. So the signature protects all of it at once: the amount, the recipient, the fee, the account nonce. There's no need to sign each field separately, and no way to alter one in transit.

docs.title: How a signature is made
docs.text:
The thing doing the work deserves naming — and so do its three outputs, which appear everywhere once you start looking at transactions.

Signing and recovery are done with ECDSA, the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (SECG, 2009). It isn't an Ethereum invention or a cryptocurrency one; it's a long-standing standard behind TLS certificates and software signing. Ethereum's contribution is the curve it runs on, and the use it makes of recovery.

docs.title: The three operations, side by side
docs.text:
signing:      message hash  +  private key          ──►   r, s
    verifying:    message hash  +  r, s  +  public key   ──►   yes or no
    recovering:   message hash  +  r, s  +  v            ──►   the public key

The first two are ordinary ECDSA, used across the internet. The third is the one Ethereum leans on, and it gets a section of its own below.

The rest of this section covers signing. Recovery follows after it.

docs.title: Where r and s come from
docs.text:
Signing a message hash z with a private key d goes like this:

  1. Pick a random secret number, called k, used once and then thrown away. It has a second name you'll meet constantly — the signing nonce — on which see the warning below.
  2. Compute the curve point k × G, the same multiplication from the public keys page. Call it R.
  3. r is the x coordinate of R.
  4. s is computed from the message hash, r, the private key and k:
    s  =  k⁻¹ ( z  +  r · d )      mod n

Every term there has already appeared on this site:

Symbol What it is z the message hash, from Keccak-256 d the private key — the only secret in the equation r the x coordinate from step 3 k the random number from step 1, also called the signing nonce n secp256k1's order, from the private keys page

k⁻¹ means the modular inverse — the number that multiplies by k to give 1, working modulo n. Not a fraction; there are no fractions anywhere in this.

So the two halves have distinct jobs. r is a commitment to the random point: it depends on k and nothing else. s is the half the private key enters, mixed with the message hash so that the pair is bound to this message and no other.

And notice that d appears exactly once, multiplied by r and buried under a k⁻¹ you don't know. That's what makes the equation safe to publish.

Neither value reveals d, and neither reveals k. And because k is fresh every time, r and s are completely different on every signature — which is what you see when you press Sign again below.

docs.title: Two different things get called a nonce
docs.text:
Worth separating before going on, because this page needs both senses and they could hardly be less alike.

What it is Secret? Chosen how k, the signing nonce the random value above, thrown away immediately yes, always unpredictably, never repeating the account nonce a counter of transactions an account has sent, checked when a transaction is validated no by counting

They share only the literal sense of the word: number used once. Everything else is opposed — one must be unguessable or your key is recoverable, the other must be guessable or your wallet couldn't build a transaction. The account one has its own page and appears later in this one, when we get to what a node checks.

k must never repeat — and here is exactly why

If one key signs two different messages using the same k, the private key falls out of the two signatures. Not eventually, not with effort: immediately, with two subtractions and two divisions.

Here's the whole attack.

Since r depends only on k, two signatures sharing a k also share the same r. So you have two equations:

s₁  =  k⁻¹ ( z₁ + r·d )
s₂  =  k⁻¹ ( z₂ + r·d )

Subtract them. The r·d terms are identical in both, so they cancel — and d vanishes along with them:

s₁ − s₂  =  k⁻¹ ( z₁ − z₂ )

Now k is the only unknown left, and it's trivially isolated:

k  =  ( z₁ − z₂ ) · ( s₁ − s₂ )⁻¹

Everything on that right-hand side is public — the two hashes are the messages, and the two s values came with the signatures.

Then put k back into either original equation and solve for d:

s₁ · k  =  z₁ + r·d

d  =  ( s₁·k − z₁ ) · r⁻¹

And that is the private key.

A worked example, with real secp256k1 values. One key signs "pay Anna 1 ether" and "pay Bob 2 ether", reusing k:

r   (identical in both)  fd1b7de8c449eecd…
s₁                       e1df25a5e5f1ccc9…
s₂                       e78cef03efaf0bd8…

recovered d  1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef
actual    d  1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef

Note that r being the same in two signatures is visible to anyone. It's the public signal that this attack is available.

This is not hypothetical. Sony's PlayStation 3 code-signing key was recovered in 2010 in exactly this way — the same k on every signature. In 2013 a flaw in Android's random number generator made Bitcoin wallets repeat k, and keys were emptied.

Which is why serious implementations don't leave k to chance at all. RFC 6979 (Pornin, 2013) derives it deterministically from the private key and the message hash: the same message always gives the same k, two different messages never do, and no random number source is involved anywhere.

docs.title: How the signer is recovered
docs.text: The third operation, and the reason a transaction needs no sender field at all.

docs.title: Why not simply verify the signature?
docs.text:
A fair objection, and worth answering before going further: verification would work perfectly well. It's what the rest of the internet does. So why does Ethereum bother with recovery?

Because verification needs the public key, and recovery doesn't.

Look again at what each operation takes in:

    verifying:    message hash  +  r, s  +  public key   ──►   yes or no
    recovering:   message hash  +  r, s  +  v            ──►   the public key

To verify, you must already have the public key. On the open internet that's usually free — a TLS certificate hands it to you, having been issued in advance by somebody you trust. Ethereum has no certificates and no issuers, so there's nowhere for a verifier to get your public key from. It would have to travel with every transaction.

And that costs:

Bytes carried r and s 64 plus a public key, to verify + 64 plus v, to recover + 1

So verification would cost 128 bytes of signature data per transaction, where recovery costs 65. Sixty-three bytes saved, every transaction, forever, in storage held by thousands of nodes.

Put against a whole transaction the difference is stark. A plain ether transfer is on the order of 110 bytes; carrying the public key would push it past 170 — more than half again as large, for information the network can work out by itself.

That's the trade. One extra byte of v instead of sixty-four bytes of public key, paid for with a slightly more involved calculation. On a system where every byte is stored permanently and everywhere, it's not a close call.

Is recovery slower than verification?

Not meaningfully. Verification works out to two point multiplications; recovery needs a modular square root to rebuild R from r, plus comparable multiplication. The same order of work either way.

Which is why the decision came down to bytes rather than speed. Had recovery been dramatically more expensive, 64 bytes might have been the cheaper thing to pay.

docs.title: So Ethereum never verifies a transaction signature at all
docs.text:
Worth being precise about, because the natural assumption is that recovery happens first and verification then confirms it. It doesn't — and the cleanest way to say why is this:

Verification is recovery followed by a comparison.

Recover the public key from the signature, then check it's the one you were expecting. Ethereum does the recovery and has nothing to compare against, so it stops there.

That matters because it settles the obvious worry. Skipping the comparison isn't a weakened check — the two operations establish exactly the same fact, and verification succeeds precisely when recovery returns the expected key. There is no version of this where a forgery slips through recovery but would have been caught by verification. The comparison is omitted because there's no expectation to test, not because a check was dropped.

Compare the two mental models:

    the familiar one      "here is the claimed sender —
                           check the signature matches them"

    Ethereum's            "here is a signature —
                           it determines who the sender is"

In the first, there are two pieces of information that might disagree, so there's a check, and the check can fail. In the second there is only one piece of information. The sender isn't claimed and then confirmed; the sender is defined as whoever the signature recovers to.

So the question "is this signature valid for this sender?" is never asked — and therefore can never fail. That's why, as the tool below shows, a tampered message doesn't produce an invalid-signature error. There's no such error to produce. It produces a different sender.

A few things can still fail outright

Recovery replaces the signature check, but it doesn't make a transaction unconditionally acceptable. Some structural conditions remain, and a transaction breaking any of them is rejected before recovery is even attempted:

  • r and s must each be at least 1 and below the curve order
  • s must be in the lower half of its range, per EIP-2 — see malleability
  • r must actually be the x coordinate of a point on the curve, or there is no R to rebuild and recovery has nothing to work with

These are checks on whether the numbers are well-formed, not on whether they're yours. Nothing here compares anything to a sender.

docs.title: Which is not the same as saying nothing gets checked
docs.text:
An important line to draw, because "verification" covers two different jobs and this page only ever discusses one of them.

Signature verification asks a single narrow question: did the holder of this key sign this exact data? That's the cryptographic operation, and it's the only thing recovery replaces.

Transaction validation asks whether the transaction is acceptable at all — and that happens in full, every time, unchanged.

And here is the part that matters. Some of those checks can be made by looking at the transaction on its own. Others are about the sender — and so cannot even be attempted until recovery has worked out who the sender is:

What the node asks Can it ask yet? Is this well-formed — the right fields, the right shape? yes Are the signature's numbers within their permitted range? yes ← recovery happens here, and produces an address Has this account already used this transaction number? only now Does this account hold enough ether to pay? only now Is the offered fee acceptable to the network? yes Is this transaction even meant for this network? yes

Which recasts the whole section. Recovery isn't an alternative to checking a transaction — it's the step that makes the important checks possible at all. It answers who, and the account-specific questions are then asked of that answer.

The proper names for those checks

Each of those questions has a technical name, and each gets a page of its own later. Listed here so the terms aren't a surprise when you meet them:

The question What it's called Has this account already used this transaction number? the account nonce Does this account hold enough ether to pay? the balance Is the offered fee acceptable? gas limits and fee parameters Is this meant for this network? the chain id

The glossary has a one-line definition of each. Nothing on this page depends on knowing them — they're here only to show which checks need a sender and which don't.

Valid, versus included-and-failed

Worth separating while the distinction is in view, because the two get conflated constantly.

  • Invalid — fails one of the checks above. Never enters a block, costs nothing, as though it never existed.
  • Valid but failed — passes every check, is included in a block, and then fails during execution: it runs out of gas, or the contract rejects what it was asked to do. It happened. It's permanent. You paid for it.

A failed transaction is not a rejected one. The work was genuinely performed by every node on the network, so the fee is genuinely owed. Why that has to be the case is the subject of why metering is necessary.

docs.title: Where the comparison does happen
docs.text:
Which brings the other half of that formulation into view, and it's the case you'll meet as a user.

When a website asks you to sign a phrase to log in, it does compare. It knows which address it expects — the one you claimed to own — so it recovers the address from your signature and checks the two match.

That is verification, assembled exactly as described above: recovery, then a comparison. Not a different mechanism, and not an exception to anything. The site simply has an expectation to test, so it performs the second step that a node processing a transaction has no use for.

So the same operation underlies both. What differs is only whether anyone had an answer in mind beforehand.

docs.title: Why recovery is possible at all
docs.text:
Here is the part worth understanding, because it looks like magic and isn't.

Verification and recovery are the same equation, solved for different unknowns.

ECDSA's check is a relationship between four things: the message hash, r, s, and the public key Q. Ordinarily you are handed all four, substitute them in, and see whether the relationship holds — that's verification.

But an equation with one unknown can be rearranged. Leave Q out, and the relationship can be solved for Q instead:

    Q  =  r⁻¹ ( s·R  −  z·G )

where R is the point whose x coordinate is r. Everything on the right is public: r and s come with the signature, z is the message hash, G is the fixed generator. So the public key falls out directly.

Recovery isn't a feature bolted onto ECDSA. It's the same algebra read in the other direction — and since the signing equation is written out above, that claim can be checked rather than taken on faith.

The formal version: from the signing equation to Q, in six lines

Start from the equation in the previous section, and remember that the public key is Q = d·G.

s   =  k⁻¹ ( z + r·d )          the signing equation

s·k =  z + r·d                  multiply both sides by k

k   =  s⁻¹ ( z + r·d )          divide by s instead

R   =  k·G
    =  s⁻¹ ( z·G + r·d·G )      multiply through by G
    =  s⁻¹ ( z·G + r·Q )        because d·G is just Q

s·R =  z·G + r·Q                multiply by s

r·Q =  s·R − z·G                move z·G across

Q   =  r⁻¹ ( s·R − z·G )        divide by r

Six steps of ordinary rearrangement, and nothing cleverer than multiplying both sides by the same thing. The only substitution that matters is d·G = Q on line four: that's where the private key disappears and the public key takes its place.

Which is the whole point. The signer's equation and the verifier's are the same statement; the signer knows d and k and solves for s, while everyone else knows s and solves for Q.

All of this was checked numerically before publication: both the signing equation and the final rearrangement hold for every random key, k and message tried.

docs.title: Which is where v comes in
docs.text:
One snag. Recovery needs the point R, and the signature only gives you r — its x coordinate. As the public keys page showed, an x coordinate has two possible y values, one even and one odd.

y is evenone candidate keyy is oddthe other onex = rr is only an x coordinate, and one x has two y values

Two candidate points give two candidate public keys, and so two candidate addresses. Only one of them signed.

One caveat the public keys page already made: this smooth curve is a visual aid. Over Ethereum's finite field the two solutions aren't mirror images in any geometric sense — they're two numbers, and what separates them is that one is even and one is odd. Parity is the thing v records.

So v is one bit saying which: the y was even, or the y was odd. That's its whole job. Without it you'd recover two addresses with no way to choose between them.

History: v used to carry more than one bit

In early Ethereum, v was 27 or 28 — the parity bit plus an offset inherited from Bitcoin.

Then came a problem. A transaction signed for Ethereum was equally valid on any other chain using the same curve, so a payment could be taken from one network and replayed on another, where the same key controlled the same address. EIP-155 (Buterin, 2016) fixed it by folding the chain id — a number identifying which network a signature is for — into v, so a signature became valid on exactly one chain.

Modern typed transactions dropped that trick. They carry the chain id as its own field and store the parity plainly as 0 or 1 — which is what the tool below shows. Cleaner, and the same protection.

So if you meet v = 27, v = 37 and v = 1 in different places, none is wrong; they're three generations of the same bit.

docs.title: Recovering an address, step by step
docs.text:
Spelled out as a procedure, so the tool below isn't a black box:

recover(message, r, s, v):

    1.  z  =  keccak256(message)        the hash that was actually signed

    2.  R  =  the curve point whose x coordinate is r
              — two points qualify, one with even y and one with odd,
                so use v to pick the right one

    3.  Q  =  r⁻¹ · ( s·R  −  z·G )     solve the signing relation for Q

    4.  address = last 20 bytes of keccak256(Q)

Step 3 is the rearrangement from above. Step 4 is the addresses page, unchanged.

Notice what goes in: a message, and three numbers. Every one of them public. No key, no secret, nothing that has to be kept safe — which is exactly why any stranger can run this, and why every node does.

docs.title: Nothing in this is secret
docs.text:
Worth pausing on, because signing is routinely confused with encrypting.

The message is public. A transaction is broadcast to every node on the network in plain text — the amount, the recipient, the data, all of it readable by anyone. Nothing is encrypted at any stage. A block explorer showing you somebody's transfers isn't breaking anything; it's reading what was published.

What a signature provides isn't secrecy, it's authorship. It answers who authorised this, not what does it say. Those are different questions, and Ethereum only needs the first one answered.

The only secret anywhere is the private key, and it never leaves your machine. What travels is r and s, which reveal nothing about it.

So when the tool below hands the verifier the message openly, that isn't a simplification for the demonstration — it's how the system works. If the message were secret nobody could check it was valid, and a network that can't check transactions has nothing to agree on.

This page doesn't derive any of it. The three properties from the private keys page are what matter: anyone can check it, it reveals nothing about the key, and it's bound to one message.

Try it: sign, then recover the signer

Message to sign Private key (hex) Sign again Message the verifier checks

Step 1 — note what the verifier was not given. Not the address, not the public key, not any claim about who signed. Just the message — public, as always — and three numbers. The address underneath is computed from those alone, and it matches.

Step 2 — press Sign again, several times. The signature changes completely every time, and the recovered address never does. That's k being fresh on each signature, and it's the claim from the private keys page made concrete: a signature is computed, not held.

Step 3 — alter the lower field only, so the verifier checks a different message from the one that was signed. Change "Anna" to "Anne", or 1 ether to 2.

Recovery doesn't fail. It returns a different address. That's the surprising part, and it's worth following through why.

  1. The signature was computed over keccak256("…to Anna").
  2. The verifier now computes keccak256("…to Anne") — a completely different z, because of avalanche.
  3. Step 3 of the procedure above uses z. Feed in a different z and the equation returns a different Q.
  4. That Q is a perfectly valid point on the curve, so it's a perfectly valid public key, which gives a perfectly valid-looking address. Just not the signer's.

So there is no error state, and there couldn't be. Recovery isn't checking anything — it has no idea what answer was expected, and nothing to compare against. It is a calculation, and it always returns an answer. Tamper with the message and the answer is simply a different address.

Which raises the obvious question: if nothing fails, what stops the tampering working?

The address it recovers to is a random point in a space of 2¹⁶⁰. Essentially certainly, nobody holds the key for it, it has never been used, and it holds no ether. So when a node treats that address as the sender — as it must — it finds an account with a nonce of zero and a balance of nothing, and rejects the transaction for the dullest possible reasons: the account nonce doesn't match, and there's nothing there to pay the fee with.

The tampering fails, but not because a signature check said "invalid". It fails because the altered transaction is now claimed by a stranger who has no funds and no history. Which is a stronger guarantee than a check, because there's nothing to get wrong.

docs.title: Replay protection needs two different things
docs.text:
A signed transaction is a standing instruction. Unless something stops it, anyone who has seen it can submit it again — and it will still be valid, because it's still correctly signed by you. Two different versions of that problem exist, and each needs its own defence.

Replayed on the same chain. Someone rebroadcasts your payment hoping it executes twice. The account nonce stops this: it's part of what you signed, and once an account has used a given nonce the network will never accept that number from it again.

Note which nonce that is. k must never repeat either, but for an entirely different reason and with an entirely different enforcer: repeating k is dangerous because it leaks your key, and nothing in the protocol checks for it. Repeating an account nonce is merely futile, because every node checks it and rejects the duplicate.

Replayed on a different chain. This one is less obvious. Ethereum isn't the only network using secp256k1 and this address format — there are testnets, forks such as Ethereum Classic, and unrelated chains built the same way. Your key controls the same address on all of them. So a transaction you signed for one network could be lifted and submitted on another, where it would verify perfectly and move real funds.

The defence is the chain id: a number identifying the network, included in what gets signed. Sign with Ethereum's chain id and the signature simply isn't valid anywhere else.

Attack Defence Rebroadcasting your transaction on this chain the account nonce — once used, that number is spent forever Replaying it on another chain the chain id — the signature is valid on one network only

Neither covers the other. An account nonce means nothing across chains, since the other chain keeps its own count. A chain id does nothing about the same transaction being submitted twice on the network it belongs to.

docs.title: Malleability, and why s has to be small
docs.text:
A quirk with real consequences.

For any valid signature (r, s), the value (r, n − s) is also a valid signature over the same message — where n is the order of secp256k1, the same constant from the private keys page that bounds a valid key. The underlying maths is symmetric, so flipping s to the other side of the range and flipping v to compensate gives a second, equally valid signature.

Two things make that matter.

First, anyone can do the flip. It takes no private key — only arithmetic on a signature you've already seen. So any node relaying your transaction can alter it this way, and the result still verifies as yours.

Second, a transaction is identified by its hash, and that hash covers the signature. Change s, and you change the transaction's bytes, and therefore its hash — while the transaction still does exactly the same thing on behalf of exactly the same sender.

So before EIP-2, this could happen:

  1. You broadcast a payment. Your wallet notes its hash — call it H1 — because that's how you track a transaction.
  2. Some node along the way flips s, producing a byte-for-byte different transaction with hash H2. Still your payment. Still validly signed by you. Different hash.
  3. H2 is the version that gets included in a block.
  4. Your wallet waits for H1. It never appears. As far as the wallet can tell, the payment never happened.
  5. So it reports a failure — and if anything automatically retries, you pay twice.

The payment went through the whole time. The accounting was looking for the wrong name for it.

EIP-2 (Buterin, 2015) closed this by requiring s to lie in the lower half of its range. Of the two equivalent signatures, exactly one qualifies, so there is only ever one valid encoding and only one possible hash. The tool above applies that normalisation — press Sign again a few times and s always starts with a hex digit below 8.

docs.title: Signing things that aren't transactions
docs.text:
A private key will sign any bytes you give it, and plenty of uses have nothing to do with the chain.

"Sign in with your wallet" works this way: a site gives you a phrase, you sign it, and the site recovers your address. No transaction, no gas, no block — just a signature and a recovery, exactly as in the tool above.

Which is why a signing prompt deserves reading

Because a signature authorises whatever was signed, and your wallet can only show you the bytes.

ERC-191 (Van de Sande et al., 2016) protects against one specific confusion: a phrase you sign being replayed as a transaction you never authorised. It does so by prefixing the message before hashing. For ordinary personal messages the prefix is:

\x19  "Ethereum Signed Message:\n"  <length of the message>

So signing hello actually hashes \x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n5hello, not hello.

The leading byte is the load-bearing part. 0x19 cannot begin a valid transaction encoding, so the bytes you signed are structurally incapable of being a transaction. The signature therefore cannot be lifted out and presented as authorisation to move funds. The length is included so one message can't be reinterpreted as a different, shorter one.

That's genuine, and it's narrow: it stops signed messages masquerading as transactions. It does nothing about a message that is plainly a message and still signs away something you didn't intend — which is why reading the prompt still matters.

The tool above hashes the message directly, with no prefix, to keep the demonstration about signing rather than about framing.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A transaction has no sender field. The address is recovered from the signature, so the signature is the claim of identity.
  • What's signed is the hash of the transaction, which protects every field at once.
  • r and s are the signature; v is one bit saying which of two possible public keys to recover.
  • Verification would have worked too — but it needs the public key, and Ethereum has no certificates to supply one. Recovery buys the same guarantee for one byte of v instead of 64 bytes of public key in every transaction.
  • Verification is recovery plus a comparison. Ethereum does the recovery and has nothing to compare against, so a transaction signature is never "verified" in that sense — the sender isn't claimed and then checked, it's defined as whoever the signature recovers to. Where something does have an expectation to test, such as a website login, the comparison happens and that is verification.
  • That is not the same as nothing being checked. Account nonce, balance, gas limit and chain id are all still validated — and most of them need the sender, so recovery is what makes those checks possible rather than a substitute for them.
  • The same message signed twice gives different signatures, both recovering the same address.
  • A tampered message recovers a different address, not an error — nothing in a signature says whose it should have been.
  • Replay needs two defences: the account nonce within a chain, the chain id across chains.
  • s is restricted to its lower half, because otherwise one transaction would have two valid hashes.

Next: Wallets and seed phrases — where the keys actually come from.

docs.text:

  • Buterin, V. (2016). EIP-155: Simple replay attack protection. Ethereum Improvement Proposals. Folds the chain id into the signature so a transaction is valid on one network only. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-155
  • Pornin, T. (2013). Deterministic Usage of the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA). RFC 6979, Internet Engineering Task Force. Derives the per-signature nonce from the key and message, removing the reuse failure described above. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6979
  • Standards for Efficient Cryptography Group (2009). SEC 1: Elliptic Curve Cryptography, version 2.0. Specifies ECDSA signing, verification and public key recovery. https://www.secg.org/sec1-v2.pdf
  • Van de Sande, A., Nita-Rotaru, C., & Logvinov, L. (2016). ERC-191: Signed data standard. Ethereum Improvement Proposals. Prefixes signed messages so they cannot be confused with signed transactions. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-191

docs.title: Who decides, when nobody is in charge
docs.text:
Stub — not written yet

This page is an outline. Delete this box when you fill it in.

Current as of: (fill in the fork and date)

The structure of the problem is permanent: no authority, no vote, no appeal, yet the rules change anyway. Who currently holds influence is not — teams, foundations and funding move. Describe roles and incentives; keep named organisations and personalities to a minimum and date them.

Mostly permanent. That changing the rules requires persuading independent parties with no formal mechanism is structural. The particular parties are not.

docs.title: The thesis this page exists to argue
docs.text:
The site's first page says nobody is in charge, and then every page after it assumes that's settled. It isn't. The rules do change — roughly twenty times since 2015 — so somebody is deciding something, and the interesting question is what kind of power that is when it isn't authority.

The answer: it's the power to propose, and the power to refuse. Nobody can make the network adopt a change. Anybody running a node can decline one. Everything else follows from that asymmetry.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• If nobody is in charge, how did twenty upgrades happen? (A process with no vote: proposals, argument, implementation by independent teams, and finally node operators choosing to run the new software — or not.)
  • What is an EIP, as a social object rather than a document? (A standing invitation to be argued with. Worth connecting to the EIPs cited throughout this site — the reader has been reading governance output all along.)
  • Where does real influence sit? (Client teams, who decide what the software does; researchers, who shape what's considered; large stakers and infrastructure providers, who can decline in ways that matter. None of them rule, and the distinction is the page's substance.)
  • What happens when agreement fails? (The chain splits. The DAO fork in 2016 is the worked example, already described on losing your keys — and Ethereum Classic still runs the original rules, which is what "refusing" looks like in practice.)
  • So what are the limits on change? (Not technical. The constraint is the cost of coordinating thousands of independent parties, plus the belief that acting arbitrarily destroys the property that gives the network value. Social, not technical — the conclusion the losing-your-keys page reaches from the other direction.)
  • Could the supply be changed? Could balances be edited? (Yes, in the sense that a fork can do anything. No, in the sense that getting agreement is the whole difficulty — and the one time it was tried at scale it split the chain permanently.)
  • How does this compare to governance people already know? (Standards bodies, central bank independence, open-source maintainership. The closest honest analogue, and where the analogy breaks.)

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• This is the institutional page the economics part was always meant to hold — the nav comment has said "pricing, money and institutions" since the section was planned.
  • Argue it in the why accounts register. The thesis is the proposal/refusal asymmetry; everything else is evidence for it.
  • The outside frame that fits best is rules versus discretion, which is Davide's own field — a system designed to make discretion expensive, and the question of whether that is credible when the rules can still be changed by agreement. Pick whichever treatment of credible commitment you know; don't let me choose it for you.
  • Be scrupulously fair here. This is the page where it would be easiest to editorialise, in either direction — "decentralised governance is a myth" and "nobody can change anything" are both wrong and both popular. State what the mechanism is, what it has actually done, and let the reader judge.
  • Verify every historical claim against primary sources, especially around the DAO fork and the client-diversity incidents. Contested events attract confident retellings.
  • Don't let this become a list of governance controversies. The structure is permanent; the controversies date.

Next: Glossary — every term the site uses, defined in one place. That's the end of the reading path; the rest is reference.

docs.title: Why security has to be paid for
docs.text:
Stub — not written yet

This page is an outline. Delete this box when you fill it in.

Permanent. The requirement is structural: it follows from the design, not from any particular fork's rules.

This is the root of the Economics section. Everything else here depends on it, so it's worth getting exactly right.

docs.title: The argument to make
docs.text:
The chain of reasoning, which the page should establish in order:

  1. Someone has to decide the order of transactions. The state machine is deterministic given an order, so ordering is the only genuinely contested decision in the system.
  2. Whoever holds that power could abuse it — reorder, exclude, or rewrite recent history.
  3. So the system must make abuse more expensive than it's worth.
  4. Making it expensive means the honest work has to be rewarded, continuously. An unpaid network is a cheap network to capture.
  5. Therefore security is a recurring cost, not a one-off property. It has to be paid for every block, forever.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• What is actually being bought? Not secrecy, not correctness of computation — ordering that is expensive to change.
  • Why can't security be a one-time investment? What makes it a flow rather than a stock?
  • What determines how much security is enough? (Roughly: the cost of attacking must exceed the gain from attacking. Both sides of that are hard to measure, which is itself worth saying.)
  • Where does the money come from? Only two possible sources — see who pays.
  • What's the relationship between the value secured and the amount paid? This is Budish's question, and the uncomfortable part of the answer is the heart of the page.

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• This is the page where being an economist shows. Most Ethereum writing treats security as a technical property. It's a budget, and framing it that way reorganises everything downstream.
  • Budish (2018) is the load-bearing reference. Read it before writing, and be careful to represent the argument accurately rather than as a slogan — it's a claim about the relationship between flow payments and the value a chain can safely secure, with explicit assumptions.
  • Be careful with proof-of-work versus proof-of-stake here. The requirement to pay is common to both and is what makes this page Tier 1. How each mechanism makes attacks expensive is Tier 3 and belongs elsewhere. Resist the temptation to compare mechanisms on this page.
  • State plainly what is unknown: whether fee revenue alone can fund security in the long run is an open question, not a settled one. That honesty is worth more than a confident answer.

docs.title: References to work from
docs.text:
Verify before citing.

  • Budish, E. (2018). The Economic Limits of Bitcoin and the Blockchain. NBER working paper 24717.

Next: Who pays: issuance or fees

docs.title: Fixed cap or flexible supply
docs.text:
Stub — not written yet

This page is an outline. Delete this box when you fill it in.

Permanent. The trade-off is permanent, even though each chain's current issuance is not.

Bitcoin capped its supply at 21 million. Ethereum has no cap. This is the single clearest design disagreement between the two, and it follows directly from the previous two pages: if security must be paid for and the money comes from issuance or fees, then capping supply means eventually paying for security out of fees alone.

docs.title: The argument to make
docs.text:
The trade-off is real and neither side gets it for free.

A hard cap delivers a credible scarcity guarantee — the supply schedule is knowable in advance and politically very hard to change. The cost is that issuance tends to zero, so the security budget must eventually come entirely from transaction fees. Whether fee revenue is sufficient and stable enough to secure a large amount of value over decades is an open question.

No cap means the protocol can always pay for security, and can adjust what it pays as conditions change. The cost is that there's no scarcity guarantee: the supply schedule depends on parameters that governance can revise, so holders are relying on restraint rather than arithmetic.

Say plainly that this is unresolved. Both communities present their choice as obviously correct; neither has run long enough to know.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• What exactly does a supply cap guarantee, and what does it not? (It constrains quantity; it says nothing about demand, price, or security.)
  • Why does a cap force reliance on fees? Work through the arithmetic.
  • What would have to be true for fee-only security to work? (Sustained demand for block space at a level that funds the budget — and demand for block space is not the same thing as demand for the currency.)
  • What does "no cap" actually mean in practice — unlimited, or merely unconstrained in advance? What does constrain it?
  • How credible is each commitment? A cap is credible because changing it is politically unthinkable; an uncapped schedule is credible only insofar as governance is trusted. Credibility is the real variable here, not the number.
  • Is "scarcity" doing economic work, or is it a narrative? Worth addressing directly, because the reader will have met the narrative version.

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• This is the page most at risk of becoming advocacy. It's the inflation debate, and both sides have slogans ready. The discipline: describe each mechanism, state who bears which risk, and name what's unknown. Do not reach a verdict the evidence doesn't support.
  • Avoid the loaded vocabulary entirely — "sound money", "ultrasound money", "debasement". Each carries a conclusion inside it.
  • Keep current numbers off this page. Issuance rates and the burn are fork-dependent and usage-dependent; they belong in the later Ethereum-specific page, with a date stamp. This page is about the structure of the choice.
  • Worth noting that the question isn't unique to crypto: the trade-off between a credible nominal rule and discretionary flexibility is a very old one in monetary economics. That connection is the kind of thing almost no Ethereum writing makes, and it's yours to make.

docs.title: References to work from
docs.text:
Verify before citing.

  • Budish, E. (2018). The Economic Limits of Bitcoin and the Blockchain. NBER working paper 24717. Relevant to whether fee-funded security scales.
  • The monetary-policy-rules literature on rules versus discretion is the natural comparison. Pick whichever treatment you know best — this is your field, not mine.

Next: Who decides, when nobody is in charge — the question every page has assumed an answer to.

docs.title: Who pays: issuance or fees
docs.text:
Stub — not written yet

This page is an outline. Delete this box when you fill it in.

Permanent. There are only two sources of revenue, and that's arithmetic rather than protocol rules.

Given that security has to be paid for, the next question is who pays. There are exactly two possibilities.

docs.title: The argument to make
docs.text:
Issuance creates new currency and gives it to whoever did the work. Nobody is billed, so it looks free — but the existing holders now own a smaller share of the total. The cost is real and it's borne by them.

Fees charge the people who actually transact. Visible, voluntary in the sense that you can decline to transact, and paid only by users.

Both are taxes. The useful move is to treat this as a question of tax incidence — who really bears the cost, as opposed to who hands over the money. That framing is standard in public economics and almost absent from writing about blockchains, which is exactly why it's worth bringing.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• Why are there only two sources? (Value has to come from somewhere: either dilute the existing stock or charge the flow.)
  • Who actually bears the cost of issuance? Holders — but is that uniform? Consider who holds, who stakes, and who merely transacts.
  • Who bears the cost of fees? Users directly — but how much is passed on to the end users of applications built on top?
  • Why might a system prefer one over the other? Issuance charges everyone a little without them noticing; fees charge users visibly but spare holders. Those have different political economies.
  • What happens as issuance falls toward zero? The burden shifts entirely onto users. Is that sustainable, and what does it imply about required fee levels?
  • Is there a third option? (Treasury funding, inflation of a separate token, external subsidy — all tried elsewhere. Worth a sentence on why neither of the big two chains does this.)

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• Keep this page mechanism-free. It should read as applicable to any chain. Ethereum's specific mix of issuance and burn is Tier 3 and belongs in a later page.
  • The incidence framing is the page's whole contribution. Lead with it rather than burying it.
  • Resist moralising. "Inflation is theft from holders" and "fees are a tax on users" are both advocacy. Describe who bears what, and let the reader weigh it.
  • A small table — who pays / who benefits / visible or not — would do a lot of work here.

Next: Fixed cap or flexible supply

docs.title: The Merkle Patricia Trie
docs.text:
Mostly permanent. The structure has not changed since 2015, and everything it achieves — a single root committing to everything, cheap updates, small proofs — is permanent regardless of how it is built. The way it is built is the part under long-running attempts at replacement.

Current as of Fusaka (December 2025)

A replacement called a verkle tree has been proposed for years, to make proofs dramatically smaller. It has not shipped, and its specification (Buterin et al., 2023) is currently marked Stagnant — which is itself the useful status report. Treat verkle as a direction rather than a plan, and check before relying on anything about it.

Merkle Patricia Trie

The structure behind every root on Ethereum: the state root, each account's storage root, and a block's transactions and receipts roots.

It is a tree in which the path to a value is determined by its key, and every node is identified by the hash of its contents. The first makes it a lookup table. The second makes the single hash at the top a commitment to every value inside.

docs.title: What it has to do
docs.text:
Four requirements, and no simpler structure meets all four. The state page set out the first three; the fourth is the one usually left out and is arguably the most important.

1. Commit to everything in 32 bytes. Change one wei in one account and the root must change. Otherwise two nodes could hold different states and agree.

2. Be cheap to update. A block changes perhaps a few hundred accounts out of hundreds of millions. Re-hashing everything per block would be absurd.

3. Support proofs about parts. Somebody holding only the root should be able to be shown that one account holds one balance, without receiving the rest of the state.

4. Depend on the contents and nothing else. Two nodes that applied the same transactions in different internal orders — different insertion sequences, different storage layouts, different software — must still arrive at the same root. The structure cannot depend on history or implementation, only on what is in it.

That fourth requirement rules out most of the obvious answers. A sorted list depends on nothing but contents but fails (2) and (3). A hash of everything concatenated fails (2) and (3) too. A binary search tree meets (2) and (3) and fails (4), because its shape depends on the order things were inserted.

docs.title: First, the Merkle part
docs.text:
Take a set of values. Hash each one. Then hash the hashes in pairs, and the results in pairs, until one hash is left. That top hash is the root, and the arrangement is a Merkle tree — the idea comes from Merkle's work on signing many messages with one public value (Merkle, 1988).

Two properties fall out, and they're the two that matter.

The root commits to every value. Change any one of them and its hash changes, so its parent's hash changes, and so on to the top. There is no way to alter a value and leave the root alone — that would require a hash collision.

Ah(A)Bh(B)Ch(C)Dh(D)Eh(E)h(AB)h(CD)h(ABCD)ROOTno partner,so it ridesup as it isfive values — an odd number, so somebody has to decide what happens

And you can prove one value belongs without revealing the others. To convince somebody who knows only the root that a particular value is in the tree, you hand them the value plus the sibling hash at each level on the way up. They redo the hashing and see whether they arrive at the root they already trust. For a million values that's about twenty hashes — not a million.

That second property is the whole reason this structure exists rather than something simpler. Verification without possession, which is the same principle the node page used to explain why pruning is safe.

docs.title: What happens when the count is odd
docs.text:
Five values, as above, and pairing leaves one hash with no partner — twice over. Something has to be decided, and the diagram shows one answer: carry the lonely hash up unchanged until it finds a partner.

That is a choice, not a consequence. Other systems make different ones: Bitcoin duplicates the odd hash and pairs it with itself; some schemes pad the level out with a fixed dummy hash. All three work.

What matters is that the rule is fixed and the same everywhere. If one implementation promoted and another duplicated, the same five values would give two different roots — and the fourth requirement above would be broken. The odd case is a small thing that has to be nailed down precisely because it is small and easy to leave to taste.

Ethereum doesn't actually pair things up

Worth saying before the picture sticks, because the binary tree above is a teaching device rather than a description.

Pairwise hashing is the classic Merkle construction and the easiest way to see why a root commits to everything. Ethereum's execution layer doesn't use it. Its structure branches sixteen ways, not two, and a node hashes its children's references rather than pairing siblings — so the odd-number question never arises there at all. A branch node has however many children it has, and empty slots are simply empty.

What carries over from Merkle is the idea: hash-linked nodes, a root that commits to everything beneath it, and membership provable from the values along one path. What doesn't carry over is the pairing.

(Ethereum's consensus layer is a different matter — it does use a binary construction, padded out to a power of two. Which is one more way the two halves of a node differ, on top of the encodings the RLP page mentioned.)

docs.title: Second, the trie part
docs.text:
A Merkle tree commits to a list. Ethereum needs a mapping: given an address, find its account. So the second ingredient is a structure for looking things up.

Forget hashes for a moment and forget Ethereum. Suppose you want to store three words — cats, cars, dog — so that you can find any of them again.

A trie stores them by spelling them out. Start at the root. Take the first letter of your key and follow the branch marked with that letter. Take the second letter, follow that branch. Carry on until the key runs out, and whatever you find there is the value.

rootcdaotrgsends catssends carsends dogTen nodes. The five dashed ones have a single child and say only “keep going”.With 64-nibble keys, almost every node in the tree looks like one of those.

Two things to notice, and they're the reasons Ethereum wants this.

Nothing is ever searched for. You don't look through the structure comparing keys — you spell your key and the spelling walks you there. cars means: root, then c, then a, then r, then s. Four steps, no comparisons — and it would still be four steps with a billion other words in the tree.

And the shape comes from the keys alone. Insert the same three words in any order and you get the identical tree, because where a word sits is decided by its letters and nothing else. There is no rebalancing, no first-come advantage, no history.

That second point is requirement (4), met for free — and it is why two nodes that have never communicated compute the same root. Not by agreeing on anything: there was only ever one possible shape for those keys.

docs.title: What Ethereum does instead of letters
docs.text:
Same idea, two substitutions.

The keys aren't words, they're 32-byte hashes — keccak256 of an address, as the accounts page described.

And the "letters" aren't letters. Ethereum reads a key four bits at a time, a unit called a nibble — half a byte, which is exactly one hex digit. So instead of 26 possible branches at each step there are sixteen, one per hex digit, and a 32-byte key is 64 nibbles long: a 64-letter word in a sixteen-letter alphabet.

Which is why the structure is drawn with hex digits on its branches. a7f3… is just a word spelled a, 7, f, 3, and finding its account means spelling it out.

docs.title: Third, the Patricia part
docs.text:
Look again at the dashed nodes in that diagram. Five of the ten exist only to say keep going: c has one child, d has one child, o has one child. They hold no value and make no decision. They are pure overhead.

With real keys this is not a minor inefficiency — it is nearly the whole tree. A key is 64 nibbles. Once a key's path diverges from everybody else's, every remaining nibble gets a node of its own, each with exactly one child. A single account could easily account for fifty such nodes, every one of them storing one nibble and a pointer.

The fix is to collapse any run of single-child nodes into one node that holds the whole run. Instead of d → o → g, a single node saying "the rest of this path is og".

Applied to the same three keys:

BRANCHslots c and d usedEXTENSIONshared letters: aLEAFrest of key: ogvalue for dogBRANCHslots t and r usedLEAFrest: scatsLEAFrest: scarsd, o and g becameone leaf holdingthe whole tailSix nodes instead of ten, holding exactly the same three keys.

Walk it and nothing has changed about what's stored. cars still means root → c → a → r → s; it just takes three nodes to say it rather than five, because the shared a sits inside one node and the final s sits inside a leaf.

What's been removed is every node that had nothing to contribute. Ten nodes became six, and with 64-nibble keys the same move turns tens of thousands into a handful.

That technique is where the middle word of the name comes from: Morrison (1968) called it PATRICIA — Practical Algorithm To Retrieve Information Coded In Alphanumeric — twenty-six years before the web.

So the full name describes its three parts: Merkle for the hashing that makes it a commitment, Patricia for the compression that keeps it shallow, and trie for the keys deciding the path.

docs.title: Building the node types one at a time
docs.text:
The compressed structure needs exactly three kinds of node, and the easiest way to see why is to build a trie from nothing and add what each step forces.

Step 1 — one key. You have a single key and a single value, and nothing to divide. So you need a node that says "the rest of the path is this, and here's the value". That's a leaf: a remaining path plus a value. With only one key in the whole structure, the root is that leaf, and its remaining path is the entire key.

Step 2 — a second key that goes elsewhere. Add a key whose first nibble differs. Now the first nibble has to choose between two destinations, so you need a node that offers a choice. That's a branch: sixteen slots, one per possible nibble, each holding either nothing or a reference to the node you'd go to. Taking a step through a branch consumes one nibble of the key.

Step 3 — two keys that agree for a while. Add a key that shares the first twenty nibbles with an existing one. Branching on each of those twenty in turn would give twenty branch nodes with one slot filled each — the waste the previous section removed. So you need a node that says "the next twenty nibbles are all this, then continue". That's an extension: a run of shared nibbles plus a single child.

Step 4 — one key that stops where another carries on. Here's the case most explanations skip. Suppose one key ends exactly at a point where other keys divide — the path a7 has a value, and so do a7f1 and a7c2. The branch at a7 has to hold both the choices and a value for the key that finished there.

Which is why a branch has seventeen places rather than sixteen: sixteen slots for the nibbles, and a seventeenth for a value belonging to a key that ended right here. It's empty almost always — on hashed keys, one being a prefix of another is vanishingly rare — and the slot has to exist regardless, because the structure must handle it.

So, assembled:

Node Holds Exists because Leaf the rest of the key, and a value the path ends here Extension a run of shared nibbles, and one child a stretch of path divides nothing Branch sixteen slots, plus a value the path divides here

All three are specified in Appendix D of the Yellow Paper (Wood, 2014), along with the encoding trick that tells a leaf from an extension — both hold a path and something else, so a flag in the encoding distinguishes them.

keys, as nibbles: 1234 → alice 1256 → bob 789a → carolBRANCHslots 1 and 7 are usedEXTENSIONshared nibble: 2LEAFrest of key: 89avalue: carolBRANCHslots 3 and 5 are usedLEAFrest: 4aliceLEAFrest: 6bobEvery box is RLP-encoded and hashed, and each parent stores its children’shashes — so the hash of the top box depends on all three values.

Follow 1256 through it, nibble by nibble, and all four steps above appear in order:

  1. 1 — the root is a branch. Slot 1 holds a reference, so take it. One nibble used, three left: 256.
  2. 2 — next is an extension saying the shared run is 2. It matches what you hold, so continue past it. Two nibbles left: 56.
  3. 5 — a branch again, because this is where alice and bob part company. Slot 5 takes you onward. One nibble left: 6.
  4. 6 — a leaf, whose remaining path is 6. It matches, so its value is the answer.

Four nibbles, four nodes, no comparisons and no searching. And had you asked for 1299, step 3 would have found slot 9 of that branch empty — which is how the structure says no such key without looking anywhere else.

docs.title: Why RLP is the prerequisite
docs.text:
Each node is turned into bytes with RLP, and the hash of a node is the hash of its RLP.

Which is why the previous page had to come first, and why its obsession with canonicality was not pedantry. If a node could be encoded two ways, it would have two hashes, so its parent would have two hashes, and the root would not be a function of the state. The root is well-defined only because the encoding is.

Two details that surprise people

Small nodes are inlined, not referenced. A parent normally stores its child's 32-byte hash. But if a child's RLP comes to less than 32 bytes, the child is embedded in the parent directly instead — because a hash would be larger than the thing it points at. So the structure is not uniformly hash-linked, and a node's encoding can contain whole subtrees rather than references to them.

The empty trie has a root anyway. It is the hash of RLP's empty string — keccak256(0x80):

56e81f171bcc55a6ff8345e692c0f86e5b48e01b996cadc001622fb5e363b421

That constant is the storageRoot of every account with nothing stored, which is where the accounts page met it. It is the same arrangement as keccak256("") being the code hash of an account with no code: emptiness still has to have a fingerprint, or "nothing stored" could not be distinguished from "anything at all".

docs.title: What a proof actually is
docs.text:
This is the payoff, and the reason the structure is worth its complexity.

A proof that some account holds some value is the chain of nodes from the root down to that account's leaf. Nothing more.

Given it, somebody holding only the root can check the claim themselves:

  1. Hash the leaf, and confirm the node above references that hash.
  2. Hash that node, and confirm the node above references it.
  3. Continue to the top, and confirm the final hash is the root you already trusted.

If every link holds, the value is in the state — and if any byte of it had been altered, some hash along the way would not match.

The size is the point. A proof is one node per level, and the depth is bounded by the key length, so it is a handful of kilobytes regardless of whether the state holds a thousand accounts or a billion. Which is what makes a light client possible: software that stores no state at all, keeps only block headers, and asks others for proofs it can verify. It isn't trusting the answers. It's checking them against a root it obtained independently.

docs.title: Why the keys are hashed — and where they aren't
docs.text:
The accounts page established that the state trie is keyed by keccak256(address) rather than by the address, as a defence: creating an account needs no key, so an attacker could otherwise dust a million addresses sharing a long prefix and force one branch of the trie to be pathologically deep.

What's worth adding here is the contrast, because it shows the hashing is a targeted defence and not a reflex.

A block's transactions and receipts also live in tries. Their keys are not hashed — they are the transaction's index, 0, 1, 2, encoded with RLP. And they don't need hashing, because nobody can choose them. Indices are assigned by position in the block, so there is no way to craft one, and therefore nothing to defend against.

So the rule is sharper than "Ethereum hashes trie keys":

Hash the keys where an adversary picks them. Don't where they are assigned.

Which is also a useful test to carry into other systems: ask who chooses the key, and the need for hashing answers itself.

docs.title: The four tries
docs.text:
Trie Key Value Keys hashed? State an address the account's four fields yes Storage, one per contract a 32-byte slot number the stored value yes Transactions, one per block the index in the block the transaction no Receipts, one per block the index in the block the receipt no

The first two are the ones this site has been building towards: the state root in the block header, and each account's storage root inside its entry — a trie whose leaves contain the roots of other tries. Change one storage slot in one contract and that contract's storage root changes, so its account entry changes, so the state root changes. One number at the top, all the way down.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The structure must do four things: commit to everything in 32 bytes, update cheaply, prove parts, and depend only on contents. The fourth rules out most alternatives, because it forbids any shape that depends on insertion order.
  • Merkle: hash the values, hash the hashes, up to one root. Changing any value changes the root, and one value can be proved with the sibling hashes along its path.
  • Trie: the key is the route, read a nibble at a time, sixteen directions per branch. Lookup needs no search, and the shape comes from the keys rather than from history.
  • Patricia: collapse single-child runs, so 64-nibble keys don't mean 64 levels.
  • Three node types — leaf, extension, branch — and a branch has seventeen slots because a key can end where another divides.
  • Nodes are hashed after RLP encoding, so the root is well-defined only because the encoding is canonical.
  • A proof is the chain of nodes from root to leaf: a few kilobytes whatever the state's size, which is what makes light clients possible. Verification without possession, again.
  • Keys are hashed in the state and storage tries and not in the transactions and receipts tries — because the first two have keys an adversary can choose and the last two do not. Hash the keys where an adversary picks them.
  • Storage roots sit inside account entries, so it is tries inside a trie, and one slot changing reaches the top.

Next: Transactions — what's actually in one, now that there's a way to write it down.
