docs.title: RLP encoding
docs.text:
Permanent. Recursive Length Prefix has not been revised since Ethereum launched in 2015, and cannot be: every hash the network has ever agreed on was taken over bytes it produced.

RLP

Recursive Length Prefix. A way of turning nested lists of byte strings into one flat sequence of bytes, reversibly.

It encodes exactly two things: a byte string, and a list of items which may themselves be strings or lists. Nothing else — no integers, no booleans, no names, no types.

Its defining property is canonicality: each value has exactly one valid encoding, and anything else is rejected.

docs.title: It encodes two things, and nothing else
docs.text:
Start with what it refuses to do, because that is most of the design.

RLP has no integers. No booleans, no decimals, no field names, no types, no maps. The two things it knows about are a run of bytes and a list.

So nonce: 3 isn't something RLP can express. What gets encoded is the byte 0x03, in a particular position in a list, and the position is what makes it the nonce. Anything wanting to encode a number converts it to bytes first; anything wanting to label a field relies on the reader knowing the order.

That sounds like an omission and is a deliberate narrowing. A format that describes types has to have opinions about them — how big an integer may be, how text is encoded, what a missing field means — and every opinion is something two implementations could implement differently. RLP has almost nothing to disagree about.

docs.title: The entire specification
docs.text:
What follows is not a summary. These five cases are RLP's entire definition — the normative content of Appendix B of the Yellow Paper (Wood, 2014), plus the canonicality rules further down. There is nothing else to the format.

Everything turns on the first byte, which says which of five cases applies and how long the thing is.

First byte Decoding — what that byte tells you Encoding — how to produce it 0x00–0x7f the byte is the data a byte under 0x80 is left as it is 0x80–0xb7 a string of 0–55 bytes; length = byte − 0x80 prefix = 0x80 + length 0xb8–0xbf a longer string; byte − 0xb7 = how many bytes of length come next prefix = 0xb7 + number of length bytes 0xc0–0xf7 a list with 0–55 bytes of contents; length = byte − 0xc0 prefix = 0xc0 + length of contents 0xf8–0xff a longer list; byte − 0xf7 = bytes of length coming next prefix = 0xf7 + number of length bytes

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
The same five rows serve both jobs, approached from opposite ends.

You have bytes and want the data. Take the first byte, find the row whose range contains it, and read the middle column. Say the byte is 0x83: it falls between 0x80 and 0xb7, so it's a short string, and 0x83 − 0x80 = 3 means the next three bytes are the data. Done — 83 64 6f 67 is "dog".

You have data and want bytes. Measure what you're encoding, pick the row that fits, and read the right column. Three bytes of string: short-string row, so the prefix is 0x80 + 3 = 0x83, followed by the three bytes.

So the subtraction and the addition are one fact read in two directions, and that's the thing to keep hold of. "dog" encodes to 0x83 because 0x80 + 3; a decoder meeting 0x83 subtracts to get the 3 back. It is never 0x80 − 3.

Two values worth memorising, because they turn up everywhere: 0x80 is the empty string and 0xc0 is the empty list.

docs.title: One thing that looks like a mistake and isn't
docs.text:
The long-string row subtracts 0xb7 while its range begins at 0xb8. The bases and the range starts don't line up, and that's deliberate.

A short string may be empty, so 0x80 has to mean "length 0" — the base and the range start coincide. A long string, by contrast, always carries at least one byte of length; there is no such thing as zero length bytes. So the smallest value that case ever expresses is 1, and 0xb7 + 1 = 0xb8. The base sits one below the range because the count starts at one rather than zero.

Same for lists: 0xc0 can mean an empty list, so its base is its range start; 0xf7 is one below 0xf8 for the same reason as 0xb7.

The arithmetic behind the table

The whole format is squeezed into one byte's worth of possibilities, and the five cases divide those 256 values exactly:

Range Values Spent on 0x00–0x7f 128 bytes that encode themselves 0x80–0xb7 56 string lengths 0 to 55 0xb8–0xbf 8 long strings: 1 to 8 bytes of length 0xc0–0xf7 56 list lengths 0 to 55 0xf8–0xff 8 long lists: 1 to 8 bytes of length 256 nothing spare, nothing overlapping

Why 55, and not a rounder number? It isn't chosen — it falls out. Half the byte values go to self-encoding bytes, leaving 128. Those split into two halves of 64 for strings and lists, and each half keeps 8 values at the top for the long form, leaving 56. Fifty-six slots counted from zero reach 55.

Why 8 for the long form? Because eight values is all the space left, and eight is more than enough. Eight bytes of length count to 264 − 1, about 1.8 × 1019 — eighteen exabytes in a single field.

So what happens to something longer than that? It cannot be encoded. The first byte stops at 0xbf for strings and 0xff for lists, so there is no way to say "nine bytes of length": the format has no case for it and an encoder simply cannot express the value. The same hard ceiling applies to both strings and lists.

This is a limit in the strict sense and irrelevant in practice. A single field of eighteen exabytes is about a million times the whole of Ethereum's state, and every field here is something a node must store and a block must carry. The ceiling exists; nothing will ever reach it.

Worth keeping the two thresholds apart, since they're easy to conflate: 55 bytes is where a value switches from the short form to the long one, and happens constantly. Eight length bytes is where the long form itself runs out, and never happens.

And the whole design is one trade. Short things — which is nearly everything — pay a single byte of overhead. Long things pay two to nine. A format that used a fixed four-byte length would be simpler to describe and would waste three bytes on every small field, in a system that stores and hashes billions of them.

docs.title: Worked, byte by byte
docs.text:
"dog" → three bytes of data, so the prefix is 0x80 + 3:

83 64 6f 67
^^ ^^^^^^^^
|  d  o  g
prefix: short string, 3 bytes

["cat", "dog"] → encode each item first, then wrap the results.

"cat" is three characters, and encodes to four bytes: 83 63 61 74 — a one-byte prefix plus three of data. "dog" is the same shape, 83 64 6f 67. So the contents of the list are 4 + 4 = 8 bytes, and the list prefix is 0xc0 + 8 = 0xc8:

c8 83 63 61 74 83 64 6f 67
^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^
|   4 bytes      4 bytes
prefix: list, 8 bytes of contents

What the 8 counts is the thing most easily got wrong. It is not the number of items, and not the number of characters. It is the length of the already-encoded contents, prefixes included — so each item's own 0x83 is part of what the list is measuring. A list of two three-letter words comes to eight bytes because each word costs four.

1024 → first becomes the bytes 0x04 0x00, then encodes as a two-byte string: 82 04 00.

The single byte 0x0f → 0f. It's below 0x80, so it encodes as itself with no prefix at all.

The single byte 0x80 → 81 80. It is not below 0x80, so it needs the prefix, and the result is two bytes where the input was one.

Try it: take any RLP apart

RLP bytes, as hex "dog" ["cat","dog"] nested lists empty string non-canonical

Highlighted bytes are prefixes — structure rather than content. The number at the start of each line is the byte offset, so you can find any piece in the original hex.

Step 1 — press nested lists. c7c0c1c0c3c0c1c0 is eight bytes and contains six lists, three of them nested two deep. Every byte is either a prefix or a prefix inside a prefix: there is no data at all.

Step 2 — press non-canonical. 8100 says "a one-byte string containing 0x00". That value already has an encoding — the byte 0x00 on its own — so this one is rejected rather than tolerated. The refusal is the feature, for reasons the next section explains.

Step 3 — break something deliberately. Change c8 to c9 in the second example: the list now claims nine bytes of contents and only eight follow, so it fails. RLP has no padding and no end markers, which means a single wrong byte is detected rather than silently reinterpreted.

docs.title: Why not JSON?
docs.text:
The obvious question. JSON exists, every language reads it, and it would have been free.

Because of what Ethereum does with these bytes: it hashes them. The state root, every transaction hash, every block hash — all are hashes of RLP-encoded data. And Keccak-256 gives a completely different output for a single changed byte.

Now consider two programs encoding the same transaction as JSON. One writes {"nonce":3,"gas":21000}, the other {"gas":21000, "nonce":3}. Same data, different bytes, different hash. Add whitespace, key order, 3 versus 3.0, escaped versus literal characters, and you have dozens of ways to write one value.

For an API that is harmless. For Ethereum it is fatal: two nodes with identical state would compute different state roots and reject each other's blocks, and the network would stop. The state page's whole argument — two nodes agreeing on 32 bytes agree on everything — holds only if identical data always produces identical bytes.

So RLP is built around the opposite priority. One value, one encoding, and every alternative rejected. It isn't a better JSON; it's a format for a job JSON cannot do.

docs.title: Which is why there are no leading zeros
docs.text:
The same reasoning, applied to numbers.

The number 1 encodes as the byte 0x01. It must not also be encodable as 0x0001, or 0x000001 — because those are different bytes, and different bytes hash differently. So the rule is that a number's byte form carries no leading zeros, and an encoder that emits them has produced something a strict decoder will refuse.

Every canonicality rule has this shape. A rule exists wherever a value could otherwise have been written two ways: no leading zeros in numbers, no leading zeros in lengths, no long form where the short form fits, no prefix on a byte that encodes itself. Together they leave exactly one path from any value to its bytes.

docs.title: What RLP doesn't tell you
docs.text:
A thing people assume and shouldn't: the bytes don't say what they mean.

Decode a transaction and you get a list of byte strings. Nothing in it says which is the nonce, which is the recipient, or that the twenty-byte one is an address at all. A decoder returns structure; interpretation comes from the reader knowing what shape to expect.

Which is not in tension with what the first section said about position. RLP preserves order faithfully, and order is exactly what a convention can attach meaning to — the second item really is the nonce, every time, reliably. What the bytes never carry is the convention itself. Position is where the meaning is kept; it is not where the meaning is written down.

Which is why the tool above can tell you that something is a three-item list of strings and not what any of it is for. Meaning lives in the specification and in the code, never in the encoding — the same division as the ABI, where the protocol sees bytes and the convention supplies the names.

docs.title: Where it's used
docs.text:
Everywhere the execution layer writes something down:

  • Transactions, so that signing has a defined set of bytes to sign
  • Block headers, so that a block hash is the hash of something definite
  • Account entries in the state, which is why the accounts page described a state value as RLP[nonce, balance, storageRoot, codeHash]
  • Every node of the trie — the next page builds on this one for exactly that reason

So RLP is underneath every hash this site has mentioned. It is also the reason the trie page has to come after this one.

RLP is no longer the only answer

Worth knowing, because "Ethereum uses RLP" is close to true and not quite.

Newer transactions are not plain RLP. Since EIP-2718 (Zoltu, 2020), a transaction may be a single type byte followed by a payload, and the specification deliberately treats that payload as opaque bytes so that future types need not use RLP at all. Current types do use RLP inside the envelope, so in practice you decode the first byte, then decode the rest as RLP.

And the consensus layer doesn't use RLP at all. It uses a different serialisation, chosen partly because RLP is awkward to produce proofs about. So the two halves of a node described on clients and the two layers differ even in how they write bytes down.

Neither changes anything on this page. RLP still encodes what it encodes, unchanged — it simply isn't the only format in the building any more.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• RLP turns nested lists of byte strings into one flat byte sequence. It encodes strings and lists, and nothing else — no integers, no names, no types.
  • A field is identified by its position, not by a label.
  • Four rules, keyed on the first byte: self-encoding bytes below 0x80, short strings from 0x80, long strings from 0xb8, lists from 0xc0. 0x80 is the empty string; 0xc0 the empty list.
  • Lengths under 56 fit in the prefix; beyond that the prefix says how many bytes the length takes.
  • The reason for all of it is canonicality: one value, one encoding. Ethereum hashes these bytes, so two spellings of the same data would mean two different hashes and a network that cannot agree.
  • Hence no leading zeros, no long form where short fits, no prefix on a self-encoding byte. A rule exists wherever a value could have been written two ways.
  • JSON cannot do this job — key order and whitespace alone give one value many spellings.
  • RLP carries no meaning. Decoding gives structure; what the fields are comes from the specification, like the ABI.
  • Used for transactions, block headers, account entries and every trie node — so it sits underneath every hash on this site.
  • Not universal any more: typed transactions wrap an opaque payload, and the consensus layer uses something else entirely.

Next: The Merkle Patricia Trie — what the state root actually is, built out of RLP and hashes.

docs.text:

docs.title: Ether, wei and gwei
docs.text:
Permanent. There have been 1018 wei to one ether since Ethereum launched in 2015, and changing it now would break every wallet and contract in existence.

Ether · wei

Ether is Ethereum's native currency, ticker ETH. You need it to pay for anything the network does on your behalf.

Wei is the unit it is counted in — 1018 wei to one ether. Every amount on Ethereum is a whole number of wei. The protocol has no decimals anywhere.

docs.title: Ethereum is the network. Ether is the currency.
docs.text:
Ethereum is the network — the state machine, the computers running it, the rules they follow. Ether is what moves across it.

So "I sent you 2 Ethereum" is wrong in the same way "I paid you 50 Visa" is wrong. You send ether; Ethereum is the thing that moves it.

One consequence worth having early: ether isn't only money for buying things. You need ether to do anything at all, because every transaction costs a fee and fees are payable only in ether.

This has a consequence people meet in practice. Suppose an account holds a large amount of some token — a stablecoin, say — and no ether. It can still receive things, since receiving requires no transaction from you. But it cannot send anything, including the tokens it holds, because sending means submitting a transaction and there's no ether to pay the fee with. The tokens are visible, owned, and stuck until somebody sends a little ether to the account.

What is an ether worth?

Whatever people are currently willing to pay for it. The price is set by markets, it moves constantly, and it has ranged over several orders of magnitude across Ethereum's life.

There's deliberately no number on this page. Any figure written here would be wrong within hours, and a reference page that quietly goes stale is worse than one that declines to answer. For a current price, any exchange or market tracker will tell you.

The more useful thing to understand is what the price means. Because you pay for computation in ether, the price of ether is also the cost of using Ethereum. When ether gets more valuable, every transaction gets more expensive in real terms — which is why fees are discussed so obsessively, and why the network's capacity matters so much.

Two structural points, which don't change with the price:

  • There is no fixed supply cap. Bitcoin has one; Ethereum does not. New ether is issued to reward validators, and some is destroyed when fees are paid, so the total can rise or fall over time.
  • Ether is not backed by anything and makes no promise of value. It's useful because the network is useful, and valuable because people want it. Nothing more solid than that.

docs.title: Wei is the smallest unit
docs.text:
There are 1018 wei in one ether — a billion billion. Wei is the unit the specification itself counts in: the Yellow Paper defines balances and fees in wei throughout, and treats ether as a denomination on top (Wood, 2014).

1 ether = 1,000,000,000,000,000,000 wei

It's named after Wei Dai, a cryptographer who in 1998 described b-money (Dai, 1998), one of the ideas that fed into cryptocurrencies. Several other units were defined early on with similar namesakes, and almost nobody uses them. In practice you'll meet three: wei, gwei, ether.

docs.title: Yes — wei is Ethereum's satoshi
docs.text:
The comparison is exact in role, and the difference is only in scale:

Bitcoin Ethereum Currency bitcoin ether Smallest unit satoshi wei How many per unit 108 (100 million) 1018 (a billion billion) Decimal places 8 18

Both systems do the same thing for the same reason: pick a smallest unit, count only in whole numbers of it, and let software display the friendly version.

And wei is genuinely indivisible. There is no sub-wei unit and no way to hold half a wei — not because nobody has defined one, but because balances are whole numbers and a fraction of the smallest unit cannot be represented. One wei is the atom.

docs.title: Ethereum never stores a decimal point
docs.text:
This is the part that matters, and it's not a detail.

Every balance, every transfer, every fee is a whole number of wei. Your wallet showing "2.5 ETH" is doing a presentation trick. What the chain actually holds is:

2500000000000000000

The decimal point is a display choice made by software. It does not exist anywhere in the protocol.

docs.title: Why integers? Because of determinism
docs.text:
Recall what the previous page established: thousands of computers each apply the rules independently and must arrive at an identical answer. That's what makes checking possible, and therefore what makes trust unnecessary.

Now try computing 0.1 + 0.2 on a computer. In most programming languages you don't get 0.3 — you get 0.30000000000000004. Computers store fractions in binary, and plenty of ordinary decimals have no exact binary form, so there is always rounding. Worse, exactly how it rounds can differ between processors, compilers and languages (Goldberg, 1991).

For most software a rounding error in the seventeenth decimal place is harmless. For Ethereum it is fatal. If two nodes computed the same balance and got answers differing by one part in a quadrillion, they would disagree about the state — and there would be no single answer for the network to agree on. The whole structure depends on arithmetic that comes out the same everywhere, every time.

Integer arithmetic has no such problem. It is exact, and identical on every machine ever built. 2500000000000000000 − 1000000000000000000 is the same number in every language, on every processor, forever.

So the rule, and it's a consequence rather than a preference:

Count in the smallest unit. Use integers only. Let the display layer put the dot in.

Why 1018, and not as fine as the machine allows?

A fair question: the EVM works on 256-bit unsigned integers, so it could represent roughly 1.16 × 1077 distinct values. Why stop at 1018 subdivisions rather than using everything available?

Because you need arithmetic headroom. Contracts don't just store balances, they compute with them — multiplying an amount by a price, by an interest rate, by a share. Multiplication is where it hurts: multiply two numbers that each use half the available bits and the result overflows.

The numbers work out comfortably. Total ether supply is on the order of 1026 wei, which occupies about 87 of the 256 bits available. That leaves roughly 169 bits spare for intermediate results — enough that ordinary arithmetic on realistic balances cannot overflow. Had ether been subdivided as finely as the type allows, every balance would consume the whole word and any multiplication would be unsafe.

And more precision would be useless. 18 decimal places already lets you express a quantity far smaller than any amount anyone could meaningfully transact. The constraint on usefulness is economic, not arithmetic.

18 is also simply convenient. It's a round power of ten, so converting is moving a decimal point rather than doing a calculation, and "18 decimals" became the convention most tokens follow in turn.

docs.title: Why fees are quoted in gwei
docs.text:
One gwei is 109 wei — a billion wei. The prefix is giga, so written out in full the unit is gigawei.

It exists for one reason: readability.

An example will make that obvious far quicker than an argument would — and setting one up needs just a single piece of background.

A fee on Ethereum isn't a flat charge. It's a price per unit of computational work, and that unit is called gas — which gets a page of its own later. All that matters here is that a fee comes out as a price, and prices need a unit to be quoted in.

Write one such price three ways and the choice makes itself:

Unit The same gas price wei 20000000000 ether 0.00000002 gwei 20

Gas prices land naturally in the single-to-low-hundreds range when written in gwei, so that's what wallets and fee trackers use. Nothing deeper than that: it's simply the scale at which the numbers are readable.

Gwei, gwei or gigawei?

All three appear in the wild, and no standard settles it. Two things can be said definitely.

Spelled out in full, it's one word: gigawei. Metric prefixes never take a space — gigawatt, not giga watt — so "giga wei" isn't right.

In code it is always lowercase. Solidity accepts wei, gwei and ether as suffixes on a numeric literal, and those keywords are case-sensitive (Solidity documentation, v0.8.26):

assert(1 wei == 1);
assert(1 gwei == 1e9);
assert(1 ether == 1e18);

That list has itself shrunk, incidentally, which is some evidence for how unsettled the naming is: szabo and finney were once valid suffixes too, and have since been removed from the language.

That's the reason this site writes lowercase everywhere. Prose and code then agree, and there's no sense in spelling the same unit two ways inside one project. Capitalised Gwei is perfectly defensible — block explorers and market sites commonly use it — but choosing it means every code example on the site contradicts the surrounding text, for no gain.

Lowercase also happens to match how SI writes spelled-out units named after people: volt, watt, newton. That's a weaker argument though, since wei is not an SI unit and the analogy is just an analogy. The compiler is a rule.

docs.title: The conversion table
docs.text:
Unit Wei In ether 1 wei 1 0.000000000000000001 1 gwei 1000000000 0.000000001 1 ether 1000000000000000000 1

Going from ether to wei means moving the decimal point 18 places right. From gwei to wei, 9 places right. That's the whole arithmetic.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Ethereum is the network, ether is its currency. You need ether to use the network at all.
  • Wei is the smallest unit: 1018 per ether, and genuinely indivisible. It's Ethereum's equivalent of Bitcoin's satoshi, just far finer.
  • The protocol holds only whole numbers of wei. The decimal point you see is added by software.
  • That's required, not stylistic: decimal fractions round differently on different machines, nodes would disagree, and determinism would break.
  • Fees are quoted in gwei (109 wei), the scale at which they read most easily.

Next: Hex and bytes — how those numbers are actually written down.

docs.text:

  • Goldberg, D. (1991). What every computer scientist should know about floating-point arithmetic. ACM Computing Surveys, 23(1), 5–48. https://doi.org/10.1145/103162.103163
  • Solidity documentation, v0.8.26. Units and globally available variables. Documents wei, gwei and ether as case-sensitive suffixes on numeric literals. Version-pinned deliberately: the latest URL moves, and szabo and finney were removed from earlier versions. https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/v0.8.26/units-and-global-variables.html
  • Wood, G. (2014). Ethereum: A secure decentralised generalised transaction ledger. Ethereum project yellow paper. Defines wei as the base unit of account. https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf

docs.title: Hex and bytes
docs.text:
Permanent. This isn't an Ethereum rule at all — it's how computers represent data.

Everything on Ethereum is eventually a string of characters like this:

0xd8dA6BF26964aF9D7eEd9e03E53415D37aA96045

This page is about how to read that. It's short, and it exists so that later pages can say "32 bytes" and have it mean something.

Byte · hexadecimal

A byte is eight bits — one of 256 possible values, conventionally read as a number from 0 to 255.

Hexadecimal, or hex, is base 16: the digits 0–9 plus the letters a–f. One byte is exactly two hex characters, and that single fact is the only reason anyone writes data this way.

docs.title: A byte is eight bits
docs.text:
A bit is a single one or zero. A byte is eight of them in a row:

0 1 1 0 1 0 0 1

How many different bytes are possible? Each position is independently a 0 or a 1, so every position you add doubles the number of patterns. Small cases first, because the pattern is easier to see than to state:

Bits Patterns All of them 1 2 0 1 2 4 00 01 10 11 3 8 000 001 010 011 100 101 110 111 8 256 00000000 … 11111111

Each extra bit doubles it: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256. That's 28.

By convention each pattern is read as a number, counting up from zero:

00000000  =    0
00000001  =    1
00000010  =    2
00000011  =    3
   ...
11111110  =  254
11111111  =  255

So "one byte" and "a number from 0 to 255" are two descriptions of the same thing. The byte is the unit everything gets measured in — not because eight is mathematically special, but because it's what hardware settled on, and the whole stack has counted in bytes since.

docs.title: How a pattern becomes a number
docs.text:
The same way a decimal number does, except each position is worth twice the one to its right instead of ten times. So the place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 — the powers of two.

Take the byte from the top of this section, 01101001. Multiply each bit by its place value and add up:

0 × 128  =    0
1 ×  64  =   64
1 ×  32  =   32
0 ×  16  =    0
1 ×   8  =    8
0 ×   4  =    0
0 ×   2  =    0
1 ×   1  =    1
            ────
             105

A bit is either 0 or 1, so each position either contributes its place value or contributes nothing. Reading a byte is just adding up the place values wherever there's a 1: 64 + 32 + 8 + 1 = 105.

Which also shows where the 0-to-255 range comes from. The largest possible byte is 11111111, every position contributing:

128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255

And the smallest is 00000000, contributing nothing at all. Zero to 255, with every value in between reachable exactly once.

docs.title: Hexadecimal
docs.text:
Base 16 needs sixteen digits, and since we only have ten, the first six letters fill in. The encoding is standardised, as Base16 (Josefsson, 2006), though you'll never see it called that outside a specification:

Hex Decimal Hex Decimal 0–9 0–9 d 13 a 10 e 14 b 11 f 15 c 12

So f is 15, and 10 in hex is sixteen.

docs.title: Reading a hex number
docs.text:
Exactly the same trick as the bits above, with a different multiplier. Each position is worth 16 times the one to its right — where in binary it was twice, and in decimal ten times.

So the place values are the powers of sixteen: 1, 16, 256, 4096. Take 0x2f:

0x2f
  │└─ f  = 15,  in the ones place      →  15 × 1   =  15
  └── 2  =  2,  in the sixteens place  →   2 × 16  =  32
                                                      ──
                                                      47

And a four-character example, 0x1234:

4 × 1     =     4
3 × 16    =    48
2 × 256   =   512
1 × 4096  =  4096
             ─────
              4660

That's all there is to it. Nothing about hex is conceptually different from decimal — only the number of digits available.

Try it: convert between decimal, hex and binary

Type into any field and the other two follow. It starts on 0x1234, the example above.

Decimal Hex Binary

Things worth trying:

  • 255, then 256. One byte becomes two, because 255 is the largest value a single byte holds.
  • ff, then 100 in the hex field — the same boundary from the other side.
  • A real address, like 0xd8dA6BF26964aF9D7eEd9e03E53415D37aA96045. It reports 20 bytes, and the decimal equivalent is an absurd number nobody would ever want to read. Which is the point of the next section.
  • 10101010 in binary. Note it comes out as aa — each hex character is exactly four bits.

docs.title: Why base 16, and not 10
docs.text:
Because of one tidy coincidence: one byte is exactly two hex characters.

A byte holds 256 values. Two hex characters give 16 × 16 = 256 possibilities. They correspond perfectly, with nothing left over:

Bits Hex Decimal 00000000 00 0 00001111 0f 15 00010000 10 16 10101010 aa 170 11111111 ff 255

Notice that two hex characters also split the byte neatly in half: the left character is the first four bits, the right character the last four. aa is 1010 then 1010.

Decimal has no such alignment, and the consequence matters.

To see why, put yourself on the receiving end. A program sends you some characters and tells you they're three bytes. Your job is to work out what those three bytes were — and you don't know their values in advance. That's the whole task.

In hex, every byte is two characters, whatever its value:

The byte In hex 5 05 255 ff 7 07

So it arrives as six characters:

05ff07

Six characters, two per byte, three bytes. Cut after every second character and you're done: 05 ff 07. And that procedure would have worked for any three bytes, which is the important part.

In decimal, how many digits a byte takes depends on its value:

The byte In decimal Digits 5 5 one 255 255 three 7 7 one

So it arrives as five characters:

52557

Now where do you cut? You have five characters to divide into three bytes, and several ways to do it are perfectly legal:

Reading Bytes Valid? 5 25 57 5, 25, 57 yes — all ≤ 255 52 5 57 52, 5, 57 yes 5 255 7 5, 255, 7 yes — the right one 52 55 7 52, 55, 7 yes

Four readings, all legitimate, and nothing in the string tells you which was meant. To know that each byte took one, three and one digits, you'd have to already know the values — which is precisely what you were trying to find out.

That's the alignment hex has and decimal hasn't. In hex the boundaries are implied by position, because every byte is the same width. In decimal they aren't implied at all, so they'd have to be sent separately — and at that point you've invented a worse version of hex.

d8 dA 6B F2 69 64 aF 9D 7e Ed 9e 03 E5 34 15 D3 7a A9 60 45

That's the address from the top of the page, as the twenty bytes it actually is.

Hex is also case-insensitive as a number — aF and AF are the same value. (Mixed case in an address does carry meaning, but as a checksum rather than as part of the number. That's covered under addresses.)

docs.title: The 0x prefix
docs.text:
0x means "what follows is hexadecimal". That's all. It is not part of the value — it's a label, so that 0x11 isn't mistaken for eleven.

The convention comes from the C programming language and is used nearly everywhere. Ethereum tooling puts it on essentially everything.

docs.title: The two lengths worth memorising
docs.text:
Almost every long string you meet on Ethereum is one of two sizes:

Bytes Hex characters What it usually is 20 40 an address 32 64 a hash, or one slot of contract storage

Worth doing once, by hand: count the characters after the 0x in the address above. There are forty. That's twenty bytes, and from now on "20 bytes" and "40 hex characters" should feel like the same statement.

The 32-byte figure turns up constantly because it's the output size of Keccak-256, Ethereum's hash function, and also the width of a single machine word in the EVM.

docs.title: One trap worth knowing about
docs.text:
0x1234 can mean two different things, and conflating them causes real bugs.

As a number, it's 4660 — the calculation from earlier.

As bytes, it's two bytes: 0x12 and 0x34.

Both readings are valid. Which is meant depends on context — and the context is really what you intend to do with it.

A number is a quantity. You add to it, subtract from it, ask whether it's bigger than another one. A balance is a quantity: 2.5 ether plus 1 ether is a meaningful thing to compute.

A byte string is an identifier. You compare it for equality and you check its length. That's all. An address isn't a quantity — the only questions worth asking are "is this 20 bytes?" and "is this the same address as that one?"

Which is why "is this address larger than that address?" is not a meaningful question, even though both look like enormous numbers. It's the same category error as asking whether one phone number is bigger than another: the digits are there to identify, not to count.

So: balances are numbers. Addresses, hashes and storage keys are byte strings. Nothing good comes of doing arithmetic on the second group.

Leading zeros, and why they sometimes matter

The distinction above has a sharp edge: as a number, leading zeros are meaningless; as bytes, they are not.

0x01 and 0x0001 are the same number — one. But they are different byte strings: one byte versus two. So a 32-byte hash beginning 00 has not somehow lost a byte, and padding a value to 32 bytes changes its length without changing its value.

This matters more than it sounds. RLP requires that integers be encoded with no leading zeros, precisely so that each value has exactly one valid encoding. Without that rule, 0x01 and 0x0001 would both be valid encodings of the same number, two nodes could hash the same data and get different answers, and consensus would break.

So "is this a number or a byte string?" isn't pedantry — the answer determines whether 0x0001 is well-formed.

Big-endian, and why the direction is a choice

Here's the problem. Take the two bytes 0x12 and 0x34, in that order, and read them as one number. There are two defensible answers, because you first have to agree which end carries the large part.

Big-endian treats the first byte as the most significant:

0x12 × 256  +  0x34        =  18 × 256 + 52  =  4660

Little-endian treats the last byte as the most significant, so the same two bytes are read in the other order:

0x34 × 256  +  0x12        =  52 × 256 + 18  =  13330

Same bytes on disk. Two different numbers. Which is why it has to be agreed rather than assumed.

Ethereum is big-endian — integers are serialised most-significant-byte first throughout the specification (Wood, 2014).

The convenient consequence is that hex strings read in the direction you already expect. In decimal 1234, the leftmost digit carries the largest place value; big-endian does the same thing with bytes, so 0x1234 is 4660, exactly as the place-value calculation earlier gave.

You can go a long way without thinking about this. It becomes unavoidable the moment you write code converting between numbers and bytes, which is where most beginner mistakes in this area live.

docs.title: Why not binary?
docs.text:
You could write everything in bits, and occasionally that's clearer — it's the only way to see a single flag being set.

But bits are unmanageably long. The address at the top of this page is twenty bytes, which is 160 bits:

1101100010011010011010111111001001101001011001001010111110011101...

Forty hex characters, or a hundred and sixty ones and zeros. Hex is the compromise: compact enough to read aloud, and still exactly aligned to byte boundaries.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A byte is 8 bits, holding one of 256 values.
  • Hex is base 16, using 0–9 and a–f.
  • One byte is exactly two hex characters — the reason hex is used at all.
  • 0x means "hex follows" and isn't part of the value.
  • 20 bytes = 40 characters = an address. 32 bytes = 64 characters = a hash.
  • Whether a hex string is a number or a byte string is a real distinction, and leading zeros are where it bites.

Next: Keccak-256 — the function that turns any input into 32 of these bytes.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Josefsson, S. (2006). The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings. RFC 4648, Internet Engineering Task Force. Specifies Base16 — hexadecimal — as a data encoding. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4648
  • Wood, G. (2014). Ethereum: A secure decentralised generalised transaction ledger. Ethereum project yellow paper. Appendix B sets out the big-endian convention and the no-leading-zeros rule for integer serialisation. https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf

docs.title: What is Ethereum?
docs.text:
Ethereum is a shared computer that nobody owns.

That sentence is doing a lot of work, so let's take it apart properly. The most useful way to understand Ethereum is not as a currency, or a blockchain, or a network. It's as a state machine — and once that clicks, most other things about it stop being surprising.

Ethereum

A state machine run in step by thousands of computers: a shared record of what every account holds and what every program has stored, plus rules for changing it that are identical everywhere.

Because those rules are deterministic, anybody can recompute the result and check it. That is why the system needs nobody in charge.

docs.title: A state machine
docs.text:
A state machine is just two things:

  1. State — everything that is stored as of now.
  2. Rules — which changes are valid, and what the state becomes after one.

A chess board is a state machine. The state is where the pieces are. The rules are the legal moves. Given a board and a move, everyone in the world can work out the new board and they'll all get the same answer. There's no ambiguity, and there's no need to trust the person who told you the move was made — you can work out the result and check it yourself.

This isn't a metaphor invented to help beginners, incidentally. Ethereum's formal specification — the Yellow Paper, Wood (2014) — describes it in exactly these terms: a transaction-based state machine. The framing is the protocol's own.

The formal version: the state transition function

Wood (2014) writes the state transition as a function. If σ is the world state and T a transaction:

σ(t+1)  ≡  Υ(σ(t), T)

Υ (upsilon) is the state transition function: it takes a state and a transaction and returns the next state. Because Υ is a deterministic function, every node computing it on the same inputs necessarily arrives at the same output — which is the formal statement of the "no need to trust anyone" property described above.

The same idea applies one level up, at the level of a block — a batch of transactions, bundled together and added to the chain as a single unit. (Blocks get a section of their own later; for now, a batch is all you need.) Writing B for a block, there is a block-level function Π that applies each of the block's transactions in order and then finalises the result:

σ(t+1)  ≡  Π(σ(t), B)

This is why state is committed per block rather than per transaction: Π is the function whose output gets recorded, and Υ is applied internally along the way.

Ethereum works exactly like this. Its state is every account and what each one holds:

Address Nonce Balance Code? 0x5aAe...b48 12 2.5 ether no 0xA0b8...Eb48 1 0 ether yes 0xd8dA...6045 847 1,337 ether no

Its rule for changing that state is the transaction. One transaction in, one new state out.

graph LR
    A[State 1] -->|transaction| B[State 2]
    B -->|transaction| C[State 3]
    C -->|transaction| D[State 4]

Thousands of computers each hold a copy of that state. When a transaction arrives, each one applies the rules independently — and because the rules are deterministic, meaning the same state and the same transaction always produce the same new state, they all arrive at an identical answer. Any machine reporting something different would be caught immediately, the same way you'd catch someone lying about a chess position.

That property is the whole point, and it's worth stating bluntly: nobody has to trust anyone, and nobody is in charge. Not that everyone trusts each other — trust is simply not required, because anyone can recompute the result and check.

That's Ethereum. Everything else on this site is detail about what's inside the state, what's inside a transaction, and how thousands of computers agree on which transactions happened and in what order.

Two simplifications in the table above

The address isn't one of the account's fields. It's the key you look an account up by — like a name in an index — not something the account stores. So that table has four columns but shows only three stored values.

An account stores exactly four things: the nonce, the balance, and two 32-byte fingerprints — one standing for everything the account holds in storage, one for its code. The Code? column above is a yes-or-no stand-in for that second fingerprint. Both fingerprints need groundwork to explain, so they wait for the accounts page.

State is recorded per block, not per transaction. Transactions really are applied one at a time, exactly as the diagram shows. But transactions travel in blocks — batches of a hundred or two, added to the chain as a single unit — and Ethereum only records the state once per block, after every transaction in it has run.

It's the difference between typing and saving. Every keystroke changes your document; only hitting Save writes anything to disk. The states in between genuinely existed, but nothing kept them.

So the states between transactions are real, and no one has a record of them. Only the state at a block boundary is permanent and agreed on — which is why the block is the unit the network agrees about, and why you'll see everything from finality to reorganisations discussed per block rather than per transaction.

History: why not record state per transaction? They tried.

It's a fair question, and Ethereum's first answer was the opposite of the current one.

Before the Byzantium upgrade in 2017, every transaction carried its own post-transaction state root — exactly the per-transaction snapshot the design now lacks. You really could point at a single transaction and prove the state immediately after it.

Johnson (2017) removed that and replaced it with a one-bit success-or-failure status code. The reasoning was practical: computing and storing a full state fingerprint after every single transaction was expensive, and almost nothing used them.

So the answer to "why not per transaction?" is that they did, and it wasn't worth the cost.

One thing is still kept per transaction: its receipt, recording gas used, any logs emitted, and whether it succeeded. So per-transaction outcomes are committed; per-transaction state snapshots are not. That's the precise line.

docs.title: What makes it different from Bitcoin
docs.text:
Bitcoin is also a state machine, with a narrower job.

It's often said that the difference is that Ethereum has code and Bitcoin doesn't. That's not true. Bitcoin has a scripting language, called Script, and it's used for real things — wallets that need several people to approve a payment, or payments that can't be collected until a particular date.

The difference is what the code is allowed to do.

A Bitcoin script answers one yes-or-no question: may this particular piece of money be spent, by this person, right now? It runs, it gives its answer, and it forgets everything. It has nowhere to store anything, and no way to look at what happened last week.

An Ethereum program has a memory of its own. It gets its own space to write things down, and what it writes survives — so it can keep a count, record who did what, and read back a year later something it wrote today. It also isn't confined to a single yes-or-no answer; it can work through any calculation you can describe.

That's the real divide. Not code versus no code, but a one-off check versus a program that remembers.

The formal version: stateless versus stateful

In the usual terminology: Bitcoin's Script is stateless and deliberately not Turing-complete — it has no loops or recursion, so every script provably terminates, and its only output is whether a spend is authorised. Bounded execution comes free from the restricted language.

Ethereum's contracts are stateful — each has a persistent key–value store, addressed by 32-byte keys, that survives between calls — and the EVM is Turing-complete. Termination therefore cannot come from the language, so it's imposed economically instead: every operation costs gas, the caller fixes a limit in advance, and execution halts when the limit is reached.

The design trade is explicit. Bitcoin buys guaranteed termination by giving up expressiveness. Ethereum keeps expressiveness and buys termination with metering.

Two things follow from this, and both matter.

docs.title: Accounts have persistent memory
docs.text:
In Bitcoin, the state is a collection of separate chunks of money (Nakamoto, 2008). Each chunk was produced by some earlier payment, and each can be spent exactly once, in full. There is no stored balance anywhere: your wallet works out "you have 0.4 bitcoin" by adding up the chunks it's able to spend. Spending one destroys it and creates new chunks — one for the recipient, one returning your change.

The name for those chunks: UTXOs

They're called UTXOs — unspent transaction outputs. You'll meet the term constantly in comparisons between the two systems, and it's worth knowing even though nothing on Ethereum uses it.

In Ethereum, accounts are the state. Your balance is a single number recorded against your address, and it goes up and down. Much closer to a bank account.

Both halves of that comparison in one picture, with Alice paying Bob 6:

BITCOIN · coinsETHEREUM · balances532what Alice holdsAlice pays 6622to BobchangeuntouchedThe 5 and the 3 no longer exist.New coins replaced them.Alice  10Bob    0Alice pays 6Alice   4Bob    6Two numbers changed.Nothing created, nothing destroyed.

Read the left side first. Alice holds three coins — a 5, a 3 and a 2 — and she owes 6. No coin is worth 6, so she hands over the 5 and the 3 together, and those two cease to exist. In their place the payment creates a new 6 for Bob and a new 2 as her change. Her 2 at the end is not the 2 she started with; it's change from coins that are gone. This is why Bitcoin transactions are described as consuming their inputs.

The right side has none of that machinery. Alice's balance falls from 10 to 4 and Bob's rises from 0 to 6. No object was consumed and none was created — two numbers were edited. Which is also why there's no change to receive: she paid 6, not "a 5 and a 3 and please give me 2 back".

This sounds like a small implementation difference. It isn't — Buterin (2014) argues the case for accounts over separate outputs at length — and it's why we cover accounts early on this site. It means an address is a thing that persists — somewhere to attach a balance, a counter, and eventually storage and code. Bitcoin has no equivalent place to put any of that, because it has no lasting object to attach it to.

docs.title: Accounts can hold code
docs.text:
Some accounts have a program attached. These are smart contracts.

When you send a transaction to a contract account, you're not just moving money — you're calling the program, and it runs. It can check conditions, do arithmetic, store results, and send ether onward. Every node on the network runs the same code on the same state and gets the same answer.

Every step of that execution is metered and capped. The caller pays for each individual operation, and sets a ceiling in advance on how much work they're willing to pay for. (The unit that work is counted in is called gas; it gets a page of its own later.) When the ceiling is reached, execution stops — which is why an infinite loop in somebody's contract can't hang the network.

That's the actual novelty. Bitcoin lets you agree on who owns what. Ethereum lets you agree on what a program computed.

So where does the 'world computer' phrase come from?

This is the kernel of truth in it. Ethereum really does execute programs, and the whole network agrees on the results.

But it's a terrible computer by any normal measure — it's slower than a phone from 2007, every operation costs real money, and all its data is public. It isn't useful because it's powerful. It's useful because tampering with it is extraordinarily expensive, and no single party decides what it computed.

Worth being precise about that, though: it's hard to stop, not impossible. Validators can decline to include particular transactions, and the concentration of the firms that assemble blocks is a live, openly-debated concern. Daian et al. (2019) document how profitable it is to control transaction ordering — evidence that the position is contested rather than neutral. Censorship resistance is a matter of cost and probability, not a guarantee.

docs.title: Why would anyone want this?
docs.text:
Because the expensive part of a lot of agreements isn't the computing — it's the trusting.

Suppose you're buying a second-hand camera from a stranger in another country. You'd rather not send the money before the camera arrives. They'd rather not post it before they've been paid. Someone has to go first, and whoever goes first carries all the risk.

Normally an institution solves this: a marketplace that holds the payment until delivery, a bank, a card issuer who will reverse the charge. These work — but they cost money, take time, can refuse you, and only exist in some countries.

On Ethereum you can instead put the money somewhere neither of you controls, with the release rule written as code. Neither of you has to be trusted to hold it, and neither does any third party.

docs.title: But there's a catch, and it's a big one
docs.text:
A contract can hold the money and release it without trusting anyone. It cannot know whether the camera arrived.

Contracts can only see what's on the chain. They have no internet connection, and they can't look anything up — if they could, two nodes might get different answers and the determinism that makes the whole system work would collapse.

So something outside has to report the result. That reporter is called an oracle, and the moment you need one, you're trusting it. You've moved the trust rather than removed it. Zhang et al. (2016) set the problem out formally.

This is worth being honest about, because it's the gap most introductions skip. What smart contracts genuinely eliminate is the need to trust a custodian — whoever would otherwise hold the money. They do nothing about trusting whoever supplies facts about the outside world.

Which is why the applications that work best are the ones where every relevant fact is already on-chain: swapping one token for another, lending against on-chain collateral, an escrow both parties sign off on. No oracle needed, nothing to trust.

Whether the trade is worth it depends enormously on the situation. Plenty of things built on Ethereum would be better as an ordinary database. But when you genuinely can't agree on who should hold the money, it's a real answer.

docs.title: The two layers
docs.text:
One last thing before we move on, because it explains a lot of confusing terminology.

Modern Ethereum is split in two:

  • The execution layer holds the accounts and runs the code. This is the state machine described above.
  • The consensus layer decides the order of transactions, using Proof of Stake.

Here's how it ended up that way, because the history is counter-intuitive.

Until 2022, Ethereum mainnet did both jobs in one system, ordering transactions by mining. Meanwhile a second, separate chain called the Beacon Chain had been running since December 2020 — doing Proof of Stake consensus with no accounts and no transactions on it at all. It was a consensus layer with nothing to order, deliberately run in parallel so the mechanism could be proven before anything of value depended on it.

In September 2022, an upgrade called The Merge connected the two: the execution layer stopped running its own mining-based consensus and began taking its ordering from the beacon chain instead (EIP-3675, 2021). Hence the name — two existing systems were joined together, which is why "merge" and not "split".

You'll see this division everywhere once you notice it — it's why Ethereum has two kinds of client software, and why blocks have two sets of fields. Clients and the two layers takes the split apart properly, including why it exists at all. The consensus mechanism itself is still to come, for reasons explained in how this site handles forks; Edgington's Upgrading Ethereum is the most thorough treatment available in the meantime. For now, just know that execution and ordering are separate jobs.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Ethereum is a state machine: everything stored as of now, plus rules for what may change it.
  • Those rules are deterministic, so anyone can recompute the result and check it. Nobody has to trust anyone, and nobody is in charge.
  • Its state is every account and its balance — not coins.
  • Accounts can hold code, so the network can agree on the result of a computation. That code is stateful and general-purpose, unlike Bitcoin's, and every step of it is metered.
  • Its value isn't speed. It's that tampering is prohibitively expensive and no single party decides the outcome.
  • Contracts remove the need for a trusted custodian. They don't remove the need to trust whoever reports facts from outside the chain.

Next: Ether, wei and gwei — the units, so the numbers on later pages mean something.

docs.title: Clients and the two layers
docs.text:
Mostly permanent. How the work of a node is divided, and why several independent implementations of it exist on purpose, are both structural. Which particular implementations exist is not.

Current as of Fusaka (December 2025)

Which implementations exist, who maintains them, and what share each has will all have moved by the time you read this — teams start and stop. So this page names roles and reasons rather than products, and any figure that does appear carries its date.

Client

The software that implements Ethereum's rules. Not an app, not a wallet — the program itself.

So node and client are not two words for one thing. A node is what a machine does: hold the state, check every arriving block, reject anything invalid. A client is the program it runs in order to do that. The same relation as web server and the particular software serving the pages.

Several independent clients exist, written by different teams in different programming languages. They must agree exactly, because a disagreement about the rules is a disagreement about what happened.

docs.title: One node, two programs
docs.text:
Now the complication. A node doesn't run one client — it runs two, side by side, and needs both.

They do different jobs, and neither can do the other's. One holds the accounts and checks what the transactions did; the other works out which block comes next. They talk to each other over a defined interface, and the pair of them is what makes one node.

ONE NODE · one machineexecution clientholds the accountsruns the codekeeps the stateconsensus clientorders the transactionsvotes on other blockstalks to other nodesother nodes’ consensus clientsNeither program is a node on its own.

The execution client is the state machine this site has been describing. It holds the accounts, runs contract code, keeps the state, and checks that transactions follow the rules.

The consensus client works out which block comes next — the problem that has to be solved by somebody because the rules don't settle it. It talks to other nodes' consensus clients, and tells its own execution client which block to apply.

Neither is a node by itself. The execution client can check whether a block is valid but has no opinion about which block is the real one. The consensus client can tell you which block the network has agreed on but cannot check whether its contents make sense. A node is the pair.

History: they were separate systems first

The division looks like an architectural decision. It's a historical accident that turned out well.

Until 2022, Ethereum did both jobs in one program: one piece of software held the accounts and also ordered the transactions, by mining. Meanwhile a second, entirely separate network — the Beacon Chain — had been running since December 2020, doing nothing but practising consensus. It held no accounts and processed no transactions. For about twenty-one months it ran alongside the real thing, agreeing on the order of nothing in particular.

In September 2022 the two were connected: the old system stopped ordering transactions and started taking its order from the Beacon Chain instead. EIP-3675 (Kalinin et al., 2021) is the specification for that change, and the event is called the Merge.

Which is why the split exists at all. Nobody set out to build a node from two programs; two systems were built separately and then joined, and the seam is still visible in every node today.

docs.title: Why several of each, rather than one official one?
docs.text:
Here is the part worth understanding, because the obvious intuition is backwards.

It would seem simpler — and safer — to have one correct implementation that everybody runs. One codebase to audit, one team to fund, no risk of two programs disagreeing about the rules.

That arrangement has a fatal property: a bug in it is a bug in Ethereum.

If every node runs the same software and that software accepts a block it shouldn't, every node accepts it. There is no one left to notice. The rules of Ethereum would no longer be the specification — they would be whatever that program happened to do, bugs included, and nobody could tell the difference.

Several independent implementations change the shape of that failure. A bug in one is a disagreement rather than a catastrophe: the affected nodes reject blocks the others accept, the discrepancy is visible immediately, and the remaining network carries on. The bug becomes a problem for that client's users instead of a rewriting of the rules.

So diversity here is a safety property, not an absence of standardisation. The duplicated effort is the point, in the same way a second opinion is not an inefficiency.

docs.title: How real is that risk?
docs.text:
Not hypothetical, and not rare enough to be reassuring.

Researchers at Seoul National University and Georgia Tech built a tool that feeds the same transactions to different clients and watches for disagreement — differential fuzzing. It found two previously unknown consensus bugs in a single widely used client, and one of them later caused a split on the live network (Yang et al., 2021).

That one sentence contains the whole argument. The bugs existed. They were found by comparing implementations against each other, which is only possible if more than one exists. And one of them went on to do real damage anyway.

docs.title: The sharp edge: when one client has most of the network
docs.text:
Diversity is only protective if it exists in practice, and it hasn't always.

On 11 November 2020, a consensus bug in the client then running most of the network caused exactly the failure described above. A fix had been released earlier but not flagged as urgent, so many operators hadn't applied it. A single transaction triggered the bug, and nodes on the old version split away from the rest — following a different chain, reporting different balances, and in some cases serving wrong answers to the applications built on them (De, 2020).

Two things about that incident are worth separating, because they're usually run together.

It was a version split, not a client-diversity failure in the strict sense — old and new releases of the same client disagreed. But the reason it mattered so much is dominance: because one implementation held most of the network, a mistake in its release process became most of the network's problem.

And this is why client share is counted and published. It isn't a popularity contest. Under proof of stake the thresholds become sharper still — a client with a large enough share of validators can stall the network's ability to settle anything, or in the worst case carry an invalid chain to settlement. The exact fractions are parameters and belong on that page; the structural point is that share is a safety variable, and a client being popular is a risk rather than an endorsement.

docs.title: Who writes them, and who pays?
docs.text:
A fair question once "nobody is in charge" is taken seriously, and the answer is less tidy than people expect.

Each client is built and maintained by its own team, independently, in different languages, funded variously — foundation grants, company sponsorship, public goods funding, and in some cases unpaid work. No team can compel the others to do anything. The specification is the shared reference, and agreeing with it is voluntary in the sense that nothing but consequence enforces it.

Which produces a situation worth stating plainly: the rules of Ethereum are maintained by several small groups of people who are not obliged to continue. Who decides what those rules become is a different question again, and gets its own page.

docs.title: Do you ever choose a client?
docs.text:
Running a node: yes, and it's the one decision an individual operator makes that affects everybody else. You pick one execution client and one consensus client. Choosing a less common one slightly increases your own risk — fewer users means bugs are found later — while reducing the network's. That tension is real and worth naming rather than smoothing over.

Using Ethereum through a wallet: no. You're relying on somebody else's node, running somebody else's client, chosen by them. The previous page made this point about nodes; it applies one level down as well. Most people have never chosen a client and never will, which is precisely why the share figures matter to people who aren't running anything.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A node is two programs: an execution client holding the accounts, state and code, and a consensus client deciding the order and voting on blocks. Neither program is a node alone.
  • The split is historical, not architectural. The consensus system ran as a separate chain from December 2020 and was joined to the execution system in September 2022 — the Merge.
  • A client is an implementation of the rules — the program, not the machine. Several independent ones exist for each of the two jobs, written by different teams in different languages.
  • One official implementation would be more dangerous, not safer. If everyone runs the same software, a bug in it isn't a bug — it silently becomes the rules.
  • With several, a bug is a disagreement rather than a rewriting: visible immediately, survivable by the rest of the network. The duplicated effort is the point.
  • The risk is documented: differential fuzzing across clients found two unknown consensus bugs in one client, and one later split the live chain.
  • Dominance is the danger. In November 2020 a bug in the most-used client split the network, which is why client share is treated as a safety variable rather than a popularity measure.
  • Clients are maintained by independent, variously funded teams that nothing obliges to continue.
  • Running a node means choosing clients; using a wallet means somebody chose for you.

Next: Running one yourself — what it actually takes, and why that number is an argument rather than a footnote.

docs.title: Running one yourself
docs.text:
Expect this page to age. It is about cost, and cost is the thing a growing state changes. The argument is built to survive its own figures going stale, which is why there are almost none.

Why this page gives shapes, not specifications

A page that prints "2 TB" is wrong within a year and confidently wrong, which is worse than vague. So this one describes the shape of the requirement — which resource binds first, what order of magnitude, and which way it moves — and sends you to a maintained source for today's numbers (ethereum.org, 2026).

If a figure here contradicts that source, trust the source.

Syncing

Getting a new node from nothing to current: holding the state as it is now, and able to check the next block against it.

It is not downloading the chain. The state is the result of applying every transaction ever sent, so a node arriving late must either redo that work or obtain the state and verify it. How much of the past you re-derive is the choice being made, and it decides how long this takes.

docs.title: What it takes, in shape
docs.text:
Four requirements, and they are not equally binding.

Disk is the one that rules machines out. The other three requirements are rarely what stops somebody; this is. And the useful facts about it aren't the quantity — they're the kind and the direction. You need terabytes rather than gigabytes, on a solid-state drive rather than a spinning one, because the work is constant small random writes rather than bulk reading. And the requirement only ever rises, because nothing removes an account from the state.

Memory and processor are ordinary. A small desktop machine of recent vintage is enough. This is the reassuring part and the part people get wrong in both directions — you don't need a server, and a ten-year-old laptop won't do.

Bandwidth is continuous rather than large. A node is always talking: receiving blocks, forwarding them, answering peers. The monthly total is unremarkable; the requirement is that it never stops.

And the real cost is that last word. A node that runs for eight hours a day is a node that spends every morning catching up. The expense isn't the hardware, it's a machine that stays on — electricity, a corner of a room, and the fact that you now own something that breaks.

So the honest summary: the cost of a node is not a purchase, it's a standing commitment. A few hundred euros of disk is the easy part.

docs.title: Why catching up is the slow part
docs.text:
The chain is large, but downloading it is not what takes the time.

Having every block is not the same as having the state. To know what an account holds, you either apply every transaction that ever touched it — redoing a decade of arithmetic — or you obtain the current state from somebody and verify it against the state root, which is exactly the trick the state page sets up. The second is far faster and gives up nothing, because a state you can check against the root is a state you don't have to trust.

So "how long does syncing take" has no single answer. It depends on how much of the past you choose to re-derive, which is the same decision as how much history you keep — described on the previous page. Hours if you verify a state you were handed; far longer if you insist on recomputing it; longest of all if you want every intermediate state ever.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
Three things, and only the first is the point.

You stop trusting anybody's answer. Your balance is a number you computed, not a number you were told. Nobody can serve you a stale state, misreport a transaction, or quietly answer a different question from the one you asked.

You stop revealing what you care about. Querying somebody else's node tells them which addresses interest you and when. Running your own removes that audience — a privacy property most people don't realise they're giving away, and the one the privacy page treats properly.

You can't be rate-limited or cut off. No API key, no terms of service, no provider deciding you've asked too often.

docs.title: What you don't get
docs.text:
Any money. This needs saying plainly, because it's the single most common expectation people arrive with.

Running a node pays nothing. There is no reward, no registration, nothing in the protocol that knows you exist. The paid role is being a validator, which is a node plus staking ether plus additional duties, and which the node page distinguishes and proof of stake will describe. The hardware requirements for staking are higher, and the money comes from the stake and the duties — never from running the node underneath.

So if you are weighing this up as an investment, the answer is that it isn't one. It's an expense that buys you a property.

docs.title: Why the cost is an argument, not a footnote
docs.text:
Here is why this page exists at all, and it has nothing to do with your hardware.

Every page on this site has leaned on the same claim: nobody has to trust anybody, because anyone can check. The node page was blunt about what that rests on — not on people being honest, but on particular computers in particular rooms being able to redo the work.

That claim has a price, and this page is it.

While a node costs a few hundred euros and a spare corner, the claim is true: checking is available to anybody who wants it badly enough, and the people who most need certainty — exchanges, builders, the suspicious — can have it. If the requirement reached the point of needing a datacentre, nothing in the rules would change, and the claim would quietly become false. Verification would still be possible, in the way that auditing a central bank is possible. It would no longer be available.

That is why node counts get watched, and why "what does a node cost" is a question about Ethereum rather than about computers.

docs.title: What keeps it affordable?
docs.text:
Nothing automatic, and this is the uncomfortable part.

The state only grows, because nothing removes an account from it. So every operator's disk requirement rises for as long as the network runs.

And notice where the money sits. Writing something into the state is paid for once, by whoever writes it, at a price set by how congested the network is that day. Keeping it is paid for indefinitely, by every operator, including everyone who starts a node years later. Those are not the same people, and the second group was never asked.

That mismatch is a question about pricing, not about hardware — which is why no amount of cheaper disk resolves it. Cheaper hardware changes how fast the requirement bites. It does not change which way it moves.

It's also not this page's argument to make: it needs the account model, and so it's taken apart properly in why accounts, and what they cost, two parts ahead. What's worth carrying there from here is the concrete end of it — the cost is real, it's denominated in disk, and it only goes one way.

EIP-4444 (Kadianakis et al., 2021) addresses the other half: making old history somebody's deliberate job rather than everybody's default, so a node need not carry a decade of blocks it will never read.

docs.title: If you're not going to run one
docs.text:
Most readers won't, and that's a reasonable decision rather than a failure of duty. The useful thing isn't guilt — it's knowing what is being assumed on your behalf.

When your wallet shows a balance, somebody's node computed it and your wallet is repeating the answer. That somebody is almost certainly honest and almost certainly competent, and you have no way to know. The protocol's guarantee — you need not trust anyone — is a guarantee you have declined to exercise.

Which is fine, and worth being conscious of. It also means you have a stake in other people being able to run one cheaply, even if you never do. The cost of a node is a question about your position whether or not you ever buy a disk.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Disk is the binding constraint: terabytes not gigabytes, solid-state not spinning, and rising every block because nothing leaves the state.
  • Memory and processor are ordinary. The real cost is a machine that stays on, not the hardware in it.
  • Syncing is slow because of arithmetic, not download. How long depends on how much of the past you re-derive — and a state verified against the state root needs no trust, so there's no need to recompute it.
  • What you get: your own answers, no audience for your queries, and nobody able to cut you off.
  • What you don't get: money. Nodes earn nothing; the paid role is a validator, which is a node plus stake plus duties.
  • The cost matters because the site's central claim depends on it. While a node is affordable, "anyone can check" is true. If it needed a datacentre, the rules wouldn't change and the claim would quietly stop being true.
  • Nothing keeps it affordable automatically. Writing to the state is paid for once; keeping it is paid for indefinitely, by different people. That's a pricing mismatch rather than a hardware problem, and why accounts takes it apart two parts ahead.
  • If you don't run one, the useful thing is knowing what you're assuming on somebody else's behalf — and that you benefit from nodes staying cheap regardless.

Next: Accounts — what all these machines are actually storing.
