docs.title: What a node is
docs.text:
Permanent. What a node does, and why checking rather than trusting is the whole point, follows from the design and has not changed. The software it runs, and what it costs, are the next two pages.

Node

A computer running Ethereum's rules. It keeps its own copy of the state, receives blocks from other computers, applies each block's transactions to its own copy, and rejects any block that breaks the rules.

It holds no keys, signs nothing, and is paid nothing. Those are different jobs, done by different things.

This part comes early on purpose. It would read better after state and blocks, whose detail makes the argument sharper — but "node" is load-bearing from the signatures page onward, and a word the site leans on repeatedly cannot stay undefined that long.

So it borrows two things from later and states them plainly: the state is the record of every account and what it holds, and a block is a batch of transactions added to the chain as one unit. Both were introduced on What is Ethereum?. Everything else here is built on what you already have.

docs.title: What a node actually does
docs.text:
Four steps, repeated indefinitely.

  1. Receive a block from another computer.
  2. Check it — are the signatures valid, the nonces in order, the balances sufficient, the rules followed?
  3. Apply its transactions to its own copy of the state, in the order the block gives.
  4. Keep it, or throw it away. A block that breaks any rule is rejected outright. Not flagged, not reported to anybody. Discarded.

That is the entire job. The interesting part is what isn't in the list: at no point does the node ask another computer whether the block is good. There is nobody to ask, and asking would defeat the point.

one blockof transactionsnodeapplies the rules to its own stateroot 3a7f…c91nodeapplies the rules to its own stateroot 3a7f…c91nodeapplies the rules to its own stateroot 3a7f…c91… andthousandsmoreSame block, same starting state, same rules — so the same answer. None asked the others.

The three results match because the rules are deterministic, which is the property the state machine page opened with. A node doesn't discover that it agrees with everyone else. It computes the only answer the rules allow, and therefore agrees by construction.

docs.title: What it refuses to do
docs.text:
The shortest accurate description of a node:

A machine that refuses to take anybody's word for anything.

Every other property follows. It won't accept a balance it was told — it computes balances. It won't accept that a block is valid because a well-known company says so — it checks. It won't accept a chain because that chain arrived first — it applies the rules and sees what survives.

This is what the site has meant, page after page, by nobody has to trust anybody. It isn't a claim about people being honest. It's a claim about a particular computer in a particular room being able to redo the work — which means the number of such computers is the extent to which the claim is true at all.

docs.title: Node, validator, miner, wallet
docs.text:
The distinction most worth getting straight, because nearly all confusion about "who runs Ethereum" is one of these four mistaken for another.

What it does Paid? Holds keys? Node checks blocks, keeps the state no no Validator proposes blocks and votes on others' yes yes, staking keys Miner the pre-2022 name for that paid role yes yes Wallet holds your keys, builds transactions no yes, yours

Three things fall out of that table.

Nodes are unpaid. No reward, no registration, and nothing in the protocol that knows you exist. This surprises people, and it's why what it costs gets a page of its own.

A validator is a node plus a job. It must run a node — you cannot vote on the validity of blocks you haven't checked — and then additionally proposes and attests, for which it is paid and for which it stakes something it can lose. So every validator is a node; almost no node is a validator.

"Miner" is a historical word. Mining was the paid proposing role under the old consensus rules, retired in 2022. Meeting it in current writing means the author means a validator, or is working from old material.

A wallet is none of the above. It holds keys, as the wallets section laboured, and usually keeps no copy of the state at all — it asks somebody else's node. Which is worth sitting with: most people using Ethereum are trusting a node they don't run.

So who gets to propose a block, and when?

Deliberately not answered here. That's the consensus mechanism — proof of stake — and it needs its own treatment.

The reason it can wait is that nothing on this page depends on it. The checking role is identical under any consensus rule: receive, verify, apply, keep or reject. Change how proposers are chosen and every sentence above still holds — a good sign the two subjects separate cleanly.

docs.title: Where blocks come from
docs.text:
There is no server. Worth saying flatly, because "connecting to Ethereum" sounds like connecting to something, and there is nothing there to connect to.

A node connects to a handful of other nodes — peers — which are connected to further nodes. Blocks and transactions are passed along those links, each node forwarding to its neighbours, until they've reached everybody. The pattern is called gossip, and the word is apt: no announcement, no central source, just repetition until the news is everywhere. Bitcoin's design paper sets out the same arrangement (Nakamoto, 2008), and Ethereum inherits it.

Two consequences:

Nobody is authoritative. A node cannot ask "what is the real chain?", because no computer holds that position. It can only apply the rules to what reaches it.

And there is nothing to switch off. No operator, no address, no company — which is the practical content of a claim that otherwise sounds like a slogan.

docs.title: Each node has its own waiting room
docs.text:
Transactions arrive by gossip too, and one that's been broadcast but not yet included has to wait somewhere. That somewhere is the mempool — and the thing to notice is that it is per-node, not shared.

There is no single queue. Each node keeps its own set of pending transactions, decides how many to hold and for how long, and may discard yours while another keeps it. This is why the nonce page could say clients differ in what they'll hold onto, and why a transaction can appear to vanish and then come back: it was never in one place to begin with.

docs.title: Catching up
docs.text:
A node starting today has to get from the first block to the present, and that's the slow part — hours at best.

What makes it slow is the arithmetic, not the download. Having the blocks is not the same as having the state: the state is the result of applying every transaction ever sent, so a node arriving late must either redo that work or obtain the current state and check it against the chain. How much history you re-derive is the choice being made, and it's the distinction state draws between history and state.

docs.title: If nobody pays them, why does anyone run one?
docs.text:
The honest answer is narrower than the usual one.

To avoid trusting somebody else's answer. That's the whole return, and for some parties it plainly covers the cost: an exchange that must be certain of its own deposits, a wallet provider serving millions of lookups, anyone building something where being lied to about the chain is expensive.

For an individual it's thinner. You get certainty that nobody is misreporting your balance, and you stop revealing which addresses you care about to whoever's node you were querying. Real, but modest against an always-on machine with a lot of disk.

Which is exactly why the number of nodes is watched, and why the cost of running one is a question about the system rather than about your hardware. If running a node becomes impractical for everyone but large operators, nothing in the rules changes — but anybody can check for themselves quietly becomes anybody with a datacentre can, and the property that made trust unnecessary ends up resting on fewer and fewer people. Running one yourself takes that apart.

docs.title: Not every node keeps everything
docs.text:
Which raises a fair question: if catching up means obtaining all that, why don't nodes simply keep it? Many don't, and the reasoning is worth knowing.

They always drop the oldest, never a selection. The data a node keeps has to run contiguously backwards from the present, because checking block N requires the state left by block N−1. A node holding a scattered sample of past blocks could do nothing with it. So the only decision is how far back, and it's set by whoever runs the node — nothing in the protocol says.

Recency wins because of what each part is for. The current state is the only thing required to validate new blocks. A short recent window is needed in case the tip of the chain changes and work has to be rewound. Everything older answers questions about the past, and nothing else.

And discarding it is safe for the same reason the state root works:

A node can safely forget anything it can re-obtain and re-verify.

Old blocks are linked by hash, so a node needing one later asks a peer and checks that what arrives matches what the chain already commits to. No trust required — a lie is detectable. Verification doesn't require possession, which is also why a new node can accept a state it was handed and check it against the root instead of replaying years of transactions.

So the trade is never about how much a node can verify; it's about which questions it can answer. Pruning costs you memory, not judgement.

The catch is collective. If everybody prunes, the history is gone from the network — nobody's copy means nobody's copy. That is exactly the question EIP-4444 (Kadianakis et al., 2021) raises by proposing that clients stop serving old history: it makes keeping it somebody's explicit job rather than an accident of everyone's defaults. State sets out the three sizes of node this produces.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A node keeps its own copy of the state, applies arriving blocks to it, and rejects anything breaking the rules (Wood, 2014).
  • It never asks another computer whether a block is valid. Same block, same starting state, same rules, same answer — agreement by construction, not by consultation.
  • Shortest description: a machine that refuses to take anybody's word for anything. Every other property follows.
  • Nodes are unpaid and unregistered. A validator is a node plus a paid job, so every validator is a node and almost no node is a validator. Miner is the pre-2022 word for that job. A wallet is neither — it holds keys and usually asks someone else's node.
  • Blocks arrive by gossip from a few peers. No server, nobody authoritative, nothing to switch off.
  • The mempool is per-node, not a shared queue — which is why pending transactions behave inconsistently.
  • Catching up is slow because the state has to be re-derived or verified, not merely downloaded.
  • Many nodes keep only recent data, always dropping the oldest, because anything re-obtainable and hash-checkable is safe to forget. Pruning costs you memory, not judgement — though if everybody prunes, the history is gone.
  • Nobody pays you to run one. The return is not having to trust anybody's answer — and how many people find that worth paying for decides whether the whole arrangement means anything.

Next: Clients and the two layers — the software that does all this, and why there are two pieces of it.

Ethereum upgrades by hard fork: a coordinated rule change that every node adopts at an agreed block or slot. This page is the timeline — the one place a reader can see how the protocol got to where it is.

Verify before writing this page

Fork names, dates and contents are exactly the kind of detail that gets misremembered. Write this page from primary sources only:

  • https://ethereum.org/en/history/
  • https://eips.ethereum.org
  • https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• What is a hard fork, and why does it need everyone to upgrade together?
  • Why do forks have two names now? (Execution layer and consensus layer each get one — Paris/Bellatrix, Shanghai/Capella, Cancun/Deneb, Prague/Electra. "Pectra" is just Prague + Electra.)
  • What actually happens at the switchover block or slot?
  • What is a contentious fork, and why is the DAO fork the only one that produced a lasting split? (Ethereum Classic.)
  • Which forks does a beginner genuinely need to know about? Probably only these:
    • The DAO fork (2016) — why Ethereum Classic exists
    • London (2021) — EIP-1559, the fee market and the burn
    • The Merge (September 2022) — Proof of Work to Proof of Stake
    • Shanghai (2023) — staking withdrawals finally enabled
    • Cancun (2024) — blobs, which made rollups cheap
    • Pectra (May 2025) — account abstraction groundwork

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• Resist listing all twenty forks with full EIP inventories. That's what ethereum.org is for, and nobody reads it. A short list of forks that changed something a beginner can feel is far more useful.
  • The ice-age / difficulty-bomb forks (Muir Glacier, Arrow Glacier, Gray Glacier) are historical trivia now that PoW is gone. One line covering all of them.
  • Each entry wants: date, what changed, and why anyone cared. The third column is the one that matters.
  • This page is also your own maintenance log — add an entry each time a fork ships, and it stays current for free.

This page is an outline. Delete this box when you fill it in.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• How is the fee actually calculated? (gas used × gas price, paid in wei.)
  • What was wrong with the old system, where you just named a gas price? (Blind auction — you were guessing what everyone else would bid, and usually overpaid or got stuck.)
  • What did EIP-1559 change, in August 2021? Three pieces:
    • Base fee — set by the protocol, not by bidders. Rises when blocks are full, falls when they're empty.
    • Priority fee — a tip, which actually goes to the validator.
    • Max fee — your ceiling. You're refunded the difference.
  • Where does the base fee go? (It's burned — destroyed. Nobody receives it.)
  • Why burn it rather than pay the validator? (If validators received it, they'd be incentivised to fake congestion to drive it up.)
  • Why does the base fee adjust so predictably? (It moves by at most 12.5% per block, so you can estimate the next one reliably. This is what fixed the guessing problem.)
  • What does maxFeePerGas mean for the user in practice? (You can set a high ceiling safely — you pay the base fee, not your ceiling.)

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• The burn is the part people find strangest, so lead with the incentive argument rather than the mechanism.
  • Worth noting the second-order effect: the burn means ether supply can shrink when the network is busy. Mention it, but don't turn the page into tokenomics.
  • A worked example in gwei, with real numbers, beats the formula.

Next: Gas costs — the actual numbers, kept in one place so every other page can talk about reasons instead.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• What is gas measuring? (Computational work — not money. Gas is a unit of effort, like litres of fuel.)
  • Why does it need to exist at all? Two reasons, and both matter:
    1. Someone has to pay for the computation.
    2. Without a cost ceiling, an infinite loop in a contract would hang the entire network. (This is the halting problem, dodged by charging per step.)
  • Why does a plain ether transfer always cost exactly 21,000 gas?
  • Why do different operations cost wildly different amounts? (Writing to storage is permanent and burdens every node forever; adding two numbers isn't.)
  • What's the difference between gasLimit (what you authorise) and gas used (what you actually spend)? What happens to the difference?
  • What is "out of gas", and why do you still pay? (The work was genuinely done. Refunding it would make spam free.)

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• Keep gas and price strictly separate. Gas is the amount of work; fees are what it costs. Mixing them is the main reason beginners find this confusing — that's why fees get their own page.
  • A short table of example opcode costs makes the "writing is expensive" point instantly.
  • Good analogy, if you want one: gas is distance, gas price is the price per mile, fee is the total. Don't stretch it further than that.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• What is a transaction, in one sentence? (A signed instruction from an EOA to change the state.)
  • What's inside one?
    • nonce — a counter for the sender
    • gasLimit — the most work you'll pay for
    • to — the recipient, or empty to deploy a contract
    • value — how much ether to send, in wei
    • data — arbitrary bytes; this is how you call a contract
    • maxFeePerGas / maxPriorityFeePerGas — what you'll pay
    • v, r, s — the signature
  • Where does the sender's address live in all that? (Nowhere! It's recovered from the signature. Worth making a point of — it surprises everyone.)
  • What are the three things a transaction can do? (Send ether, call a contract, create a contract.)
  • What's a transaction hash, and when does it exist? (As soon as it's signed — before anyone has accepted it.)
  • What does it mean for a transaction to fail? (It still happened, still cost gas, but the state changes were reverted.)

docs.title: A transaction doesn't name the state it expects
docs.text:
The natural question, once roots are in view: when you sign a transaction, which state root is it computed against? And should it carry that root, so the network knows what you assumed?

It carries no state root, and no reference to one. A transaction holds a nonce, a recipient, a value, some data, gas limits, fee terms, a chain id and a signature — the field list above goes through them. Nothing in it describes the state it expects to meet.

So a transaction is an instruction, not a statement about the world. It says what to do. It says nothing about what it assumes.

The single exception is the nonce, and it's a revealing one. The nonce is a claim about state — "my account has sent exactly this many transactions" — but it constrains only your own account's position in its own sequence. About every other account, every balance and every contract's storage, your transaction is silent.

docs.title: What yours actually runs against
docs.text:
If it lands in block N, it executes against the state at the end of block N−1, plus the effects of every transaction ordered before it within block N.

That intermediate state is perfectly real, and no root is published for it. Ethereum commits to the state once per block, after all of it has run — which is the second of the two simplifications flagged back on What is Ethereum?.

History: it used to publish one per transaction

This is not how it always worked, and the change is instructive.

Until the Byzantium upgrade in 2017, every transaction receipt carried the state root as of that transaction — a published commitment after each one, not just each block. EIP-658 (Johnson, 2017) replaced that field with a plain status code: 1 for success, 0 for failure.

The reason was cost against benefit. Computing an intermediate root per transaction is real work for every node, and almost nothing used the result, whereas did this transaction succeed? was the question everyone actually asked and previously had to infer.

So Ethereum once offered exactly the per-transaction commitment this section says doesn't exist, looked at the price, and sold it for a single bit of far more useful information.

docs.title: Why you shouldn't want to send one
docs.text:
It sounds safer to pin the state you signed against. It would be close to unusable.

A transaction naming a required state root would be invalidated by any change anywhere in the state — one unrelated transfer, by a stranger, in the same block. Since the state changes every block and thousands of transactions compete for each one, yours would have a useful life of a few seconds and would usually miss. A mempool — the pool of broadcast transactions waiting their turn — could not work at all, because waiting is exactly what would kill them.

So state-agnosticism is deliberate: it's what lets a transaction sit in a queue and remain valid. The bill arrives elsewhere, though, and it's worth knowing where:

  • You cannot pin the conditions you'll meet. The state your transaction executes against is whatever exists at inclusion, not what existed when you signed.
  • Which is why contracts add their own guards. Deadlines after which a call reverts, minimum amounts a trade must return — those exist because the protocol declines to offer them.
  • And it's the gap between simulating and executing. A wallet shows you the outcome against the state as it stands now; the real outcome is against the state at inclusion, which nobody can predict. Much of what gets called front-running lives in that gap — which is this page's territory.

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• Decode one real transaction field by field. That single worked example teaches more than any amount of prose.

  • Make it a tool, and make it prove itself. Embed the raw bytes of an actual transaction, decode them in the browser with the RLP decoder, then hash the bytes and show the result equals the published transaction hash. The reader isn't told the example is real — they watch it check out. Nothing else on the site can do that.

Hard-coded bytes, not a live API: it then works offline, cannot break when somebody's endpoint dies, and makes no request that reveals who is reading.

  • Second tool: validation, split by what it needs. This is the stronger one, because the split is the lesson.

    • Stateless checks compute for real in the browser — does the RLP parse, does the signature recover to an address, is the chain id right, does it cover intrinsic gas?
    • Stateful checks need the state, which a static site doesn't have. So let the reader supply it: two inputs for the account's nonce and balance.

    The tool then reports accept or reject, and which check failed — which turns the four steps on what a node is into something you operate, and teaches the stateless/stateful distinction by making you provide one half of it. - Don't explain the signature maths here — point at the signatures page. - The data field is the gateway to the whole EVM section. Flag it as important and move on.

Next: Why metering is necessary

docs.title: Why metering is necessary
docs.text:
Stub — not written yet

This page is an outline. Delete this box when you fill it in.

Permanent. The requirement follows from running untrusted code on a shared machine. Only the prices change.

This is the problem page. Gas is the mechanism that answers it, and gas costs change at forks — the argument here does not.

docs.title: The argument to make
docs.text:
1. The network executes code written by strangers, and every node must run all of it.
  2. Some of that code will not terminate — whether by mistake or on purpose.
  3. You cannot tell in advance which. (This is the halting problem, and it isn't a limitation of Ethereum's design but of computation itself.)
  4. So termination cannot be decided by inspection. It has to be imposed.
  5. Charging per step imposes it: the caller fixes a budget in advance, and execution stops when the budget runs out.
  6. The charge also has to be paid, not merely counted — otherwise an attacker spends nothing to make every node work.

docs.title: Questions this page should answer
docs.text:
• Why can't the network simply refuse infinite loops? (Step 3 above. Worth stating properly, because it's the real answer.)
  • Why charge per operation rather than per transaction or per second?
  • Why must the price be positive even for cheap work? (Free work is free spam.)
  • Why does the caller set a ceiling in advance rather than paying whatever it takes?
  • Why is the work paid for even when it fails? (It was genuinely performed by every node. Refunding it would make failed spam free.)
  • What does Bitcoin do instead, and what does it give up? (Restricts the language so termination is guaranteed — no metering needed, no general computation either. The comparison makes the trade-off visible.)

docs.title: Notes to self
docs.text:
• No numbers on this page. Not one gas cost. Those live in the reference table and change at forks; this page has to stay true regardless.
  • The halting-problem point is what makes this more than hand-waving. It explains why metering is necessary rather than merely convenient — and almost nothing written about gas says this clearly.
  • This page is also the hinge into Economics: it establishes that computation must be paid for, which who pays then takes up.

Next: Gas

docs.title: What losing your keys means
docs.text:
Permanent. A direct consequence of how addresses are derived and how signatures are checked. No upgrade could change it without changing both.

Irrecoverable

The protocol's only test of authority over an address is a valid signature from the matching private key. There is no second test, no override, and no party holding one.

So losing the key means losing the only thing that can authorise a change to that address — permanently, and for everyone, including the people who wrote Ethereum.

The ether is not destroyed. It stays recorded at that address indefinitely: visible to anybody, spendable by nobody.

docs.title: Nothing happens to the ether
docs.text:
The first question is usually where does it go, and the answer sounds evasive until you see why it's exact: nowhere. Nothing happens at all.

A balance is a number recorded against an address by every computer on the network. Losing a key doesn't touch that number. It removes the only means of changing it. The ether sits there, as legible as it ever was, and no transaction that would move it can ever be valid again.

There is no expiry. No dormancy rule, no reversion to anyone after a period of inactivity. Unclaimed bank accounts eventually escheat — pass to the state — under laws most countries have. Ethereum has no equivalent and nowhere to put one: escheat needs a recipient with the authority to receive, and the protocol recognises no such party.

docs.title: There is nobody to ask
docs.text:
Not "nobody who will help" — nobody who could.

The addresses page established that nothing creates an address. All 2160 of them already exist; a wallet picks a number and derives one. No application, no approval, no registration.

So follow the chain of people you might appeal to, and it terminates immediately:

  • Your wallet never had your key in any sense it could restore. It derived keys from your phrase and stored them on your device. It kept no copy anywhere else — that is precisely what "non-custodial" means.
  • No issuer exists. Nobody granted you the address, so nobody holds a record connecting it to you, and nobody has the standing to reassign it.
  • The network doesn't know who you are. It has never held your name, and the address carries no claim of ownership — only a balance.
  • The developers have no privileged access. They write software that enforces the rule. They are not a party to it.

A bank can reset your password because the bank is the ledger: your balance is an entry in its database, and it decides what that database says. Ethereum's ledger is held by thousands of independent machines agreeing on rules. There is no analogous operator — which is the entire design, not an oversight in it.

docs.title: What a recovery mechanism would have to be
docs.text:
This is the part worth understanding properly, because it shows the limit is structural rather than a missing feature.

To restore your access, the protocol would need to accept a transaction moving funds out of your address without a signature from that address's key. The specification offers no route to that: a transaction is valid when the signature recovers to the sending address, and there is no alternative clause (Wood, 2014). There is no third option either — the key authorises the move, or something else does.

So suppose such a rule existed. Whatever that something else is — a committee, a court order, a company, a majority vote — it is now a thing that can move ether out of any address. Not just yours, and not just when funds are genuinely lost.

And the protocol cannot tell the difference, because:

You cannot prove you have lost a key.

Proving you hold a key is trivial: sign something. Proving you don't is impossible, because absence leaves no evidence. There is nothing you could present. Meanwhile an attacker claiming your key is lost makes exactly the same claim, backed by exactly the same nothing.

Why no clever scheme fixes that

People reach for one quickly, so it's worth walking through why each collapses into the same problem.

"Require ID." Then whoever checks the ID controls every address, and the network would have to recognise identity documents — which it cannot, having no way to verify anything that isn't a signature or a hash.

"Require a waiting period, so the real owner can object." Object with what? The only way to object is to sign — and the premise is that you can't. This protects the people who still have their keys, which is the group that needed no protection.

"Let a majority of validators vote." Then a majority of validators can take anyone's funds, which is a far larger problem than the one being solved. It also changes what the system is: the point of staking is enforcing a rule, not exercising discretion over balances.

The common structure: every mechanism able to recognise a genuine loss is equally able to manufacture one, because the evidence distinguishing them does not exist. Not hard to obtain — does not exist.

That is the whole argument. A recovery power is an expropriation power wearing different clothes, and no amount of procedure separates them.

docs.title: Losing a key, and losing a phrase
docs.text:
Different losses, different scope.

What you lose What becomes inaccessible One private key That one address, and anything only that address can authorise The seed phrase Every address in the tree — all of them, at once The passphrase, phrase intact Every address, again. The phrase alone derives a different wallet

The asymmetry runs the way you'd expect from how derivation works: a phrase regenerates every key beneath it, and no key reveals the phrase it came from. That makes the phrase strictly the more valuable secret — the worse thing to lose, and equally the worse thing to leak.

The passphrase deserves singling out because it is quietly the most dangerous item of the three. It is short, it feels like a password, and people treat it like one — but there is no reset, and a phrase without it opens a wallet that is perfectly valid and entirely empty. Which looks exactly like a wrong phrase, with no way to tell which mistake you made.

Nobody can recover a lost key, so anybody offering to is lying

This follows from the argument above rather than being general caution. Recovery would require the key, and the key is the thing you don't have. There is no service, no specialist and no tool that changes this.

So every "wallet recovery" offer is a theft attempt, and they work by asking for the one thing that still has value: your seed phrase, or a fee paid up front. Treat an unsolicited offer to help as proof of fraud, because that is what it is.

The single exception is narrow and worth knowing: if you still have the phrase and have forgotten part of it — a word, or its position — the search can sometimes be brute-forced, because the checksum tells you when you've hit it. That is a computation you run yourself, offline. It is not a thing you hire anyone for.

docs.title: "Lost" is not something the chain records
docs.text:
A point with consequences beyond the individual: the network has no category for lost funds.

An address holding ether with no known key is indistinguishable from one whose owner is simply not spending. Both are a balance that isn't moving. Nothing marks the difference, and nothing ever will, since marking it would require knowing a key is gone — see above.

So figures for "lost ether" are estimates built on heuristics — how long since the address last moved, whether it ever behaved like a wallet, whether the key was plausibly generated at all. They are inferences about absent information, not measurements, and they should be read with the uncertainty that implies.

This matters for anyone reasoning about supply. Ether destroyed by fee burning is verifiably gone: the protocol subtracts it, every node computes the same total, and the number is exact. Ether behind a lost key is still in the supply, fully counted, and merely immobile. The two are often discussed as though both reduced supply. Only one does so in a way anybody can check.

docs.title: Contracts can soften it — but look at what they move
docs.text:
A contract can hold funds and define its own rules for releasing them: three of five nominated keys, a backup key that works after a delay, a spending limit above which a second approval is needed. This is what social recovery means, and what account abstraction exists to make practical — ERC-4337 (Buterin et al., 2021) adds it as a layer, EIP-7702 (Buterin et al., 2024) lets an ordinary account take on code directly.

These genuinely help, and they're the right answer for most people holding meaningful amounts. But be clear about what changed:

The protocol's rule is untouched. The ether now sits at a contract's address, and the contract's code decides what moves it. Code can say anything; a single key cannot. That's the whole trick — the authority moved from one secret to a program.

The keys didn't go away, they multiplied. Your guardians are keys. You've converted losing one secret is fatal into losing several is fatal, which is a real improvement and not the same as elimination.

And you've accepted new ways to fail. Your guardians can collude or vanish. The contract can have a bug, and a bug in the thing holding your funds is as final as a lost key. You are trading a simple, well-understood failure for a diffuse, less predictable one — usually worth it, but a trade.

docs.title: The symmetry, stated plainly
docs.text:
It's tempting to call irrecoverability a feature. It isn't, quite. It's the cost of the property that makes the system worth using, and the two cannot be separated:

No party can take your ether because no party can move your ether. Remove the second and you have removed the first.

Every system offering recovery does it the same way: somebody else holds the keys, or holds power over the ledger. That is not a criticism — it's a description, and often the better choice. A custodial exchange sells you recovery, and the price is that it can freeze your account, be compelled to hand it over, or fail with your funds inside. Which is the older arrangement, not a new one: an intermediary absorbing settlement risk in exchange for discretion over the ledger is what the payments system already was (Böhme et al., 2015). Bitcoin's original paper made the irreversibility explicit as the thing being bought, not a side effect of the design (Nakamoto, 2008).

So the real decision isn't whether to accept irrecoverability. It's which risk you'd rather carry — your own mistakes, or a third party's conduct. Self-custody is a bet on your own operational discipline. Custody is a bet on an institution. Both are bets, and pretending either is the safe option is how people get hurt.

Couldn't a hard fork just restore it? It's been done.

It has, and this is the honest answer: the limit isn't technical.

A hard fork is everyone agreeing to run software with different rules. If enough of the network agreed to a change that credited your address, it would happen — nothing prevents it but willingness.

In 2016 something close to this occurred. A contract called The DAO was drained of a very large sum through a flaw in its code, and the network forked to move those funds to a contract from which investors could withdraw. Part of the community refused, kept running the original rules, and that chain continues today as Ethereum Classic.

Which is the point. It required a hotly contested, chain-splitting coordination of thousands of independent parties — over an amount representing a substantial fraction of all ether at the time, under genuine doubt about whether the project would survive otherwise. It has not been repeated, and the episode is widely cited as the reason it shouldn't be.

So nobody is going to fork the network for your wallet. But it's worth understanding why not: the obstacle is the cost of coordinating people, and the belief that doing it casually would destroy the property that gives the network value. Not a rule in the code. Social, not technical — and on the evidence, considerably harder to move.

docs.title: What to actually do
docs.text:
Three things, and no lecture attached. Worth saying first that these failures are well documented and mostly not carelessness — the research on key management finds people losing funds to tools that gave them no way to tell a correct backup from a broken one (Eskandari et al., 2015).

  1. Back up the phrase, not the keys. It's one item, it covers every account, and it survives losing the device.
  2. Test the restore before you fund it. Load the phrase into a different wallet and confirm the same first address appears. An untested backup is the standard way people discover a transcription error — afterwards.
  3. Treat the passphrase as a fourth thing to back up, if you use one, and store it apart from the phrase. Separately is the whole purpose; forgotten is indistinguishable from never-existed.

And one thing not to do: don't keep the only copy somewhere a single accident reaches both it and your device.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The protocol's sole test of authority is a valid signature. Lose the key and nothing can authorise a change to that address, ever.
  • The ether isn't destroyed and doesn't go anywhere. It stays recorded, visible and immobile. No expiry, no escheat.
  • There is nobody to ask, because nobody issued the address and nobody holds a record of who has it.
  • Recovery would require accepting a move without a signature — and since you cannot prove a key is lost, any mechanism able to recognise real loss can equally manufacture it.
  • Losing the phrase is worse than losing a key: a phrase regenerates every key, and no key reveals the phrase.
  • The chain has no category for lost funds, so "lost ether" figures are heuristic estimates. Burned ether, by contrast, is verifiably gone.
  • Contracts can soften this — social recovery, account abstraction — by moving authority from one key to code. The keys multiply rather than disappear, and new failure modes arrive with them.
  • No party can take your ether because no party can move it. Recovery and confiscation are the same power.

Next: What a node is — the machines this site keeps mentioning, finally defined.

docs.title: Wallets and seed phrases
docs.text:
Permanent in practice. None of this is part of Ethereum — these are conventions built on top of it. Nothing binds anyone to them, so they aren't permanent the way a protocol rule is. They have also gone unchanged since they were written, and every wallet now depends on them.

The cryptography section ended with a loose thread. A private key is one number and gives exactly one address — yet every wallet you've used shows a list of addresses, and offers to restore all of them from twelve words.

This page is how those two facts fit together.

Wallet

Software that stores private keys and signs things with them. Not a container for money, and not an account — your ether is recorded on the network, not inside any app.

A wallet's whole job is to keep your keys safe and use them when you ask. Keyring would have been the better word.

docs.title: A wallet doesn't hold your money
docs.text:
Worth unpacking that, because the usual word is actively misleading.

Your ether isn't in your wallet. It's a number recorded against your address by every computer on the network — and your wallet is not one of them. Delete the app and the number is untouched. Install a different app and it still doesn't move.

What a wallet holds is keys, and what it does is sign things with them. A better name would be a keyring.

Which explains something that otherwise seems odd: you can load the same seed phrase into three different wallets at once and see the same balances in all three. Nothing was copied between them. All three can derive the same keys, so all three can produce the same signatures — and all three are reading the same public records.

docs.title: What the phrase actually is
docs.text:
Before the tree: a seed phrase is a number, written as words. Twelve of them usually, sometimes twenty-four.

That's worth stressing, because the words look like something a person chose, and they aren't. Making a phrase goes like this:

  1. Generate random bits — 128 of them for a twelve-word phrase.
  2. Append a short checksum calculated from those bits.
  3. Chop the result into groups of 11 bits.
  4. Read each group as a number from 0 to 2047, and use it to pick a word from a fixed list of exactly 2048 words.

128 random bits — here, all zeros+44 checksum bits, worked out from those 128132 bits, chopped into 12 groups of 1100000000000abandon00000000000abandon00000000000abandon00000000000abandon00000000000abandon00000000000abandon00000000000abandon00000000000abandon00000000000abandon00000000000abandon00000000000abandon00000000011aboutEach group is a number from 0 to 2047, and it picks that word from the list.Eleven zero bits give word 0, which is abandon.The checksum lands inside the last group, making it 3 rather than 0 —which is why the phrase ends about, and not a twelfth abandon.

So abandon doesn't mean anything. It's word number 0 in the list, and it's there because eleven of your random bits happened to come out as zeros.

Nothing is remembered, chosen or looked up. The phrase is the number, in a form a human can copy onto paper without making mistakes.

docs.title: One phrase, many keys
docs.text:
Here's the structure, and the direction is what matters:

                     seed phrase
                          │
                          │  one-way
                          ▼
                     512-bit seed
                          │
          ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
          ▼               ▼               ▼
      key #0          key #1          key #2        … unlimited
          │               │               │
          ▼               ▼               ▼
      address 0       address 1       address 2

The words are stretched into a single large number — the seed — and that seed can produce an endless supply of private keys. Each key then yields one address, exactly as the cryptography section described.

So "many addresses from one thing" is true of a seed and false of a private key.

The procedure that turns one seed into many keys

Worth seeing, because "a repeatable procedure" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

Every point in the tree holds two things: a private key, and a separate 32-byte value called a chain code. The seed gives you the first of each.

To produce child number i from any point in the tree:

1.  combine  the chain code, the parent's key material, and i
2.  hash it  with HMAC-SHA512, giving 64 bytes
3.  the first 32 bytes, added to the parent key, = the child's key
4.  the last  32 bytes                          = the child's chain code

Three properties follow, and they're the useful part:

  • Deterministic. The same seed and the same i always give the same key, on any machine, forever. That's what makes a written phrase a complete backup.
  • One-way. A child key reveals nothing about its parent, so exposing one account doesn't expose the others.
  • Unlimited. i can be any of about four billion values at every level, and the levels nest. You will not run out.

This is BIP-32 (Wuille, 2012), and the tool below runs it.

the seed, 64 bytesm/44'/60'/0'/0/0one address/1one address/2one address/3one address…and on,without limitSame seed, same path, same addresses — in the same order, on any wallet.

Because that procedure is deterministic, the same phrase always produces the same keys, in the same order, on any wallet that walks the same route through the tree. That is what makes a written-down phrase a backup rather than merely a hint.

Try it: a phrase, and the addresses it produces

Seed phrase Passphrase (optional)

This is the real derivation, run in your browser — the same procedure your wallet performs.

Step 1 — look at the five addresses. One phrase, five unrelated addresses, and it would go on indefinitely. This is what your wallet is doing when it shows you a list.

Each address is shown with the private key it was derived from, in full. Those are real keys, and the only reason it is safe to print them here is that the phrase above is public. Compare any two: nothing in one hints at the other, and nothing in either hints at the phrase they both came from.

Step 2 — change one word. Every address changes completely. There's a hash at the heart of this, so the avalanche property applies here too.

Step 3 — type something in the passphrase field. Every address changes again, and you now have a different wallet from the same twelve words. More on that below.

Step 4 — type something that isn't a phrase at all. banana banana banana, or your own name. It derives addresses from that too, perfectly happily.

That is not a shortcoming of the tool; it is what the derivation does. Turning a phrase into a seed is one fixed calculation over the characters you typed, and it has no opinion about whether those characters were words. The wordlist and the checksum are checks a wallet runs before this point — which is why your wallet rejects a mistyped phrase and this tool accepts it. Worth noticing, because it's the same division as the 60 in the path: real rules, enforced entirely by software, nowhere in the protocol.

The phrase shown is the standard test vector from the specification. It is famous, publicly known, and holds nothing — a good thing to experiment with, and the worst conceivable thing to use.

docs.title: Why words
docs.text:
A seed could perfectly well be written as hex. The reason it isn't:

  • You can copy words by hand without error. Sixty-four hex characters transcribed onto paper is a mistake waiting to happen; abandon is not.
  • You can read them aloud, and spell them if needed.
  • Most typos become detectable, because the words come from a fixed list of 2048. Write abandonn and it simply isn't in the list, so a wallet can refuse it before deriving anything.
  • And part of the phrase is a checksum, so a phrase with one word swapped for another valid word usually still fails.

docs.title: Where the numbers come from
docs.text:
The list holds exactly 2048 words, and 2048 is 211. That number was chosen for precisely that reason: picking one word out of 211 carries exactly 11 bits, with nothing left over.

That makes the arithmetic tidy:

Words Bits total Of which random Of which checksum 12 132 128 4 18 198 192 6 24 264 256 8

Which is where the twelve and the twenty-four come from. They aren't arbitrary, and they aren't the only lengths the standard allows — they're the two that land on round numbers of random bits. Twelve words is exactly 128 bits of randomness; twenty-four is exactly 256. Those were the two security levels anyone wanted, so those are the two counts you meet in practice.

12 words is not half as strong as 24

It's 2128 against 2256 — and 2128 is already far beyond reach, by the same argument as on the private keys page. Both are unguessable. The difference matters only against attacks that don't exist yet.

docs.title: The path, and why two wallets can disagree
docs.text:
The seed can produce unlimited keys, so something has to say which ones. That's the derivation path — the route taken down the tree. Wallets handling Ethereum keys have settled on this one:

m / 44' / 60' / 0' / 0 / 0

Read left to right, each segment picks a branch:

Segment What it selects m the seed itself — the root of the tree 44' a standard structured layout, rather than an ad-hoc one 60' Ethereum. 60 is the number registered for it in the wallet standard 0' which account, if the wallet offers more than one 0 ordinary receiving addresses 0 the address index — 0, 1, 2, … the list your wallet shows you

Note what that 60 is and isn't. It's an entry in a registry wallet software keeps, so that two wallets don't derive different keys for the same chain. Ethereum doesn't publish it, doesn't read it, and doesn't know it exists. The path is a convention among wallets about where to look — not something the protocol specifies.

Walk a different path and you get entirely different keys from the same seed. Which is exactly why the same phrase can show different addresses in two different wallets — not a bug, and not a lost wallet. The phrase was fine; the wallet was looking somewhere else in the tree.

The standards underneath, and what each one does

Three separate specifications stack up here, all of them originally Bitcoin's:

Does what BIP-39 (Palatinus et al., 2013) words ⇄ seed. Defines the 2048-word list, the checksum, and the function that stretches a phrase into a 512-bit seed BIP-32 (Wuille, 2012) seed → a tree of keys. Defines how a parent key and an index produce a child key BIP-44 (Palatinus & Rusnak, 2014) which branches to use. Defines the m/44'/coin'/account'/change/index layout and the registered coin numbers

The apostrophes mark hardened derivation — a variant that uses the parent private key rather than the public one, so a leaked child key and chain code can't be walked back up the tree.

Stretching the phrase into a seed is deliberately slow: 2048 rounds of PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512. That's not for elegance, it's to make guessing phrases expensive, which matters because human-chosen phrases would otherwise be weak.

Then what is the optional passphrase?

A thirteenth secret, mixed in when the phrase is stretched into a seed. Change it and you get a completely different tree — different keys, different addresses, everything.

Which has an unusual consequence. Any passphrase is valid, so one phrase plus one passphrase is one wallet, one phrase plus a different passphrase is a different wallet, and there is no way to tell from the phrase alone which passphrase, if any, was meant. There's no "wrong passphrase" error, because there's nothing to check against — you simply land on an empty wallet.

That's deliberate: it means a phrase found in a drawer doesn't necessarily unlock anything. It also means a forgotten passphrase is indistinguishable from a lost phrase. Try it in the tool above.

docs.title: Ethereum knows about keys. It has no idea how you got them.
docs.text:
That sentence is the whole boundary, and it's worth being exact about, because the claim gets both over- and under-stated.

Keys are protocol. Three things on the previous pages are written into the specification and enforced by every node: that an address is derived from a public key in one particular way, that a public key comes from a private key on one particular curve, and that a signature from that key is the only thing which can authorise a change to that address. Those rules are Ethereum.

Where your key came from is not. Nothing on this page — not seed phrases, not the key tree, not derivation paths — appears anywhere in Ethereum. The protocol cares that you hold a key. It has no interest in how you came by it.

docs.title: What a node actually sees
docs.text:
When you send a transaction, a node receives the fields plus v, r and s. It recovers an address, checks that account's nonce and balance, and executes.

Nothing in that sequence mentions a seed, a phrase, a path or a wallet. The node cannot tell whether your key came from twelve words, a hardware device, or a number you made up — and it has no way to ask.

docs.title: The dice test
docs.text:
Here's the version that settles it.

Roll a die 256 times. Write the results down as bits. Treat that number as a private key, derive the public key, derive the address, and send ether to it.

Ethereum accepts that key exactly as readily as one from any wallet. There's no registration step, no scheme to declare, nothing to opt into. There is no field anywhere that says "this key was generated properly", because there would be nothing to put in it.

If the protocol cared where keys came from, that wouldn't work. It does work. So it doesn't care.

Don't actually do that

The dice test is sound as an argument and a poor idea in practice. Real dice are slightly biased, counting 256 results by hand goes wrong, and you'd have no checksum to catch the error — so you could lose everything to a miscount you never notice.

It demonstrates what the protocol will accept. It is not a method.

docs.title: Then what is a seed phrase for?
docs.text:
It solves a human problem, not a protocol one.

A 64-character hex key is miserable to write on paper and verify, and you would need a fresh one for every account you wanted. So BIP-39 turns one number into words you can transcribe by hand, and BIP-32 turns one secret into a whole tree of keys so you never need to back up more than once.

Both are conveniences. Neither makes anything possible that wasn't possible before — you could always have written down raw keys, one per account, and Ethereum would have been equally content.

docs.title: Three things this explains
docs.text:
Each of them looks like a defect until you see where the line falls.

Two wallets can show different addresses for the same phrase.

Each wallet picks a path down the tree, and nothing forces two wallets to pick the same one. If Ethereum defined paths, they would all have to agree, because disagreeing would mean breaking the rules. Ethereum doesn't define them, so a wallet is free to look somewhere else — and some older ones did. Your keys weren't lost. The second wallet was reading a different branch of the same tree, and the addresses it showed you were real, just unused.

A hardware wallet and a browser extension can share one phrase.

Not because Ethereum coordinates them — it has no idea either exists. Because both vendors independently chose to implement the same three published standards. That's co-operation between competitors, which can be relied on in practice and could in principle stop at any time.

Anyone could invent a different scheme tomorrow.

A new way of turning a backup into keys would need no permission, no proposal, and no change to Ethereum — because Ethereum only ever sees the finished keys. It would need other wallets to adopt it to be useful, but nothing about the protocol would resist it.

That last point is the test for whether something is protocol or convention: could you replace it unilaterally? Seed phrases, yes. The curve that turns a private key into an address, no.

docs.title: What it does not mean
docs.text:
Not that wallets are unimportant. They're the only reason any of this is usable, and a flaw in one costs you everything. The point is narrower: the protocol doesn't define them — so they vary, compete, and improve without anyone needing to change Ethereum.

History: the boundary is starting to move

The clean story above is becoming less clean, and it's worth knowing which direction it's going.

Account abstraction is, in part, about pulling wallet logic into contract code — so that "what authorises a transaction" can be a rule rather than a single key: several signers required, spending limits, a recovery procedure, fees paid by somebody else.

That is the protocol beginning to care about something it had left entirely to software. The layer this page describes doesn't go away — a contract still ultimately checks signatures made by keys — but "one key, one account" stops being the only arrangement available.

Everything in the cryptography section stays exactly as described. What changes is how much gets built on top of it.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A wallet holds keys, not money. Your ether is in the state; the wallet can only sign.
  • A seed can produce unlimited private keys; a private key still gives exactly one address.
  • Because the procedure is repeatable, the phrase is a complete backup.
  • The word list is 2048 = 211, chosen so each word carries exactly 11 bits. That's why 12 words comes to 128 bits of randomness and 24 comes to 256, plus a checksum in each case.
  • The derivation path decides which keys. Two wallets disagreeing about your addresses are walking different paths, not losing your money.
  • The optional passphrase makes a different wallet from the same words, with no way to detect a wrong one.
  • None of it is part of Ethereum. It's convention on top, and the protocol would not notice if it changed.

Next: What losing your keys means — the other side of holding the only secret.
